Furthermore, since the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) is the first to enter the state of a noble one, it is said that the mind takes itself as its object;

however, this refers to taking oneself as the object within the same moment of thought. If it were to take another person as its object or if there were an interval between moments of thought, even the Mahāyāna would grant that such is possible.

Furthermore, regarding the charge that [the reason] "because it can produce consciousness" is an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntika*): suppose a Sautrāntika master were to formulate a formal inference (*prayoga*) as follows:
"External forms (*rūpa*) are definitely the direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for at least one among the five sensory consciousnesses, because they can produce consciousness;

just as, for example, sound and so forth. In this case, one would then point out that [the reason] is inconclusive because it applies to other conditions such as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and so on, which also act as producers of consciousness.
The fallacy of the "undetermined" (anaikāntika) can be understood from the commentary.
As for the statement, "If one does not negate that [the object] exists externally to the mind and is transformed by being relied upon by other consciousnesses," the meaning is this:

here we are negating the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) position that external dharmas serve as the direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); if one were to negate the indirect [condition], that would contradict what the Mahāyāna itself admits regarding the eighth consciousness.
If one were to take another consciousness as the objective support (*ālambana*), it would immediately result in self-contradiction.

Now, the intent in taking this as an analogy is to adopt only a partial aspect; since the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) states that "even if there is no objective support, there is no cognition of a second moon," it is called a "partial" [property] because the thesis-property consists only of the portion where there is no cognition despite the absence of an objective support.
Regarding the claim that the five consciousnesses suffer from the fallacy of having no thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*):

if one takes the "conjunction" (*sāmagrī*) as the subject (*dharmin*) of the five consciousnesses and posits "that which is not a causal condition despite being an object of cognition" (*ālambanatve saty apratyayatvam*) as its property (*dharma*), then taking this as the thesis (*pratijñā*), there is no fallacy of having no thesis because a similar example (*sapakṣa*) exists.

However, if one takes "conjunction" itself as the subject and posits "being an object of cognition despite not being a causal condition" with respect to the five consciousnesses [as the property], [the fallacy remains].
To establish the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) upon the corroborative instance (sapakṣa) would be equivalent to having no property to be established there; why is this so?

Because the "second moon" is apprehended solely by the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), whereas since [the reason] is stated as being present in the five sensory consciousnesses (pañcavijñāna), there is nothing to be established upon the corroborative instance.

Furthermore, regarding the reduction of the text for the sake of meaning to the point where five characters must be removed: [The opponent] asks, "This [passage] is precisely refuting that the 'conjoined color' (*saṃghāta-rūpa*) of the Sautrāntika school is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the five consciousnesses.
Now, by removing these five characters, it becomes difficult to maintain that conjoined color is not the object-condition of the sixth consciousness.

Since this exceeds your own fundamental tenet, how can it constitute a valid refutation? [The respondent] answers: "The original intent was precisely to refute that a 'conjoined provisional color' (*saṃghāta-prajñapti-rūpa*) can function as an object-condition. Even if [the text were otherwise],..."

The meaning that [the five] are not objects for the consciousness of mental cognition is also established; furthermore, since this is currently a commentary on the treatise composed with skillful wisdom, we provisionally set aside the five [objections] as being non-contradictory to reason.

That which lacks a substantial basis (*bhāva*) and is not the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) refers to the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), which must rely upon a substantial basis when perceiving objects;

because they apprehend objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they obtain the self-nature of phenomena. Since empty flowers lack a substantial basis, they are not objects perceived by the five [consciousnesses].

Regarding the statement "only the five consciousnesses take what is real as their object," there are two interpretations below it. Since taking what is real as the object of the five consciousnesses is the established correct meaning, we shall now rely on this explanation, in which case there is no uncertainty.

However, among the sense bases (*āyatana*), those that reach the stage of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are designated as "rough" when the earth element is predominant and "smooth" when the water element is predominant;
because the body faculty perceives them only as the four great elements, they are different from [the perception of] length and so forth.

If it is said that when the five consciousnesses reach this [object], they are "within consciousness," even if one grants that the five consciousnesses take long [forms] and so forth as their objects, because the direct objective condition (*sākṣādālambanapratyaya*) does not depart from the mind, they are said to be "within consciousness.
This differs from other schools which maintain that the five consciousnesses directly grasp external, composite, conventional form (*saṃvṛtirūpa*).
This can be understood by citing examples such as the case of taking the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as an object.

Although form (*rūpa*) and other [objects] exist, those that constitute the objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) are as follows: among the five objects apprehended by the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), each individual object possesses many characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

These include the characteristic of form, the characteristic of atoms (*paramāṇu*), the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha*), the characteristic of impermanence (*anitya*), and characteristics such as long and short, or defiled and pure.
Among these, the characteristic of form and the characteristic of atoms may be the objects of the five consciousnesses in the present; the others are not, and for this reason it is so stated.
One part:

regarding the "aggregation like solidity" and so forth, "solidity" refers to earth. The intended meaning is that although earth, water, and so forth are indeed subtle particles (*paramāṇu*) in their characteristics, they can serve as conditions to produce visual consciousness and other cognitions;
however, because the characteristic of solidity does not exist within the visual consciousness itself, [it is considered thus].

Question: Now, these [qualities] such as solidity (*khara*) are precisely the objects of the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) that apprehends the composite aggregate, and thus they are exactly what is being refuted within the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Why, then, are they used as an analogy? Answer: In this context, earth, water, and so forth are apprehended solely by the body-consciousness.

If one refutes the object of the body-consciousness, it falls within the scope of the thesis. For now, we shall refute the objects of the other four consciousnesses; regarding solidity and the rest, there exists both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).

Therefore, for the time being, let us take this as a common analogy. Question: If one refutes the object of touch by means of the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), what shall be used as the analogy?

Answer: One uses the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) itself as the analogy. However, in the treatise on the objects of cognition (*ālambana-śāstra*), it is not possible to cite all the faculties as analogies;

rather, it speaks only of "solidity" (*khara*) and so forth. Since "solidity" and the rest are the very nature of the various faculties, the general analogy is cited here; thus it says that "solidity" and so forth belong to them.
The meaning of the treatise is as follows: regarding the mutual correspondence of the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the four consciousnesses, "activity" refers to the mode of activity;
the intent is that a consciousness whose mode of activity is coarse cannot take an object with a subtle mode of activity as its cognitive object.
Regarding the question that the eye’s perception of the mind up to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) is likewise so, the intent of the objection is as follows:

If the perceived image-part (*nimittabhāga*) does not further transform its own image, then it would be identical to the Saṃmitīya school’s view of directly apprehending the external object; furthermore, it would be like the Sarvāstivāda school’s view of perceiving the combined color-form (*saṃghātarūpa*) without transforming the image of the ultimate atoms—that is, perceiving the ultimate atoms themselves.
Regarding the phrase "suddenly manifesting as a single mark" (*ekalakṣaṇādi*), the commentary cites the third [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. That treatise states:

"Furthermore, within an aggregate of matter (*rūpa-saṃghāta*), there has never been the production of an atom (*paramāṇu*). When it arises from its own seeds, it arises only as a collection—whether subtle, medium, or large—and it is only through conceptual designation (*prajñapti*) that these are established as atoms.
Thus, one should know that [matter] transforms suddenly according to whether it is subtle, medium, or large.
This is not like the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which achieves results through the accumulation of small [factors].

Regarding the statement that "the former are like anger (*krodha*) and so forth, while the latter are like regret (*kaukṛtya*) and so forth": anger is simply another name for an increase in hatred (*dveṣa*) and delusion (*moha*);
regret, however, is not a distinct entity from delusion, as it possesses its own separate substantial nature (*svabhāva*).

Question: Length and so forth do not exist in dependence upon shortness and the like; yet, since blue and the like do exist in dependence upon one another, how can there be a distinction between the conventional (false) and the real?
Answer: When length and the like are in dependence, there is no time when shortness is absent, and thus length necessarily exists.

However, when blue is contrasted with other colors, there is no time when yellow is absent, and yet blue still exists. Question: Since blue does not arise from yellow, how can you say it is dependent? Answer: This... [text ends]

However, names and designations depend upon one another, whereas their essential natures do not; this differs from cases such as "long" and so forth, where both name and nature depend upon one another—thus there is a distinction between the two.

Nevertheless, because they are dependent [on causes and conditions], they may be said to be real; yet when analyzed through conceptual construction, they transform into subtle characteristics, and thus they are "dependent."
In the fifty-fourth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is stated that for five reasons the Buddha spoke of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

According to the intended meaning of that treatise: first, by way of conceptual analysis; through the analytical wisdom of discernment, one analyzes all forms (*rūpa*) until reaching their ultimate limit, thereby establishing the atom.
Second, by way of differentiation; these consist of fifteen kinds, namely the five atoms of each of the sense faculties and their five corresponding objects. Fourth... [text fragment].
The great [elements] constitute four bases of dharmas (*dharmāyatana*), while actual matter constitutes one; all of these are derived by analyzing gross matter down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).
This is due to three reasons: first, because they are established as independent entities, meaning that the substantial ultimate atom establishes its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);

second, because of their association, meaning that within the location of a single ultimate atom of earth or another element, there are other ultimate atoms gathered together in one place without being separated.

Regarding the statement that "the name 'companion' [is used] because of the fivefold absence of conceptual differentiation": this means that those atoms have no further parts and are not of a composite nature.
This refers to the yogi reaching a state consistent with reason; the term "consistency with the Dharma" is a general explanation of yoga.

The term "yoga" (*yoga*) is a general designation for a practitioner who is in accord with the Dharma. Now, to analyze gross matter down to its ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) is precisely the third principle of being in accord with reality.
Some interpret this as "being in accord with the object of yoga," but that is incorrect;
if it were merely being in accord with the object, it would not contradict the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena. Here, one portion is analyzed.
If one treats [matter] as an ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), does this not contradict the intrinsic nature (*dharmasvabhāva*) of phenomena?

What is meant here by "corresponding to principle" refers to the conventional establishment of truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through the analytical disintegration of atoms. Therefore, it should be understood that one merely adopts a mind that analyzes and deconstructs in accordance with principle;
such a mind does not contradict the principle of conventional truth.
Because the substance of an atom arrives [at its location] and yet possesses spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*), there is no further differentiation;
thus, the substance itself is differentiated, and since it still has the four cardinal directions as well as above and below, it is said to "possess spatial dimensions.
Regarding the question that these are not objects of the internal divine eye (*divyacakṣus*): if the divine eye has no obstruction to external forms, why is the atom not its object?

Answer: Although one may see what lies beyond an obstruction, the remaining three [types of matter] can be analyzed into atoms (*paramāṇu*), whereas this [manifest form] cannot; therefore, it is an object of the dharma-sphere (*dharmāyatana*).
Previously, the analysis of manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) up to its refutation of non-manifest form (*avijñapti*) was completed;

now, since the refutation of the resistant (*sapratigha*) matter within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) has already been concluded, this passage further refutes manifest form specifically so that it is shown to be non-existent. Hence, it says "furthermore."
This would contradict the [doctrine of] non-manifest form (*avijñapti*).
Alternatively, it would imply that atoms possess distinct elongated shapes; this further refutes the notion that distinct elongated shapes exist upon spherical atoms.
Regarding the Saṃmitīya school’s position as presented in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the *Karma-siddhi-śāstra* states:
"Some say that bodily intimation has motion as its nature. What is meant by "motion"? It refers to the transition to another location. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* further states:
"Other schools maintain that movement is called bodily intimation; for when the body moves, it is moved by karma. The above passage summarizes the position of the Saṃmitīyas.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* itself refutes this, stating: "If something arises in this very place and ceases in this very place, it cannot possibly move from here to another location;
therefore, one cannot say that motion constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)."

Regarding the statement that among existing phenomena one must speak of the "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*): if one does not speak of the conditioned, others would likewise admit that cessation is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) because it does not depend on a cause;
thus, one would incur the fault of contradicting what is mutually accepted.

As for the claim that there is no fallacy of "indefiniteness" (*anaikāntika*) regarding abiding (*sthiti*) and so forth because they depend on causes, this passage is difficult to understand; for although abiding and so forth are not... [the text continues].
Since this cessation does not arise again, the reason (*hetu*) operates within the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) of the thesis; why then would it not be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)?
Now, by interpreting the meaning according to this text, both of the aforementioned two types of inference are simultaneously shown to be free from inconclusiveness.

The former inference based on the treatise stated: "Cessation should not be cessation, because it abides; if it were to depend on causes, it would be exactly like the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). Therefore, this [text] says: "However..."
It is not the case that because "cessation" (nirodha) is a negation of the preceding inference, one may claim that "abiding" (sthiti) is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, because it is not universally established (*asiddha*), it cannot serve as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*). This is because within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the inference regarding cessation is also not inconclusive;
since the Mahāyāna does not admit that "abiding" is a dependent cause, and since a non-cause cannot serve as a similar instance, one cannot take "abiding" and so forth as such.

[Question: It is not fixed. According to the ten causes discussed below, such as the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*), it is stated that they all function within the context of arising, abiding, accomplishing, and obtaining results.
Since this is so, how can you say that the "abiding" in the Mahāyāna is not universally established (*aprasiddha*)?

[Answer: For example, the great earth and other things abide upon the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). However, the wind and so forth serve only as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and are not the direct causes (*hetu*). Thus, [the abiding of the Mahāyāna] is likewise.

The fact that arising and ceasing are not identical is accepted by others as being dependent upon causes and further conditions; since the ten causes and so forth are not all direct [causes], there is no contradiction.
Regarding the refutation of the *Raviprabhā-śāstra*, the *Xiyuji* states: "The master of śāstras, Dharmapāla (Tongshou), was a native of the country of Takṣaśilā."
He would daily recite thirty-two thousand words and simultaneously write thirty-two thousand characters. The treatises he composed numbered several dozen;

these are included at the end of the section on the Sūtras. At that time, there were Ārya Aśvaghoṣa in the East, Ārya Deva in the South, Nāgārjuna in the West, and Ārya Kumāralāta in the North, who were known as the "Four Suns Illuminating the World. According to this, the name of Kumāralāta is stated in full.

Regarding the commentaries on the dozens of treatises he composed, four masters have written sub-commentaries; some say he authored the *Navāśata-śāstra* (Treatise of Nine Hundred Verses), while others speak of five great masters—though it remains uncertain what these accounts are based upon.

First, it is because those who follow the teachings of the Hīnayāna schools, such as the Sarvāstivāda, maintain that the substance of form and sound encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Second, it is to distinguish the inner mind from external objects such as fragrance and other sensory qualities that support the faculties;

for while one (fragrance) cannot represent the inner mind, the other (sound) does not arise in accordance with the mind’s wholesome or unwholesome states. Thus, these are excluded, as is also discussed in the treatises.
"That which acts as the cause" and so forth refers to the sixth consciousness; "that which causes the transformation of consciousness" refers to the eighth consciousness;
"the manifesting mind" also refers to the sixth.
This [sixth consciousness] is that which can manifest and comprehend the meaning intended to be expressed; as previously stated, while it manifests the mind, it can also manifest that body.

The phrase "performing an action" (*kṛtya*) expresses the intended meaning; it also indicates that [the action] is manifested in the mind, such that they mutually reveal one another. Regarding the formal argument (*pramāṇa*):

if it is said that "in speech, for instance, there is the Buddha’s single-moment speech," this refers in the Mahāyāna to the Buddha’s single moment as a conventional manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), whereas in the Sarvāstivāda it is considered real.
Therefore, we now raise an objection: if that were so, others should challenge you by saying, "In your Mahāyāna, the Buddha..."

Question: If it is said that vocal sound in a single moment possesses an artificial informative act (*vijñapti-karman*), then except for the Buddhas, the vocal sounds of a single moment should also possess an artificial informative act;

since that is not the case for them, how can this be so? Answer: It is not so. The Buddhas have attained mastery (*vaśitā*) and can accomplish an informative act in a single moment; other persons lack such mastery, and thus their single moment is not an artificial informative act. Objection: If that were so, others would be the same as the Buddhas, for the Buddhas have attained mastery in a single moment. [The answer continues: [It is not so. The Buddhas have attained mastery and can accomplish an informative act in a single moment.

Other persons lack such mastery; therefore, their single moment is not an artificial informative act. If that were so, others would likewise be the same as the Buddhas, for the Buddhas have attained mastery in a single moment.
In reality, other people lack mastery over manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) beyond a single moment; this [single moment] is not real manifest karma. This principle applies universally.
How could you possibly refute me based on this? Therefore, one should say: "Because I do not accept real manifest karma, I am merely refuting you; you cannot reverse this analogy.

According to the method of *hetuvidyā* (logic), the purpose of a negation is to establish a thesis. Since it is admitted that things exist, the Mahāyāna position—that the combination of consciousnesses is conventional (*prajñaptika*) and distinct from [independent] consciousness—is established.

The term "transformation" (*vikāra*) is used to distinguish [the Sautrāntika view] from that of the Sautrāntikas; since the Sarvāstivādins hold that sound exists as a real entity external to consciousness, the phrase "resembling sound" (*śabdābhāsa*) is used to exclude them.

Question: Since the previous section clarifying bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) required a general exclusion of the views of all masters, and since vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) belongs only to the Vaibhāṣika school, upon what basis is it here further distinguished by excluding other systems?
Answer: It must be excluded whenever there is a difference from the Mahāyāna tenets; why would one not discuss it?
Regarding existence and non-existence:

those who maintain that the body possesses courage and bodily diligence (*kāya-vīrya*) assert that there exists within the internal body a distinct, real unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) which causes the body to possess exertion, courage, and initiative;
therefore, this unmanifest form is named "bodily courage" and so forth. Question: For what reason [is it not] mental?

Regarding the question of whether vigor and so forth are not subsumed under non-informative form (*avijñapti*): among the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), diligence (*vīrya*) and application (*pradhāna*) have already been established as such.
Furthermore, because those [factors] cannot apply vigor toward matter (*rūpa*), they are not established as non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Regarding the phrase "meritorious deeds manifested as having no visible basis" (*anāśraya-pratyakṣa-puṇya-kriyā-vastu*):

for example, when a donor is at a distance such that they do not see the recipient nor the object being given, it is called "manifested as having no visible basis. At the time the object is actually consumed, [the merit] increases because the conditions are complete.
The statement "when the donor is at a distance," etc., explains the meaning of meritorious deeds manifested as having no visible basis.

When the *ācārya* performs the formal announcement (*jñapti*) up to the point where it says "or because of being without mind," one must first ask [the candidate] before they can receive the precepts.

How, then, does one immediately attain the concentration of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)? Answer: As in the case of the *śrāmaṇera* Nāgasena, who had previously attained the meditative absorption of cessation;

at the time of the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), by the power of his prior practice, his single moment of thought entered the concentration of cessation. Even though the conditions for the mental object were present, he also produced non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).

Regarding the statement that if both the new and the old are employed up to the point of "increasing" (*vṛddhi*), this text cites both the essence (*svabhāva*) and the function (*kāritra*) as increasing;
it concludes below that the increase of function is superior.

Furthermore, in distinguishing between the distant and the near, as well as the momentary: "distant" refers to deliberation (*santīraṇa*) and "near" refers to determination (*niścaya*), starting from the third [moment].

After the seeds have been perfumed by volition (*cetanā*), there subsequently arises another volition called "momentary volition" (*kṣaṇa-cetanā*). It is so named because it manifests in a continuous stream once the seeds have been perfumed;
it does not mean that the moment is defined by the time when the function of the seeds increases. Furthermore, another interpretation states:

the initial mind possesses distant and near preparatory applications (*prayoga*), which are termed "distant" and "near"; the two types of volition—thoroughly determining (*niścaya*) and resolving—are termed "momentary," [and this applies] to the second...
Because the three types of reflection (*vitarka*) are extremely close to one another, the preceding one is taken as the primary basis.
Regarding the statement in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Xianyang lun*) that "it does not manifest as dharmas" and so forth: bodily and vocal unwholesome forms are termed "non-manifesting.

That [treatise] establishes the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*) based solely upon this. Now, this treatise states that "arousing body and speech" is established based on actual manifestation (*samudācāra*).

In the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explanation of the Principles), following the establishment of the nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*), there are two intended meanings in the passage from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*:

first, that [the text] explains the reason for definitely obtaining the designation "form"; second, that it speaks of the union of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*). Regarding the phrase "the reason for definitely obtaining the designation 'form'":

among the various types of restraints (*saṃvara*), there are none that do not cease misconduct of body and speech; therefore, they are designated as "definite" because they consist of wholesome bodily and vocal actions, even when at times they are not being actively manifested.
The name "definitive manifestation" (*niyata-prakāśana*) is used because it refers to what is determined; it speaks of relying on the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*) that does not manifest.

Regarding the statement that concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*) are explained together: since the precepts of concentration and the path do not initiate bodily or vocal actions but can only restrain evil, they are said to be merely dharmas that do not manifest.

Question: Do the two types of volition (*cetanā*)—those of concentration and those of the path—not also initiate wholesome bodily and vocal actions? Answer: [They do not,] because in the eight stages...
Because Bodhisattvas above this [level] are able to produce [karmic seeds] prior to the seventh stage, whereas those who cannot do so are not necessarily thus; furthermore,
regarding the fact that those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) certainly cannot produce them,
this statement concerning the non-production of karma in the meditative and path states (*samāhita-mārga*) is likewise not contradictory when applied to the Two Vehicles.

Regarding the establishment of the precepts of the path of concentration (*samādhi-mārga-śīla*) based on the volition (*cetanā*) that restrains the manifestation of evil in body and speech: when the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) arises, it must necessarily be accompanied by concentration.
Is this manifesting volition one or two? If there were such a question, what would be the fault?

If you say there is only one [volition] and the paths of concentration each have their own non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), how can one volition establish two non-informative matters? If there were two, how could they exist within a single consciousness (*vijñāna*)?

[Objection: Two volitions answer this [question], yet here there is only one volition; why are there two together? [Response: If that were so, how could the two non-informative (avijñapti) factors of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the path (*mārga*) exist?

[Objection: How can they both rely on a single present volition? [Response: Regarding meditative concentration and the path, if they did not occur simultaneously, one might say the substance of volition is not of a single type.

However, since the arising of the path necessarily relies upon meditative concentration, why posit two present volitions? It is because the powers of both meditative concentration and the path are capable of preventing wrongdoing, even though they are [distinct].
If one present volition were to establish both [the manifest and] the unmanifest, then in the case of impure meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*), this would necessarily follow;
yet it could only be the restraint of concentration (*samādhi-śīla*), because the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*) does not exist there.
Is it then the case that a single present volition is both manifest and unmanifest? This is a counter-interrogation. Below, there are three explanations; the first two are incorrect.

Regarding the first interpretation of the first principle following the "Correct" [section], it says: "That is not 'informative' (vijñapti), but is merely called 'non-informative' (avijñapti) because that present volition does not inform others.
Second, it says: "Although it issues forth from body and speech, it is neither informative nor non-informative;
this is because when discussing its essential nature as volition, it cannot manifest itself to others and thus is not informative, yet it can know itself and thus is not non-informative. First.

Third, regarding the difference in perspective concerning that which encompasses both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*): it is called "manifest" because it can incite the manifestation of body and speech and makes them known to others;
it is called "unmanifest" because it ceases the misconduct of body and speech and does not make itself known to others. Question: Why are the first two interpretations incorrect? Answer:
The intention here is to explain that right speech, action, and livelihood have the present volition (*cetanā*) as their essence. The first two interpretations both state that this is not the case.

Since the *vijñapti* (informative action) is what is designated as "right speech," the Commentary further states: "If it were not so, there would be no *avijñapti* (non-informative action) from the eighth stage upward"; therefore, the latter [explanation] is correct.
Regarding the "one branch" or "two branches" in the Mahāyāna, this refers to cases within the Mahāyāna where one receives only a single precept, such as the precept against killing, and so forth.

The arising of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) does not necessarily require the full reception of the five precepts; this is the view of the Sarvāstivāda, which is equal to that of the Sautrāntika.
However, [the latter] maintains that it must be fully received for non-informative action to arise.

Now, one should explain that the two types of non-informative action are those of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the mundane (*vyutthita*). As for what they are made of, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:

Question 66: Regarding the Blessed One’s statement that there exists non-obstructive form (*apratigha-rūpa*) associated with views of existence and non-existence, by which primary elements (*mahābhūta*) should it be said to be derived?
Answer: If, through concentrated thought, an image (*pratibimba*) of various forms belonging to the desire realm arises, it should be said to be derived from the primary elements of the desire realm;
if, through concentrated thought, an image of various forms belonging to the form realm arises, [it should be said to be derived from the primary elements of the form realm].

Regarding its arising, it should be said that it is produced from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm; this "unseen and non-obstructive form" refers precisely to the unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) of meditative concentration, the Path, and so forth.
Furthermore, the phrase "because it does not continue uninterruptedly" explains why the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates bodily and vocal actions is not termed "unmanifest."
Regarding the application of the analogy of "form" (*rūpa*) to characterize the nature of the provisional and the real, the analogy states:

if one allows that the names "body" and "speech" are categorized as form, then since body and speech are admitted to be real dharmas (*dravyadharma*), they should not be subsumed under the category of provisional dharmas. One should consider such analogies to understand them fully.

The phrase "dissociated" (*viprayukta*), which excludes non-material phenomena such as mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), intends to convey that "associated" (*samprayukta*) means "similarity.

Because they do not resemble matter (*rūpa*), mind, or obstructive mental factors, they are termed "dissociated. Question: If this were the case, then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and the like should also be termed dissociated.

Answer: The term "formations" (*saṃskāra*) serves as a qualifier. "Formation" carries the meaning of "transmigration" or "flux"; since unconditioned phenomena are eternally abiding, they are not formations associated with flux. Thus, they are not included here.
Regarding the charge that the unconditioned meditative attainment (*asamskṛta-samāpatti*) lacks definiteness:

it is argued that the unconditioned is precisely the true nature (*dharmatā*) of form and mind, which is apprehended by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Since this is just as form and mind are apprehended through direct perception, and is not otherwise, there is no lack of definiteness.

Regarding the question: "If it is established as a thesis that [the self] is not distinct from matter and mind, and since matter, mind, and mental factors are substantially real, they serve as a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*);
yet the reason—that 'activity is found to be non-distinct from matter and mind'—occurs within this dissimilar instance.
Therefore, this reason must be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). The answer is: It is said that since the essence of matter, mind, and so forth is not... [text fragment ends].

The argument that "because a distinct color-consciousness (*rūpa-citta*) is the positive reason (*sādhana-dharma*) and not a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), there is no fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*)," is necessarily untenable.
If the very essence of color, consciousness, and so forth constitutes the positive reason, then the treatise should simply state "not a means of valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*).

Why is it necessary to subsequently state that "the activity (*kāritra*) is perceived"? Since this is the case, there is the fallacy of the contradiction of the specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*) of the probans.

The *Pramāṇa* states that acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and so forth must necessarily exist as real entities (*dravyasat*), because they are not distinct from matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and mental factors (*caitta*).

Since there is no such fault in the case of matter, mind, and so forth, we know that the [opponent’s] intention is to take something other than matter, mind, and so forth—namely, a distinct function of acquisition and the like—as the cause.
This is what is meant by "establishing a different phenomenon (*dharmāntara*) as the cause," which will be refuted below. Now, for the sake of explanation, this is our thesis (*pakṣa*).

In the middle [of the argument], one should state that acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and so forth, do not possess a substantial reality distinct from matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). This accords with what the subsequent treatise says:

"Furthermore, how does one know that acquisition and non-acquisition have a substantial reality and function distinct from matter, mind, and so forth? Therefore, this thesis should be stated as: "[Acquisition and non-acquisition] are not distinct from matter and so forth.
Because matter and mind are not included in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), there is no fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Since this objection has already been addressed...

Since unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) possess functional activity that is not distinct from form and the other aggregates, they do not possess a substantial reality separate from form and so forth;
thus, the commentary itself has already excluded the possibility of them being entirely distinct, and this cannot be considered a fault.

In the stage of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī bhūmi*) within the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are four kinds of non-existence; at the sixteenth [moment] of this stage, there are five kinds of non-existence:
(1) non-arisen non-existence (*anutpannābhāva*), which refers to future conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); (2) ceased non-existence (*vinaṣṭābhāva*), which refers to past conditioned phenomena;
(3) mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), which refers to the nature of separation from the characteristics of other phenomena, or their lack of existence as such; or...
1) The non-conjunction of remaining phenomena with other phenomena;

2) the four ultimate non-existents, which refers to that which is established by means of conventional discourse and the imputed nature of verbal expression; 3) absolute non-existence, such as the son of a barren woman and so forth.
The statement in the *Ṭīkā* that there are "four" is an error; alternatively, there may be another textual passage [stating five], which one ought to consult.
Consideration:

In this context, the word "the rest" (*śeṣa*) indicates those things not subsumed under matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth. When it says "the rest" in the statement regarding causes, it refers to the "rest" of acquisition (*prāpti*) and so on—namely, matter and mind.
Since others accept acquisition and so forth as being real entities (*dravyasat*), it says "the rest [of] the real. Furthermore, when it says "the rest" in the analogy, it likewise [refers to these].

Regarding the phrase "the remainder of what is obtained" (*prāpti-avaśeṣa*), this refers to other things such as jars and basins; for in our own school (*svasiddhānta*), the substance of "obtaining" (*prāpti*) and so forth is considered provisional (*prajñaptisat*).

Thus, when it says "the remainder," it refers to provisional causes and does not mean that [the reason] is unestablished for either party (*anyatarāsiddha*) based on what is accepted. The intended meaning of the word "accepted" (*abhyupagata*) is that which is accepted by both schools as a real entity (*dravyasat*), namely matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
If one did not say "accepted" but simply said "because it is not subsumed under real entities," then there would be the fault of the reason being unestablished for the other party (*parāsiddha*).
Because it establishes that the entities such as "attainment" (*prāpti*) admitted by others are substantially real.
Regarding the statement in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* that it is "not included in the category of non-existence": "retrogression" (*parihāṇi*) means the sense of falling away.

If the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* were to define "otherness of beings" (*pṛthagjanatva*) [as non-attainment], then because it would not include retrogression and non-accomplishment (*aprāpti*), its definition would be said to be too narrow. If, however, it refers to "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*)...
The state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and retrogression (*parihāṇi*) are fully subsumed within these [two categories] and do not constitute exceptions.

Furthermore, the term "distinct" (*anya*) indicates the sense of being different, not the sense of being inseparable. In the systems of other schools, acquisitions (*prāpti*) and so forth are all distinct from form (*rūpa*) and the like, yet they are not separate from form and the like.

If one were now to challenge that [position], one could only say that acquisitions and so forth are not distinct from matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). It is not [the case that they are not distinct].

One may say that they are not separate; however, if one were to say that your attainment and so forth must likewise not be separate from form and mind, this would incur the fault of contradicting what is already established (*prasiddha*).
Therefore, the meaning of "not being separate" is not used to refute others.
Regarding the ten dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), some claim that "right liberation" (*samyag-vimukti*) refers to the category of resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*).

This is because it is a factor (*aṅga*) [of the path], and thus not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). However, such reasoning is incorrect. Since this passage clarifies the dharmas of one beyond training, how could one beyond training fail to attain *nirvāṇa*?
Furthermore, those two dharmas of one beyond training do not enter into the factors of the noble path; therefore, to call them "factors" is a hollow statement. Thus, the tenth [point] is established.
The one of right knowledge may take up the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), the wisdom of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and so forth.
Regarding the question of why those [opponents] do not establish "possession" (*prāpti*) for other bodies or insentient things:
the answer is that they consider that if one were to establish real possession with respect to other bodies, many difficulties would arise and there would be confusion.
The fault in this position is that if one were to acquire [the state of] a ghost or an animal while in the human realm, then a human would also become a being of the non-human realms;

thus, if acquisition were established with respect to inanimate objects (*asattva*), then both animate and inanimate things would be equally accomplished, and there would be no distinction between them.

Regarding the statement, "Dharmas already abandoned, such as those of a different realm or stage, should never arise again," etc.: The questioner asks: For dharmas not yet attained, there is the possibility of further attainment;

it is difficult to ensure they do not arise. This poses no difficulty. However, regarding dharmas already lost—such as the bodies of hell-beings and so forth, which absolutely do not arise once one has entered the Path of Seeing—it is now argued that these too must be rendered non-arising. If this were the case, it would entail a logical fallacy (*prasanga*).
As for how the fault in the *Fu* [treatise] is difficult to refute, the answer in that treatise is brief;
one should state that the thesis is that dharmas which have not yet been attained and those already lost—which are capable of arising again—will never arise again, and thus there is no contradiction.
Those who all admit the existence of co-nascent acquisition (*sahaja-prāpti*) maintain that, according to their own school, dharmas of the three time periods have three types of acquisition:
past dharmas have subsequent acquisition, present dharmas have simultaneous acquisition, and future dharmas have prior acquisition.
Since they hold that the two acquisitions of the past and future cannot serve as causes for arising, they here speak only of the case where co-nascent acquisition acts as the cause for arising.

As for the claim that "because it previously existed, it subsequently ceases to exist": if the former [state] is not separate from the phenomena associated with sentient beings (*sattva-dharma*), why discuss the establishment of "acquisition" (*prāpti*)?

Since all that can be established is not separate from sentient beings, and since you yourself admit that there is no acquisition once one is separated from sentient beings, and because no phenomenon can be acquired when separated from sentient beings, both [theories] are useless.

Regarding the statement "according to the second [section] below, it is explained as two," this refers to one master (Sthiramati) among the eight variations concerning the transformation of another's faculties below [in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*], who asserts that the faculties are transformed;
and another master (Dharmapāla), who asserts that only one's own faculties are transformed, because transforming another's would serve no purpose for oneself.
Thus, the statement "there is enjoyment" means that one achieves one's own body; this is the meaning of the first master.

To state it briefly, regarding the causes that constitute the conditions for arising (*utpatti-pratyaya*) and the factors of sustenance and intensification (*parigraha-vardhana-hetu*), there are two masters’ views.

One says that both are explained in relation to seeds (*bīja*) in contrast to manifest activities (*samudācāra*): namely, that these seeds are able to produce manifest activities and are thus called "conditions for arising";

the capacity they possess to sustain the production of those manifest activities is called "sustenance"; and because the seeds, having been moistened, possess functional power, they are called "causes of intensification."
The second explanation states: "The condition for arising" refers to the accomplishment of seeds, as they manifest as the conditions for the arising of active phenomena (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
"Appropriation" refers to the accomplishment of active phenomena, as they appropriate tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) fruits.

"The cause of intensification" refers to the accomplishment of mastery, because superior dharmas arise with seeds as their cause. These three types are all described as "attainment" (*prāpti*), according to the subsequent explanation.

Regarding the attainment [of the fruit], three types of accomplishment (*siddhi*) have been explained; however, while the former interpretation is superior when considered generally, one should consult the *Yogācārabhūmi* as the definitive authority.

As for the distinction between those who possess the substance (*dravya*) and those who achieve accomplishment merely through designation (*prajñapti*), the Abhidharma already distinguishes between those who are free from desire (*vītarāga*) and those who are not.
Regarding the statement that the essence of a seed exists when it possesses the capacity for production, both are termed "established seeds";

conversely, when the essence of the seed is absent and its capacity for production is impaired, both are termed "unestablished. The *Yogācārabhūmi* merely states that because [the seeds] have not yet been subdued, it clarifies only what is established (without clarifying what is unestablished).
Following the intent of the *Abhidharma* texts, even if the essence of the seed exists, it may be termed "unestablished" provided that the manifest activity has been subdued. Why is this so?
However, the term "subdued" (*vīta*) refers exclusively to the state where the seeds are definitely not severed.

If one says that "freedom from desire" (*vītarāga*) also encompasses the meaning of severing the seeds, then within the discussion of innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*), the *Abhidharma* text is likewise abbreviated;

it does not explicitly state that a portion of the spontaneous (*anābhoga*), natural, and functional (*airyāpathika-śailpasthānika*) neutral states serve as seeds for the accomplishment of innate wholesome states, but merely speaks of their accomplishment without mentioning their non-severance.
It is also omitted because it is already established.

Regarding the phrase "because it exists in another realm and is acquired at birth," this explains that the wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) are also not possessed (*aprāpta*), just as one born in the desire realm does not possess the wholesome states acquired at birth belonging to the higher realms; therefore, they are called "not possessed" according to the Abhidharma.

It is taught that one receives the designation "accomplished" solely based on the arising [of right view], without mentioning "non-accomplishment"; this is identical to what the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
that as long as one has not been subverted by wrong view, one is merely called "accomplished" and not "unaccomplished. Therefore, it is said to be the same as the *Yogācāra*.
Regarding this "attainment of seeds" as described in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, since that treatise states:

"The mastery over the power of the conditions for production is conventionally designated as 'attainment'; the conditions for production are themselves the seeds," it is known that this passage refers only to seeds as the attainment of seeds, and does not refer to manifest activity (*pravṛtti*).

Regarding the passage "having substance and having function" up to "the name being established or not established," this text is general in its application. Its intended meaning is that when there is both substance and function, the name is established;
when there is neither substance nor function, the name is not established; and when there is substance but no function, the substance is established while the function is not established.
The reason it is not stated that the manifestation [of afflictions] constitutes the possession of seeds is as follows:

the Abhidharma treatise states, "For those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, these various afflictions and secondary afflictions are called 'possessed' (*samanvāgata*). Fearing that this term "possession" might also include the manifestation itself as the possession of seeds, this [text] reconciles it with that treatise:
regarding defiled phenomena and innate wholesome phenomena, they are termed "possessed" in terms of both their essence (*tattva*) and their function (*kāritra*).
That which is not established and does not manifest is called the "accomplishment of seeds.

Regarding the statement that this is explained based on the abandonment of desire for the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): one teacher maintains that the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) fruit does not abandon the seeds of innate self-view, while another teacher maintains that they do abandon them;
since the latter is the correct position (*siddhānta*), it is adopted here.

If [wholesome roots] are suppressed by wrong view such that they are not established, it is as follows: if one is in the desire realm and suppressed by wrong view, the innate wholesome [roots] of that realm are not established;

even if not suppressed, those belonging to other higher realms and so forth—places where they do not arise—are also called "not established," because one certainly cannot give rise to the innate wholesome [roots] of other realms.
This is not the case for afflicted states or acquired wholesome states.
Regarding the mutual correlation between the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*) and the wholesome (*kuśala*):

although the *Yogācārabhūmi* text states that those [wholesome factors] which have not been damaged or suppressed are all termed "possessed" (*samanvāgata*), here we consider that even when they are damaged, they are termed "not possessed.

Although that text does not explicitly state their essential nature (*svabhāva*), it may also be explained by correlating it with the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-paryāya); therefore, it is said that they are mutually correlated as shadows.

Regarding the second point—that [cessation] belongs to both the mundane and the supramundane paths that can attain it: according to that school, even the six mundane practices (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) that suppress afflictions can attain analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
therefore, this analytical cessation belongs to the mundane path, while its supramundane counterpart is understood by analogy.

Just as one who has ultimately reached the point where [rebirth in] evil states does not arise—such as having entered the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga), whereby rebirth in the three miserable realms, the state of a eunuch, and so forth, never arises again—the Buddha-body likewise never gives rise to false principles.

This is a non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) that belongs solely to its basis. Question: Since these are all extinguished through the power of the Path, why do they not belong to the Path? Answer: The Noble Path fundamentally intends...

At the time of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), these [afflictions] do not arise spontaneously; because this is not the "correct abandonment by means of the path" (*mārga-samyak-prahāṇa*), it does not belong to the Path.
Furthermore, as it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it does not belong to that which is attained.
Third, regarding the seeds: as long as the seeds exist, even when the six practices (*ṣaḍ-ākāra*) suppress the afflictions, they may temporarily not arise.
Question: Why does the seed not belong to the seed itself, but rather to the Path? Answer: Because it possesses superior power, it belongs only to the Path;
since other conditions are lacking, phenomena have no Path to which they can belong, and thus they belong to the seed.
Regarding the statement that there are three types of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) just as there are for acquisition, the question is asked:

"As it was already clarified previously regarding what acquisition belongs to, since non-acquisition does not exist for a dharma that has not been acquired, it is unknown to which [dharma] this non-acquisition belongs. The answer is:

Just as ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) do not possess the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*), so too they lack mastery over them; furthermore, this constitutes a lack of actualization (*samudācāra*). Thus, non-acquisition belongs to both the state of non-possession and the state of non-manifestation.
Since the seeds are not established and the manifest state is not established, this non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) belongs to the seeds of the afflictions that act as obstacles.

By analogy, one should understand that when a noble one does not possess (*asamanvāgata*) afflictions, it refers to the non-acquisition of their seeds; thus, this non-acquisition belongs to the seeds of the noble path that functions as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Other instances of non-acquisition should be considered according to this same principle.
It is not only in relation to that which can be obstructed—namely, those who possess the potential for the noble—that something is designated as an "obstructor.

If one were to establish the absence of nature (*abhāva*) based solely on the obstructor, it would not apply to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), because they lack any noble path (*āryamārga*) that could be obstructed.

Regarding the phrase "because the two vehicles’ abandonment of one portion [of obstacles] up to their inclusion in the category of 'both'": this refers to those who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]. Although they have already attained the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) and are thus termed "noble" (*ārya*), they have not yet abandoned the afflictive cognitive obscurations (*parikalpita-jñeyāvaraṇa*) and are thus termed "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*).

Therefore, they are said to belong to the category of "both. Question: As stated previously in the treatise, since identity and difference cannot coexist when their substrata are the same, how can you now allow for the identity of ordinary beings and noble ones?

Answer: [This is permissible] because it concerns the identity of their underlying nature. Since both possess the same fundamental nature (*dharmatā*), there is no contradiction. Furthermore, although they are identical in terms of their ultimate nature, they differ in terms of their conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Thus, while they are identical in essence, they are distinct in their conventional status as ordinary or noble. This is why they are said to be "both."
Answering based on a single body: the previous [objection] regarding identity and difference is untenable because they are mutually contradictory;
however, since the seeds upon which the two natures—ordinary and noble—rely are distinct, there is no contradiction.

As for the claim that "there can be no non-arising of mind because it must have an object": if a real *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) did not exist, how could the mind arise [with respect to them], and how could one take the heavenly realm (*devagati*) or the human realm (*manuṣyagati*) as an object?

Only the masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Nyāyānusāra* establish the existence of *dharmasabhāgatā*; those masters rely solely upon internal phenomena such as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Regarding the establishment of dharmas, external forms and so forth are not established as being of the same category [as internal ones].
If it is argued that external forms of outflow (*niṣyanda-rūpa*) do indeed exist, one might object:
"If the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) that is the fruit of karma exists only internally, why is it not the case that the *sabhāgatā* of outflow extends to the external as well?"

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "also because *gati* is that which goes toward" (*gamyate*), the ancient Sarvāstivādins did not establish the category of *sabhāgatā*; therefore, they challenged [the opponent] by means of the term "going toward.

Since the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* do establish *sabhāgatā*, and since the previous arguments were based on karma, its fruit, and so forth, it is known that the present argument specifically challenges the masters of the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma*.

Furthermore, there is another objection that should be formulated based on the principle of "arising" (*jāti*). Suppose the opponent further defends [the position] by saying: "Internal phenomena possess all the aggregates (*skandha*) and share the same category of existence;

therefore, 'homogeneity' (*sabhāgatā*) is established as a universal. External phenomena consist only of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and lack many similar types; thus, they have no homogeneity. To this, one should further object:

"If internal phenomena, consisting of multiple aggregates, are admitted to possess arising and so forth, then external phenomena, consisting only of form, should likewise lack arising and so forth. If...

If it is argued that external phenomena such as arising exist because of the principle of dependent origination, then since they are of the same category as matter (*rūpa*), external phenomena must also possess "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*).

If you claim that they are called "matter" and so forth because they are composed [of atoms], this interpretation loses the intended meaning of your own tenet; this is merely your attempt at a defense.

Since you have already accepted the principle that "that which is capable [of producing] is called 'having the same name' and 'having the same category' (*sabhāga*)," you ought to offer this defense: "Because they produce [derived matter], the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are called 'form' (*rūpa*);
the four great elements do not themselves produce [other great elements]. Because they are not called 'form,' they are said to have the 'same name' and 'same category.

Since those with the same category cannot possess the same category, and those with the same category do not possess a 'same category,' you cannot offer such a defense. Therefore, it is known that the four great elements are not called 'form' simply because they produce [derived matter]."
Form has no creator; it is merely designated by similarity as "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*). There is homogeneity because there is a similarity of homogeneity.
Even if one were to attempt to overturn the Vaiśeṣika position, for the Vaiśeṣika, the term "homogeneity" belongs to the Vaiśeṣika master himself.
If you now take that very term "homogeneity" to be homogeneity itself, it is still difficult to understand, since you yourself admit the existence of homogeneity. Alternatively, [it may mean]...
Even if the Vaiśeṣika were to attempt to overturn my refutation with superior arguments to establish their own excellence of reasoning, it would still be difficult to discern,

for the reasons stated previously. Nevertheless, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, since the Sautrāntikas also employ a "refutation by identical phrasing" (*samāna-pada-pratiṣedha*) against the Vaiśeṣikas,
the former interpretation should be considered correct.

This differs from the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), where it is not so at present. If one says that the meaning of "cause" refers to the substantial entity itself, while the meaning of "similarity" is merely a conventional designation—since the former is real and the latter is provisional—it is said that this is not the case here.

The Sautrāntikas and others claim that the attainment (*samāpatti*) itself is not that destiny (*gati*). Since the Sautrāntikas maintain that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is merely conventional (*prajñapti*), the Sarvāstivādins refute this, saying:

"If you have no real life-faculty, by what is the body sustained? If you say it is sustained by consciousness (*vijñāna*), then at the time of entering the mindless states (*acittaka*), by what dharma would it be sustained?
If you say it is sustained by matter (*rūpa*) itself, then upon entering the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where there is no matter, it would be sustained by something of a different category."
When the mind is [of a different level] or when it is untainted (*anāsrava*), one is no longer a sentient being belonging to that destiny (*gati*) who shares its common characteristics (*sabhāga*).

This means that when a mind of a different level arises, or when an untainted mind arises, because it is not comprised within a [specific] realm (*dhātu*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is absent, and thus one is no longer of that destiny.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "because there is no basis for a provisional life," since both form and mind are absent, your provisional life-faculty would have no locus of dependence.
Because matter and mind are not identical, they are said to be "equal. For me, there is no such fault regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Sentient beings (*sattvasaṃkhyāta*) serve as the basis for inference (*anumāna*), as follows: those in the mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) must have consciousness not separated from the body, because they are included among sentient beings, just like other sentient beings;
this is as stated in the fourth chapter below.

If it is argued that [the body] is sustained because warmth and consciousness are uninterrupted, one asks: "The original difficulty concerned why the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) does not sustain [the body];

why then do you answer that previous difficulty by appealing to warmth and consciousness? [The opponent replies: "In the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), there is no life-faculty; therefore, to rescue [the argument], one must say that in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and other states, warmth and consciousness are interrupted and cannot sustain the body, so a real life-faculty is required."
Furthermore, regarding the Sautrāntika masters' claim that the eyes and so forth cannot serve as the "support" (ādhāra),

this refers to their defense against the objection that although there is no real life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) in states such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the eyes and so forth nonetheless sustain the seeds of the body.

Regarding the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) in terms of the arisen and unarisen wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas]: this means that with respect to wholesome dharmas already arisen, one speaks of "effort for protection" (*anurakṣaṇā-prahāṇa*), which is called "protection" because it prevents the wholesome from being lost;

it is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) because it ensures that unwholesome dharmas do not arise. With respect to wholesome dharmas not yet arisen, one speaks of "effort for cultivation" (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*), which is called "cultivation" because it causes wholesome dharmas to arise;
it is called "abandonment" because it ensures that no unwholesome [dharmas] exist. With respect to unwholesome [dharmas] already arisen...

Regarding the statement that "the Dharma explains restraint (saṃvara) as the cutting off [of evil]": it is called *saṃvara* because it possesses a rule or method; it is called "cutting off" (*prahāṇa*) because it restrains evil so that it does not arise.

Regarding the cutting off of unarisen evil dharmas, it is called "cutting off" because one has already attained their cessation; furthermore, causing them not to arise again is also termed "cutting off. Question:
Since this is by means of wisdom (*prajñā*), how can it be diligence (*vīrya*)? Answer: In truth, it is wisdom; however, diligence is predominant here.

Therefore, names are established based on what is predominant; this is the explanation of their mutual proximity. Furthermore, although the abandonment of evil arises from prior wisdom, the cultivation of goodness must necessarily rely upon vigor (*vīrya*);
since the overcoming of evil follows the cultivation of goodness, it is designated simply as "vigor. Moreover, while vigor is universal among wholesome states, wisdom is not necessarily so;
thus, establishing the name based on its universality involves no contradiction or impediment.
Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) among the twenty-two faculties, some say it has no affiliation within the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

Question: Whether considering the life-faculty in its ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it should belong to the mind-base (*manāyatana*) according to its various manifestations; or if discussing it as a conventional designation (*prajñapti*), it is subsumed under the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*).
Why, then, do you say it has no affiliation? Answer: Although it is subsumed under the phenomena-base, since this is a conventional phenomenon (*prajñaptidharma*), with respect to ultimate reality—

Because it does not belong to any [of the twelve] bases (*āyatana*), although the seed is subsumed under the mind-base (*manāyatana*), there is no base among the twelve that is the seed itself. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
"not belonging" means that it has no fixed affiliation between the two categories of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

If this is so, since it is said to have no affiliation, how do we know that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) relies upon the seed? The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains that it is by virtue of the functional capacity of the seed.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth," this is not the case. The intention of the *Yogācārabhūmi* is that among the twenty-two faculties, provisional phenomena (*prajñaptidharma*) belong to real faculties (*dravyendriya*).

For example, male and female belong to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), and the three untainted [faculties] belong to the nine faculties. Therefore, the life-faculty is provisional and has no [real faculty] to which it belongs.
Thus, one should know that this refers only to its lack of affiliation within the twenty-two faculties, and does not rely on the three [untainted faculties].
The classification is established by way of mutual inclusion.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because it is maintained by the manifest consciousness," the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are the manifest [basis], while the faculties (*indriya*) are the seeds.
Since the seeds are maintained by the manifest consciousness, the term "maintained" refers to the seeds, thereby describing the abiding of the manifest consciousness that maintains them.
The functional activity is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), whereas the manifest consciousness is the entity sustained by the seeds of the life-faculty; it is not itself the life-faculty.
This should be understood as explained previously.

However, regarding the point that the functional capacity reaches the mind and its various distinctions: because the seeds of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are identical, the functional capacity and the entity are one, and thus the aspect and the seeing are unified.
Because they are distinct, matter and mind differ.

If one were to say that death would necessarily occur upon the appropriation of the seeds of the five sense faculties, [the opponent] asks: "Even if the seeds of the faculties are present, though their manifest activity has been severed, why is this called death?
[The response is: Since the seeds of the faculties no longer possess the capacity to produce manifest activity and thus lack the function of sustaining the body, one must die.
Since the formless realm consists only of the mind, it should consist only of matter; yet in the formless realm there is only mind and no other distinct phenomena.
If there were no mind, it would consist only of matter—how then could there be another distinct phenomenon capable of obstructing the mind?

Regarding the statement, "In my system, mental factors are capable of both revulsion and so forth," the following section first presents a mutual critique, followed by a critique based on mutual compatibility, as can be understood.

From the Sarvāstivāda up to the point concerning "composite form" (*saṃghāta-rūpa*) and the "provisional" (*prajñapti*): the question asks why, if the Vaibhāṣika previously asserted that both the coarse and the subtle are substantially real, [this is now contradicted].

Now, regarding the question of whether [the object] is a conventional designation of a composite (*saṃghāta-prajñapti*), the answer is as follows: That school itself admits that jars, basins, embankments, and so forth are conventional designations of composites.
These are apprehended solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and are subsumed under the sense-field of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). Although they are composites, their substance is real;
therefore, our statement that they are "conventional" does not contradict that school's own tenets.

However, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that there is a distinct dharma that acts as an obstruction; the Sarvāstivādins also employ the analogy of a dammed river for the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*).

Their intention is that, just as a river is dammed, so too is the distinct mind obstructed; furthermore, the objects of focus (*ālambana*) of that [obstructing] mind differ from those of the two attainments.
This [text] does not discuss whether these are provisional (*prajñapti*) or substantial (*dravya*).

For those who have not long practiced, it is as described; however, for those who have long practiced from the eighth bhūmi upward, any seed of mind—whether coarse or subtle—in any realm constitutes the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
As stated in the commentary on the seventh fascicle, there are two interpretations.
Regarding the distinction between the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the two attainments (*samāpatti*), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (second chapter) states:

"The attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is preceded by the mental attention (*manaskāra*) of the notion of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-saṃjñā*); the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is preceded by the mental attention of the notion of stillness (*upaśama-saṃjñā*), having transcended the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (first chapter) states: "As for the attainment of non-perception, one contemplates perception as being like a disease, like an abscess, like..."

For one who enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) by first giving rise to the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the perception of renunciation (*naiṣkramyasaṃjñā*) based on this absence of perception—

whether they enter the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) or the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*)— they previously observe *tathatā* (suchness) as the preparatory application (*prayoga*) before entering the attainment of cessation. If, however,
they are those who have attained mastery through transcendence (*atikrāntavaśitā*), they observe *tathatā* immediately following a mind of whichever stage (*bhūmi*) they are in.

Regarding the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for entry [into the meditative attainment]: if it follows the sequential order, then the mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) observing *tathatā* constitutes the preparatory application for entry.

As for the statement that "the former interpretation is superior because the seeds of the extremely subtle mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*) reach [that state]," the latter interpretation holds that the clear mind which draws forth the collective retribution (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is this very mind;
however, since this mind is not extremely sublime and has not yet transformed into meditative absorption (*samādhi*), how could it possibly draw forth that collective retribution?

Regarding the former interpretation, which holds that only the final subtle mind at the end of the fruit-phase attracts those collective and individual [results] and this mind itself transforms into meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
that former interpretation is superior.

As for the current interpretation, which maintains that the attainment (*prāpti*) receives the name "maturation" (*vipāka*), this interpretation relies on the cessation of wholesome and defiled minds within the six consciousnesses of that stage.
This seed—whether original or newly acquired—is established as the provisional designation of "non-conceptualization" (*asaṃjñika*) upon the maturation (*vipāka*).
If this is so, since these seeds are either wholesome or defiled, how can it be said that they are established based on maturation? The answer is: these seeds are not actually maturation themselves;

however, because they are subsumed under the true maturation and their function is traced back to its essence, they are also called "maturation. It is upon this maturation that non-conceptualization is established.

Furthermore, just as it is accepted that these mindless states (*acittaka*) exist solely based on the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) without being distinct from it, yet are said to be established upon the fundamental consciousness, so too is this [explanation] understood;
however, such a reasoning is difficult to accept. There is another interpretation, which is explained at length in other commentaries.

Regarding the "cessation of the constantly active mind and mental factors" (*nitya-pravṛtta-citta-caitta-nirodha*): they are called "constantly active" because they arise repeatedly as wholesome, defiled, and so forth; it does not mean...

Seventh: Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that this maturation (*vipāka*) is established [as the basis for rebirth], this interpretation is based solely on the seeds of the "innate existence" (*mūlabhava*).

This is because those acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*) are inferior and incapable of being perfumed (*vāsya*). Due to the power of the mind of revulsion toward the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), these seeds are made to persist for five hundred eons.
The power of the non-occurrence of perception and feeling is conventionally designated as "non-perception" (asaṃjñika) based on this state;
this seed, when described in relation to the true maturation (vipāka), is called the "maturation of non-perception."

The "ripening of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) may be understood through both the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) and *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds. From the perspective of the state of mindlessness when born in that heaven, it is established as a conventional ripening;

thus, "non-conception" itself is the ripening. Alternatively, if one refers to the causal stage, it is designated as "non-conception," and from the perspective of the result, it is called the "ripening of the meditative attainment of non-conception."

The Compendium of the Meaning of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Volume Two (Original).

Regarding the statement that "the signs of a young girl do not indicate whether a phenomenon is wholesome or unwholesome," there are two interpretations.

First, it is said that according to Western (Indian) secular customs, if one encounters a young girl before setting out on a journey, it indicates an auspicious event; if one encounters an ox or similar animal, it indicates an inauspicious matter.
Second, it is said that if a young girl has black hair, a fair face, red lips, small knees, and slender calves, these indicate [the fulfillment of her desires].

If one gives birth to a child who is handsome and wise, it is auspicious; however, if one sees a young girl with yellow hair, a green face, black lips, large knees, and thick calves, it indicates that the child will be ugly.
