However, regarding the requirement that [an object] must necessarily be associated with its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) when being perceived: if one takes the characteristic of "form" (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) as encompassing all forms, this is called a "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), and its substance is not ultimately real.
This is because within it, each individual form is itself termed a "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, it must necessarily be associated with [its own] perception.

Because there are no common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) existing separately from their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is by means of this transformation of consciousness that common characteristics are established as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

As for the phrase "even up to [the perception of] a self" (*ātman-ādi*), this refers to the conceptualization of a self within the aggregates (*skandha*); taking the aggregates as real dharmas, one conceptualizes a self apart from them.

The "objective aspect" (*nimitta-bhāga*) of this [perception] exists as an object; it is like perceiving a flower in the sky (*khapuṣpa*) and forming the cognition of blue and so forth. Here, the blue and so forth are taken as real, or perhaps as being real flowers. If one perceives them separately...

Regarding rabbit horns and the like, because one has previously heard of or seen things such as cow horns, rabbit horns—which are similar to them—are also termed "concurrent realities" (*sāṃvṛta-satya*).
Alternatively, because their objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is taken as a real dharma, they constitute a condition.

Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): although this explanation of the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) encompasses all phenomena, this universal characteristic is itself dependent (*paratantra*), and thus fulfills the definition of a condition.
Nevertheless, it does not accord with reality, because the essence of each phenomenon possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and does not extend to others.

It should not be able to take two or three truths as its object; rather, when taking two or two [truths] in combination among the four truths, it is all termed a "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), because within a single moment of mind it takes many phenomena as its objects, and thus it is not a "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the three extensive interpretations found in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, that treatise itself poses the question:

"If the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom is subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can it know the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena? If the objects of common characteristics are known through direct perception, why are the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) established based on two distinct aspects?
The first interpretation states: "There is a view that the two means of valid cognition exist within the state of the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*) and rely upon two [aspects]."

Regarding the mutual establishment [of these positions], it is not said that the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-citta*) takes all aspects as its object; rather, they are all subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The second interpretation holds that there is a certain meaning: the mind in meditative equipoise takes only specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

However, when it is induced by the means of common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) to take as its object the principles manifested by various common characteristics, it is designated as "knowing common characteristics" from the perspective of those means. That which is not so is called "knowing the specific."
Based on this principle, some say that *tathatā* (suchness) is called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of emptiness and selflessness of all phenomena;

others say that *tathatā* is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness and is not a common characteristic. This latter view holds that through the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*), one performs a contemplation of the common characteristic—either contemplating emptiness and selflessness, or contemplating the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena—and that this contemplation of the common characteristic serves as the skillful means for subsequently attaining specific true observation.

The *tathatā* manifested is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Now, when we call this *tathatā* "selflessness" (*anātman*) or the principle of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), these are all explained from the perspective of the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) through the preceding preparatory means.

This contemplation of *tathatā* as selflessness and so forth is called the contemplation of the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-darśana*). A third interpretation states: "To speak according to reality" is established in that treatise on logic (*hetuvidyā-śāstra*).

This differs slightly from that [previous] explanation. According to that view, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) is termed their "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), because within each phenomenon, both the specific and general characteristics are attached to its own essence and do not belong to others.

However, when the conceptualizing mind establishes a single category where the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*) are common to all phenomena—like a thread threading through flowers—it is called the "general characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). This...
That which is conceptually established through the discrimination of the distracted mind is the object of inference (*anumāna*).

All states of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that are free from such discrimination are termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Although they take as their objects such things as suffering and impermanence, because each individual phenomenon exists separately, these are called specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If the Sūtras speak of suffering, impermanence, and so forth, these are called common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Now, regarding the suffering and [impermanence] mentioned in this treatise...

Because the characteristics such as impermanence and suffering are never separate from the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, each phenomenon possesses its own distinct suffering, impermanence, and so forth;

therefore, these [characteristics] such as suffering and impermanence, together with the essential nature of phenomena, are collectively termed "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the principles of the signifier and the signified within the conceptualizing mind are all termed "general characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

The seven stages are: first, the lineage; second, the stage of practice through resolute belief (the stage prior to the first bhūmi); third, the purification of the superior intention (the first bhūmi);
fourth, the stage of practice (the subsequent six bhūmis); fifth, the stage of certainty (the eighth bhūmi); sixth, the stage of certain practice (the ninth bhūmi);
and seventh, the stage of ultimate attainment (the tenth bhūmi, the stage of Buddhahood).

Regarding "predominance as human effort" (*puruṣakāra-adhipati*) up to "established by way of conventional designation": human effort is mostly designated with respect to *niṣyanda* (outflow), and predominance is mostly designated with respect to *vipāka* (maturation).
As for "an outflow that is not a cause": the fruit produced is the "outflow" (*niṣyanda*), while the seed that produces it is called the "equal" (*sama*).
Since it is the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of the outflow, the "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) belongs to the fruit and not to the cause.
However, when this cause is cited to manifest its own essence, this meaning is the same as that of the outflow, because this name is revealed by means of the perfuming karma.
Therefore, the treatise says: "By the perfuming of the impure wholesome and unwholesome [states] within the six consciousnesses, they are caused to grow and develop."
He also asked why the two texts only take the perfuming agent (*paribhāvaka*) to manifest its own nature.

The intended meaning is that the active manifestation (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) may also be termed the "cause" and may also be termed the "transforming agent" (*pariṇāmin*), as will be explained below in the self-commentary.
Regarding the statement that each [seed] is cited as being able to perfume and produce its own essence as a fruit: in the treatise, each perfuming active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) is cited;
these two seeds, in relation to the two perfuming agents, are shown to produce their essence through those two active manifestations. Therefore, they are all *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions).

It is not said that the view of self extends to the point of being distinct from conventional expression (*vyavahāra*), because although there is the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the grasping at a self, it does not result in a real self as its fruit.
Since these seeds, perfumed by what is unwholesome and obscured (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), are not distinct from conventional expression, they are distinguished [only] from conventional expression.
Question: Do the seeds of ripening karma (*vipākakarma*) have a separate essence apart from conventional expression?
Answer: Because it is superior in producing maturation (*vipāka*), it is established [as a separate category]; self-grasping (*ātmagrāha*) is not so, and thus it is not excluded. Question:
Since the latencies of self-grasping (*ātmagrāhavāsanā*) are excluded only from the category of "nominal objects" (*nāmārtha*), why is it said here that they are not excluded from these two? Answer:
The intention is to state that these two causes encompass all types [of latencies], not that the latencies of self-grasping are present within both of them simultaneously.

Regarding the statement that "this fruit-transforming [consciousness] is precisely the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and so forth," a question is raised: Are the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) and the object-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) fruit-transformations?
If they are fruit-transformations, why are they not mentioned as such? If they are not fruit-transformations, are they not produced from causal seeds? The Commentary (*Śū*) explains this itself:

[The seeing and object portions] are phenomena possessing objects (*sālambana-dharma*) that manifest as the meaning of the object-portion; thus, both meanings [of being a fruit-transformation] are absent.

Although the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) possesses the quality of being an object-condition, it lacks the sense of "transformational manifestation" because it cannot manifest the image-part (nimitta-bhāga);
therefore, it is not a transformation of the fruit.

Regarding how many [transformations] exist within the three realms, one should reflect according to reason; as for the cause that is capable of transforming, this applies generally to the Desire Realm and so forth.

Regarding the three natures: the retributive (vipāka) nature possesses both the wholesome and the unwholesome. If it is of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*) in the two higher realms, it is not unwholesome;

its retribution is exclusively wholesome in nature. Regarding the transformation of the fruit: in the desire realm, all eight consciousnesses are present; in the form realm, the nose and tongue [consciousnesses] are lacking;

in the formless realm, there are only the three [mental] consciousnesses. Among these fruits, the three natures exist. As for their causes—the seeds of matter, mind, and so forth—one should understand the varying number of these across the three realms accordingly.
It cannot be fully explained.

It also encompasses both cause and fruit, reaching up to the term "fulfillment through karma" (*karma-vaipulya*). Regarding "fulfillment of the cause" (*hetu-paripūri*), this refers to the karma that can summon the six consciousnesses;

"fulfillment of the fruit" (*phala-paripūri*) refers to the karma that is summoned as the six consciousnesses. These are called "outflows" (*āsrava*). Among these two types of fulfillment, karma is the most preeminent. [Question: As for the previous...

If it is argued that karma which produces a collective retribution (*saṃbhāra-karma*) may be called "superior," while this [present] karma—which produces specific fruits—should not receive the name "superior," the answer is that the points of reference differ.
What was previously called "superior" was superior in terms of inducing the fulfillment (*pūraṇa*); what is now called "superior" is superior in terms of the cause relative to its fruit.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the selection of the first among the five meanings, the question asks: according to the commentary on the six explanations, why does it speak only of "five meanings"?
There are two interpretations to this: first, it is said that the final meaning is a re-examination of the preceding errors rather than a primary explanation;

second, it is said that the third explanation is not called "vipāka" (maturation), because that which is "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) is fundamentally not itself *vipāka*, and therefore it is not included here.
There are only five meanings; between these two interpretations, the latter is correct while the former is not.

Since the final meaning clarifies *vipāka* (maturation), it should be understood through inference that among these various meanings, each preceding one is narrower and each succeeding one is broader.
Regarding the first one and a half verses that clarify the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*):

the intended meaning is that the first section, consisting of one and a half verses beginning with "by means of the imaginary" (*parikalpita*), clarifies the non-existence of the imaginary nature based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Now, in this present passage, which extensively explains the characteristics and natures, the first two sections—comprising twenty-two and a half verses—are detailed expositions; since the verses here are identical to those [in the previous section], they likewise clarify only [the perfected nature].
The dependent and the imagined are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Now, this third section, consisting of one verse, clarifies the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*);
it does not elaborate extensively upon the former [two natures], because this verse only elucidates the perfected nature as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The three masters all state that the first two and a half verses of the stanza explain the first [topic], the "transforming consciousness" (*pariṇāma*).
Regarding the ten gates within this transforming consciousness, some say they correspond to the three sections of the preceding commentary on the stanza. Furthermore, another interpretation states:

the previous explanation was based on the "objects transformed by consciousness," where there were the three commentaries of Dharmapāla, Sthiramati, and Nanda; since the present [text] expands upon the "transforming consciousness" itself, it is known that [the ten gates] refer to this.
The interpretation of those three masters is correct.

Regarding the statement that they serve as mutual conditions for defilement (*saṃkleśa*), this "defilement" includes the first seven consciousnesses and their three impure natures (*sāsrava-svabhāva*) which can perfume seeds—all of these are contained therein.
[Question: Do the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, when they are untainted (*anāsrava*) within the causal state, also have the capacity to perfume seeds?

Regarding this point within the eighth [fascicle] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, why is it not accepted? The answer is: this explains that the ālayavijñāna and the defiled [consciousnesses] serve as mutual causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

However, those seven consciousnesses can perfume the seeds of the *dṛśya-bhāga* (perceived portion) and *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving portion) within the ālayavijñāna, thereby producing the eightfold manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) of the ālayavijñāna.

Since the virtue of the ālayavijñāna is able to maintain those seeds, the principle of mutual causality is established. Nevertheless, regarding the seeds perfumed by the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) sixth and seventh consciousnesses—
The seeds are incapable of producing that Ālayavijñāna in its manifest state because they lack the causal basis;

if one considers their capacity to sustain the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they may possess the sense of "containing," yet the sense of being a causal condition (*pratyaya*) is absent. Therefore, this does not refer to the uncontaminated.

Furthermore, the uncontaminated and the contaminated are distinct as the antidote and the object of the antidote respectively; it is only among contaminated phenomena that they mutually serve as conditions for one another.

It is not like the *Mahad-ādi-tantra*, which is considered supreme; for although the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth are indeed transformations that are impermanent, they are identical in essence with *prakṛti*.
Here, however, the defiled ālayavijñāna and its effects stand in a relationship of mutual cause and effect, being neither identical nor different, and thus it is unlike that [system].
Furthermore, it is distinct because the Supreme Nature (*śiva*) is eternal, whereas the ālayavijñāna is impermanent.

Furthermore, regarding the absence of a "total" apart from the two [parts], the previous explanation clarifies this by means of cause and effect, while the subsequent explanation relies on the relative meaning of essence and attributes;
although both speak of the "total" and the "particular," their intended meanings differ.

Furthermore, when mental factors (caitta) are said to have the mind-king (citta) as their "fruit of human effort" (puruṣakāra-phala), it is like the case where attention (manaskāra) acts as the cause of human effort and the mind-king is the fruit of human effort;

for it is through the power of attention that the mind arises. Thus, according to this former master, the fruit of human effort belongs to the dharma, while according to the latter master, the fruit of human effort belongs to the person (pudgala).
Regarding the point that "the fruit of the seed is narrow because it is exclusively the fruit of karma": the question asks, "Narrow in relation to what? There are two interpretations. The first says:

It is called "narrow" in relation to the present fruit. This means that the eighth consciousness in its active state (*pravṛtti*) is the fruit of both the outflowing cause (*niṣyanda-hetu*) and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
However, the seeds of the eighth consciousness are the fruit of karma alone; therefore, they are "narrow. The second says: Here, this "fruit of the seed" is considered in relation to the seed itself.
The reason the name is "narrow" is that while the characteristic of being a cause applies to all seeds, the characteristic of being a fruit applies only to the eighth [consciousness] seed;
therefore, it is called "narrow. Between these two interpretations, the former is incorrect. Why is this so?

Because both the seed and the manifest fruit are produced by two causes—namely, the *niṣyanda* (outflowing) and *vipāka* (ripening) causes—and since the seed itself is also produced from a preceding seed.
Why do you say that it is solely due to the fruit of karma? To answer this: such reasoning is not correct.

The intended meaning is that seeds and fruits are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and exclusively the fruit of karma; they differ from seeds as causes, which pervade all types of seeds. This demonstrates the distinction between the broad and the narrow. Question:
If seeds are called "narrow" because they are exclusively indeterminate and the fruit of karma, then should the manifest fruit (*dṛṣṭadharmaphala*) be the same? No.
Because it serves as a cause. Answer: This is not so. This explanation states that the two characteristics of cause and effect both apply to seeds (*bīja*) and manifest phenomena (*vyañjana*).
If one considers seeds in relation to seeds, the cause consists of only eight types of causes, as these are the only causes that apply to all [factors]; thus, the seed-cause is narrow.

If one considers manifest phenomena in relation to manifest phenomena, both cause and effect belong to the eighth category; thus, their breadth and narrowness are equal. Therefore, one does not consider a manifest effect in relation to a manifest cause.
Because they are not identical, there is no contradiction.

Regarding the fact that they mutually serve as conditions and fruits, their characteristics are also pervasive; as the *Abhidharma-sūtra* states, "All dharmas [are the fruit] for the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and the storehouse-consciousness is likewise for those dharmas.
Because they mutually function as the nature of fruit and also constantly function as the nature of cause, it is said that this is the characteristic of fruit.
"Pervading all dharmas" refers to everything produced by the eighth seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*), which is designated as the "resultant aspect" (*phala-lakṣaṇa*).
This is according to a specific interpretive principle; in reality, it is not so. Why is this?

For instance, while all seeds are subsumed under the causal aspect and may thus be called the "seed-consciousness" from the perspective of the eighth consciousness, the actual manifestation (*pravṛtti*) of various dharmas does not derive its name from the eighth consciousness.

Regarding why the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) is called the "result-aspect" (*phalalakṣaṇa*), the first interpretation in the Commentary is correct; the subsequent explanation is made from the perspective of its functional meaning.

As for the phrase "it is also co-existent with the seeds up to being their cause," this means that while the seeds of the eighth [consciousness] are co-existent with the manifesting consciousness and are also its cause, the manifesting consciousness, though co-existent with the seeds, is not their cause. This refers to the eighth [consciousness], the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Because formations (*saṃskāra*) cannot perfuse (*vāsayati*), they do not give rise to their own fundamental dharma (*mūladharma*), just as the minor life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth do not; thus, although they are co-existent (*sahabhū*), they are not causes.
Other perfuming consciousnesses (*vāsaka-vijñāna*), however, may be termed co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) in relation to the seeds (*bīja*) that are perfumed.

Furthermore, regarding its being the "purifier of seeds": this eighth consciousness is able to sustain the untainted (*anāsrava*) seeds and also serves as the seed for untainted manifest activity (*abhisaṃskāra*).
Because it is a manifest phenomenon, it is not termed a "function. [Question: Since seeds can produce manifest phenomena, they are established by the name "function."
If the present dharma can also act as a perfuming agent (*vāsanā*), why is it not established as having "functional capacity" (*sāmarthya*)? The answer is that seeds are difficult to discern;

therefore, the meaning of a seed is revealed by means of its functional capacity. Since actualized phenomena (*pravṛtti*) are easily understood, one does not speak of their functional capacity. Furthermore, because a seed can produce both another seed and an actualized phenomenon, it may be designated as having "functional capacity";
however, since a present dharma produces only a seed, it is not so designated. Thus, the former interpretation is correct.
Regarding the passage from "It is not exclusively different" up to the end of the fifty-first [fascicle], consult the fifty-second [fascicle], which states:

"That is to say, within the *ālayavijñāna*, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) resulting from the false attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of all phenomena are called 'established seeds' (*vyavasthāpita-bīja*).
However, these habitual tendencies exist as substantial entities (*dravyasat*); they exist conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*), but in relation to those phenomena, they do not [exist as such]."
It can be definitively stated that the characteristics of being neither different nor non-different are just like those of True Suchness (*tathatā*);
here, however, it speaks only of the cause and effect as being neither identical nor different, and does not speak of their essence and function as being neither identical nor non-different.

This is known because it says, "regarding those various dharmas, one cannot definitively state whether their characteristics are different or non-different. Thus, what are referred to as "those various dharmas" are precisely the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) in their active manifestation.

Furthermore, as for the term "expectation" (āśaṃsā), it refers to the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); these are capable of expecting their corresponding manifest activities (*pravṛttivijñāna*), being neither identical nor different from them.

Furthermore, the phrase "existing as a real entity" (*dravyasat*) means "real-only" (*tattvika-mātra*); the phrase "existing as a conventional reality" (*saṃvṛtisat*) means "conventional-only" (*saṃvṛti-mātra*).
Within the fifty-one textual passages, there is no place where the meaning of "neither identical nor different" is explained.
It is not only the case that seeds, in relation to the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna), constitute cause and effect;

rather, within this context, it is not only the seeds of the eighth consciousness in relation to the manifest activity (pravṛttivijñāna) of the fundamental consciousness that are subsumed under cause and effect. Indeed, all seeds in relation to the manifest activities they produce are likewise encompassed by the relationship of cause and effect.
However, dharmas are not effects because they are not produced by causes; nor are they causes because the "arising" (jāti) that produces them is not a cause.

This is because they [the dharma and its arising] either manifest simultaneously or exist as simultaneous seeds, and thus are neither cause nor effect. Furthermore, since "arising" and the like are provisional while the fundamental dharma is substantial, and because the provisional and the substantial differ, they are not cause and effect.
If one follows the Sarvāstivāda school, where arising is considered substantially existent, it might be possible [to posit such a relationship].
This treatise takes [the three natures] as cause and effect.

Regarding this, the critic An-hui (Sthiramati) and others raise an objection: they hold that the two aspects—the perceived (*nimitta*) and the perceiving (*darśana*)—are the essence of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) and are not real entities.
Since seeds are subsumed under the aspect of the perceived, they must be admitted to be unreal; thus, they formulate this objection.
Regarding the passage beginning with "If it were not an established [truth], then up to 'this reality is only... etc., the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that seeds exist conventionally (*saṃvṛti*).

In that treatise, there are four types of established truths within conventional truth, while the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is solely true suchness (*tathatā*), which should be called the non-established truth (*avyavasthāpita-satya*).
Since seeds exist only within the category of established truths, when it says "truth," it refers exclusively to conventional truth.

Because it penetrates the truth, if one relies on this treatise and holds that seeds (*bīja*) are exclusively substantially existent (*dravyasat*), then according to this treatise’s reliance upon the four ultimate truths (*paramārtha-satya*) and the four conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*), seeds are exclusively substantially existent within the realm of conventional truth; thus it says they are "exclusively real.

However, if one investigates them further within the ultimate truth, seeds are also conventionally designated (*prajñaptisat*). Therefore, the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) assists the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in reaching a harmonious conclusion.

Regarding this treatise, if one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, seeds are conventional (*saṃvṛti*). As for the term "real" (*satya*), it means real within the conventional, because they are real among conventional phenomena.
Now, as for the question: "To which part does this [seed] belong? Is it the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of this consciousness, or something else? The answer is:

These seeds have existed from beginningless time and depend upon the very substance of consciousness; thus, they are subsumed under the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*). They are not taken as objects by the seeing aspect (*darśanabhāga*), and therefore they do not belong to that.

Regarding the statement that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) is not included [within the definition of consciousness], this refers to the *nimitta-bhāga* as explained in the context of contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena. Question:

Since it does not perceive objects through the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect), it should not be considered *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Answer: This is identical to *tathatā* (suchness); because it is the very essence of consciousness and is not separate from consciousness, it is also termed *vijñapti-mātra*.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "nor is it because the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) reaches and encounters the preceding object," this is intended to refute the Master Ghoṣaka, who maintains that seeds depend upon the seeing-part because the self-cognition (svasaṃvedana) [of the seeing-part] is able to take seeds as its object.
This is incorrect, for seeds cannot depend upon the seeing-part; the seeing-part encounters objects, whereas seeds do not serve as the basis for such encounter.
Moreover, the seeing-part is merely the functional capacity of the self-cognizing part (svasaṃvedana-bhāga) to act as a perceiver. Furthermore, this...
Because the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part) does not receive perfuming, and for three reasons, it is known that the seeds do not depend upon the *darśana-bhāga*.
Regarding the statement "the *darśana-bhāga* cannot initially receive other perfumings," this cites the defense of Dharmapāla.
If it were not so, there would be no self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

If [the object] were not the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) but rather the self-substance itself that is said to be perceived based on its specific functional capacity, then it would be unnecessary to establish a fourth self-cognizing portion.
Why is this? Because the seeing-portion is itself the third fruit.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part) only takes external objects as its object: if one grants that the *darśana-bhāga* perceives and adheres to the *svasaṃvedana-bhāga* (self-verifying part), it would necessarily take the internal as its object;

why then do you say it only takes the external? Question: Since it is said that it takes the *svasaṃvedana-bhāga* as its object, how can its differentiated functional capacity not be taking the internal as its object?
Answer: Since this functional capacity is subsumed under the category of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective image part), there is no logical obstacle to the *darśana-bhāga* perceiving the internal.

Regarding the statement, "If [the self-cognizing part] protects until the end of the month, it does not exhaust the principle," this master does not allow that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes seeds as its object.

If that were so, then the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) would have no object of cognition. This master explains: in that realm, the self-cognizing part takes seeds as its object, while the seeing-part actually takes the material forms of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) of the lower realms as its object.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the eighth consciousness in the formless realm takes only internal seeds as its object.

It is not that the statement that the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part) does not take the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) of the lower realms as its object is unreasonable; rather, this [text] states that there is no internal body or vessel-world in the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* conceals the vessel-world and speaks only of taking seeds as its object.
Since this is so, regarding those who are born in the formless realm, such as non-returners (*anāgāmin*), Saṃghabhadra reconciles these contradictions.

This refers to the explanation by way of the distinction between function and capacity; that is, the functional capacity of the seeds is not of the same indeterminate nature as the substance of the eighth consciousness.
This is explained according to the gate of distinction, and is also termed the "gate of the separate discussion of nature and function."
"An untainted dharma that accords with principle and opposes birth" means it accords with the principle of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and opposes birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

Regarding the statement that this applies to all untainted seeds of the Buddha-fruit: Question: The treatise states, "It is by the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*) that [seeds] undergo transformation and maturation.
Since the Buddha has no perfuming, how can this statement be said to apply to the Buddha-fruit? Answer: This mention of "perfuming" does not refer to the Buddha.

Furthermore, because there is perfuming within the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) seeds, although the Buddha does not perfume them, when the seeds produce their manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), they must nevertheless undergo transformation;

thus, this applies universally to the Buddha as well. Another interpretation states that even for the uncontaminated seeds of a Buddha, when they produce manifest activity, it is due to the power of perfuming within the causal stage that they reach the state of Buddhahood through transformation and maturation.
The *Sub-commentary* (*Vivaraṇa*) further states: "Even if one were to exclude the Buddha, if one were to..."
This interpretation is without fault.

Regarding the present explanation of the meaning of "non-contention" (*araṇā*), all three masters mentioned below agree that it is through perfuming (*vāsanā*) that the seeds [of the mind] are protected;
even according to Candragomin, it is by means of perfuming that these seeds are caused to increase.

Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 52) that "arising from seeds" refers to the supramundane mind arising from the seeds of the untainted mind that takes suchness as its object:

because suchness is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it is said that the seeds of the wisdom that takes it as its object arise from that very object, suchness, to produce the untainted [mind].
Furthermore, it is traditionally said that this was the interpretation of Master Bao.

Taking *tathatā* (suchness) as the untainted seed (*anāsrava-bīja*), it is because this *tathatā*, acting as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), can give rise to untainted noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*).
Since it possesses the capacity to produce [wisdom], it is also designated by the name "seed. Thus, *tathatā* is the object-condition, and the object-condition is the seed.
Although there are these two interpretations, they are not yet correct in principle. One should now provide the correct interpretation: namely, that the Tathāgata...

Taking *tathatā* (suchness) as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the great samādhi, wisdom, and compassion flow forth from *tathatā*; this is the *sāmbhogika-kāya* (enjoyment body) of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body) flows forth from the *sāmbhogika-kāya*, and from this *nirmāṇa-kāya* flow the twelvefold teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma*).

This is called the "outflowing true Dharma" (*niṣyanda-saddharma*), because when sentient beings hear these twelvefold teachings, they cultivate the seeds of the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-bīja*).
It is capable of producing the supramundane, untainted (*anāsrava*) manifest activity; this refers to the supramundane mind from the perspective of its fundamental source.

Since it is metaphorically said that True Suchness (*tathatā*) arises [as the cause], True Suchness is designated as the "seed. Therefore, the statement that [the supramundane mind] arises from the seeds of the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of True Suchness is identical in intent to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Question: How do the masters who maintain that [seeds] exist only as original (*mūla-bhava*) interpret this passage? Answer: Regarding supramundane gnosis (*lokottara-jñāna*), by means of...
Tathatā serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and this wisdom arises from seeds that have existed from the beginning.

As for the proof that these [seeds] also exist [innately] rather than being newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*), such as the teaching on the "hearing-perfuming" (*śruta-vāsanā*) cited previously, I do not point to them here because those teachings include both the innate and the newly perfumed;
this will be reconciled later when it says: "At the time of hearing the True Dharma... and so forth.

Because it perfumes what is originally present, gradually causing it to increase until, through skillful means, it is described as the seed of supramundane mind, [the text] does not explicitly point to it.
When it says that [something] acts as the two types of conditions for the various consciousnesses, and that one serves as their seed, this refers to the *ālayavijñāna*.
The seed-consciousness serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the three natures and the evolving consciousnesses.

Regarding the statement that "the two serve as its support," this means that the eighth manifesting consciousness, by grasping and maintaining the material sense organs, acts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the arising of the visual and other consciousnesses.
Regarding the statement that the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) serve as two conditions:

first, "nurturing those seeds in the present life" means that all subsequent moments of the manifesting eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) are produced by the perfuming of those seeds by the preceding moments of the evolving consciousnesses;
thus, the perfuming manifesting consciousness acts as the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition) for the seeds it perfumes. Second, "gathering and planting [the seeds] in future lives."

Regarding those "seeds," it means that in the future, the resultant *ālayavijñāna* arises only by virtue of the seeds perfumed within the present evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) through wholesome and unwholesome karma acting as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

Furthermore, regarding the "present life," this refers to the evolving consciousnesses of the present, which can only nourish those seeds but do not serve as their causal condition (*hetupratyaya*). As for the "subsequent life," it refers to this very same [resultant consciousness].
It is held that the seeds newly perfumed by past moments are able to produce the manifest activities of subsequent moments; this is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The previous interpretation is correct when it states that they "mutually produce" one another: that is, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) are mutually the producers, which constitutes their nature as cause (*hetu-bhāva*), and they are mutually the produced, which constitutes their nature as effect (*phala-bhāva*).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "exhausting the substance within this context": here, the substance of causes and conditions—comprising both manifest phenomena (*vijñapti*) and seeds (*bīja*)—is exhausted;

yet, because nothing exists apart from manifest phenomena and seeds, the three dharmas and two dharmas herein both describe the mutual arising of manifest phenomena and seeds, rather than describing seeds giving rise to seeds.
Therefore, the fruit is not exhausted.
Regarding the phrase "its seeds are originally present and continue to increase," the meaning is to be read as looking upward [to the preceding context];
it clarifies that the seeds of the fruit which are increased coexist with their own karmic seeds from the very beginning.

Therefore, since the manifest karma is able to cause the seeds of the fruit to increase, it should also be called a "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*), just as manifest karma perfumes and increases its own seeds. [Question: What was the previous interpretation?
Question: This [explanation] also involves the increase of the seeds of the fruit through the perfuming of present karma; how does it differ from the previous one? Answer:

Although the previous explanation also involves the increase of the seeds of the fruit, it identifies the present karma itself—relative to the present fruit—as the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition). This current explanation, however, views the matter relative to the seeds, and for that reason it differs from the former.

Question: If that is so, even if both involve new perfuming (*navasaṃskāra*) and so forth, what is the distinction? Answer: To this objection, the proponent of new perfuming (*navasaṃskāravādin*) says: "I maintain that there is merely perfuming and growth."

If that which is called a "causal condition" (hetu-pratyaya) were to cause the seeds of karma to increase their fruit, then those seeds should indeed be called causal conditions. Suppose you argue that what is newly perfumed (navābhyasta) is called a causal condition;
yet if both the karma-seed and its fruit are equally newly perfumed, how could you allow for the present karma to be called a causal condition with respect to the seed of the fruit?
The meaning of the answer can be understood from this.

However, when examining the original intent of the latter interpretation—that it is the "original" because it follows the second among the first three interpretations and precedes the initial [interpretation]—it is clear that the Master’s original intention was to designate the increase of the perfumed seeds as the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Therefore, why not adopt the second [interpretation], which contains the meaning of increase occurring both initially and subsequently? Answer: Although there is increase in both cases, it is only in the initial and subsequent [second] interpretations that this increase is explicitly stated.

The meaning is obscure; the reason for this is as follows: first, regarding the objection that present karma serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for a present fruit, this principle is untenable.
This is because present karma lacks the capacity to increase [the fruit], and a present fruit, having already arisen, cannot be increased.

Second, regarding the objection that it would cause the seeds of karma to increase, it is likewise impossible for the seeds of the fruit (namely, *nāma-rūpa*) to increase; a present, strong seed cannot coexist with a present, weak one.
Since it has already increased, what need is there to plant it? One cannot plant that which has already increased, because it does not increase further in the present.

For this reason, it is known that the second interpretation is correct. Now, to further support this, the *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The latter interpretation is the original one. This means that both of the latter two interpretations are designated as "latter";
however, the underlying intent is simply that causing the seeds to grow is termed the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*), while the latter two [interpretations] both concern the seeds of the fruit.

Because of the increase [of the cause], the first interpretation—viewed in contrast to the present—is not the primary intention. Furthermore, the nature of the *saṃskāra-aṅga* (the link of formations) extends to both seeds and manifest [actions].

The second [interpretation] takes the manifest action as increasing the seed of the fruit; the third takes the seed of the action as increasing the seed of the fruit. Therefore, the latter two interpretations constitute the primary intention.
If one were to take only the second [interpretation], one should say that the middle interpretation is the primary one; why then call it the "latter"?
Regarding the phrase "Since this is so, these causes... and so forth: this objection implies that if something is newly produced, the old manifestation should not be produced.
When it says "this meaning should be considered," the intended sense is that the original and the new arise together as one manifestation; it is not the case that [the old] is not produced.

However, the statement "because they are equal in their category of production" is not a direct answer; rather, it merely explains that the original possesses its own kind of seed, which is termed the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*), without relying on [other factors].
The term "perfuming and increasing" refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Regarding the point that it is accepted that outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) [dharmas] can produce one another: [Question: If the opponent already accepts that they produce one another, then your thesis commits the fallacy of contradicting what is already admitted (*pratijñā-siddha*).

If the opponent does not accept it, then your reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished for at least one party (*anyatara-asiddha*). [Answer: We merely accept that the outflowing [dharmas] are capable of...

The arising of the untainted (*anāsrava*) is precisely the arising of its own characteristic; it does not require the untainted, for we allow that the arising of the tainted (*sāsrava*) may occur without a cause.
Since it is not stated that they arise mutually, there is no fault of [failing to meet] either one of the conditions.

This may be so for the Hīnayāna regarding what constitutes a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), but this is the doctrine of the Sarvāstivāda. If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa*, it speaks only of...
Wholesome five aggregates serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for wholesome five aggregates; the same applies to indeterminate [aggregates] and so forth.
This implies that wholesome form, mind, and so on are mutually accepted as homogeneous causes, though there is no explicit permission for wholesome and unwholesome [states] to be homogeneous causes.

Furthermore, according to other specific interpretations found in the *Vibhāṣā* and other texts, such cases should exist. Moreover, even if it were permitted—such as when an unwholesome mind arises immediately after a wholesome mind—that would be the case.
The claim that a preceding wholesome state gives rise to a subsequent unwholesome state constitutes a similarity of kind (*sabhāga*) is not the Mahāyāna doctrine.

Regarding the statement that "all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are likewise unimpeded [in this regard]," while it is logically unimpeded for all unconditioned phenomena to serve as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) among the four conditions,
it is logically impossible for them to serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
If you argue that because [the mind] is pure in its nature when it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) up to when it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and wholesome, you likewise claim:

"I accept that the nature of the mind is intrinsically pure even when it is evil or neutral; therefore, the unconditioned—which is associated with faith and other [wholesome factors]—must also be pure by nature and thus associated with faith and so forth," there is no fault in this.
For it is commonly accepted that the unconditioned is ultimate goodness (*paramārtha-kuśala*), not something that is associated with conditioned factors.
Because it is a wholesome mind, it cannot be made to be associated with faith and so forth.

As for the nature of the untainted (anāsrava) mind being like the nature of the tainted (sāsrava), if one were to establish this as a formal inference (*pramāṇa*), the probandum (*sādhyadharma*) would be unestablished within the corroborative example (*sapakṣa*), because the opponent accepts that the nature of the tainted mind is untainted.
Therefore, one should instead formulate the inference as follows: "Your untainted mind [is tainted]."

It should be understood that [the reason] is subsumed under either the contaminated (*sāsrava*) or the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), as its nature is contradictory [to the thesis], just like a contaminated mind.

Regarding the statement that "from the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) up to noble ones (*ārya*) such as the Buddhas, this measure of the cause allows for the manifestation of a contaminated mental nature because the nature of the mind is admitted to be pure":
the reason should simply state "because the nature of the mind is admitted to be pure," and thus there is no fault.
In the Abhidharma treatise, regarding the three transformations of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), that treatise states:

"What are the three transformations of the basis belonging to the path of no-more-learning? They are the transformation of the mind, the transformation of the path, and the transformation of the heavy residues (*dausthulya*).

As for the transformation of the mind, it means that having attained the path of no-more-learning and realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the self-nature of the mind is pure and forever free from all [afflictions]."

Because it is free from adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*), it is called "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); this is the meaning of the transformation of the basis as *tathatā*. Regarding the transformation of the basis of the path:

when one generates the mundane path, at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), it is transformed into the supramundane; this is called the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) because there is still further work to be done.
When all that is to be countered is permanently eliminated and one is forever free from the desires of the three realms, the intrinsic nature of this path is thoroughly investigated.
Finally, it is established as the complete transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parivṛtti*). Regarding the "transformation of the basis of the heavy residues" (*dausthulya-parivṛtti*):

because the *ālayavijñāna* is forever separated from all afflictive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is called the "transformation of the basis. Question: Why does that treatise state that *tathatā* (suchness) is the mind?

Answer: The mind has three meanings: first, the meaning of objective consideration (*ālambana*); second, the meaning of accumulation (*cita*); and third, the meaning of reality (*tattva*). Suchness [possesses these meanings].
Since it is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, it is called "mind" (*citta*) because it is the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*).
Regarding the passage in the fourth fascicle of the *Abhidharmapada* stating that it is also called "untainted" (*anāsrava*), I have searched the fourth fascicle and did not find this text.

However, according to the third fascicle, the explanation of "tainted" (*sāsrava*) states: "That which conforms to the outflows (*āsrava-anuloma*) refers to the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)," even though they are [associated with] afflictions...

Although it is accompanied by the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of affliction, it can be established as having the nature of being untainted (*anāsrava*), because it turns its back on all existence (*bhava*) and accords with its antidote.
Regarding this [state] that accords with penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) as being of the nature of the untainted, there are two interpretations:

first, it is said that one takes the originally existing untainted seeds belonging to the stage of penetration and designates them as "penetration" for the sake of establishing it as untainted; second, this [penetration]...

The essential nature of the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (factors conducive to penetration) is not itself untainted (*anāsrava*), yet it is designated as "untainted" because it accords with the untainted and turns away from the tainted (*sāsrava*).
Regarding the statement in the fifty-first fascicle that these induce a superior maturation (*vipāka*), that treatise further states:

"The seeds of wholesome dharmas such as the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), which are sustained by the *ālayavijñāna*, do not constitute [the cause of] accumulation (*upacaya*)."
Because the roots of goodness such as the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are contrary to the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*),
all other mundane roots of goodness arise from them and consequently become increasingly radiant and flourishing. By virtue of this causal condition,
the seeds of their own kind that they have grasped become functional and powerful, and these increasing seeds quickly reach full establishment.
Furthermore, by virtue of these seeds, those various wholesome dharmas arise with increasing clarity and vigor;
moreover, they are able to bring about future ripened fruits that are increasingly abundant, increasingly superior, desirable, and delightful.

"All are of a single category; this refers to the transformation and cessation [of seeds]" means that, for example, when entering, abiding in, or emerging from a single stage (*bhūmi*), at the initial moment of entering the stage, there exists only the seed of the inferior category.
When reaching the state of abiding in the mind, the inferior category is transformed and ceased, and the medium category arises.

When emerging from the mind, the medium category is transformed and ceased, and the superior category arises. If one adheres solely to the doctrine of the "original existence" (*mūlāstitva*) of seeds, then the preceding moment is the inferior category.
After the cessation of the middle-grade [state], the subsequent thought arises as middle-grade; after the cessation of the middle-grade, the subsequent thought arises as superior-grade.

If, according to the school that maintains only new perfuming (*navavāsanā*), at the time of abiding in the mind, a lower-grade manifestation perfumes and forms a middle-grade seed—then one should know that the manifestations produced by this seed are all termed middle-grade, and likewise up to superior-grade.
It should be understood that the same applies to the others.

Regarding the principle of "equal transformation": just as when one sees the seeds of the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga), at the time of reaching the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), they are equal to the seeds being cultivated and are both termed "middling";
and upon reaching the Path of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa-mārga), the seeds of the Paths of Seeing and Cultivation are equal to those of No-More-Learning.

Now, regarding the seeds of the Path of Seeing and those of the Path of Cultivation, which are equal, does the manifest knowledge (jñāna) produced thereby also have the power to sever the co-emergent afflictions? If this were not the case, what fault would there be?

Question: If it is admitted that [the path of seeing] can sever [afflictions], what is the use of cultivating the wisdom of the path of cultivation? If it cannot sever them, on what basis is the principle of "equal transformation" (parāvṛtti) established?

Answer: There are two interpretations. The first says: Although the seeds of the path of seeing persist through the paths of cultivation and no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), they do not manifest as active states;

therefore, it is said that afflictions are not severed. As for the term "equal transformation," this refers to the seeds, and thus there is no contradiction. The second says: The path of seeing... [text fragment ends].

Regarding the seeds of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), it is permissible that they arise as manifest [during the stage of training], yet by the time one reaches the stage of the diamond-like concentration (vajropamasamādhi), they necessarily do not manifest.

This is because the seeds of the dharmas of the path of cultivation exist inherently; furthermore, those seeds of the path of seeing (darśanamārga) do not encounter the conditions for manifestation, and once [the path of cultivation] has already been able to sever them, further effort would be useless.

Moreover, there is no single moment of mind that possesses multiple wisdoms (*prajñā*); thus, even if two types of understanding were to coexist, one must examine other texts for further clarification.

This cannot yet be established as definitive. Regarding this third master, since he maintains that both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) each possess both original and newly perfumed seeds, how does his doctrine differ from that of the previous two masters?
Why do you say they are "equal"? Answer: This master holds that because each of these three stages possesses both original and newly perfumed seeds, they can be considered equal.
Question: Since the previous masters maintain only one type [of seed], if that were so, what would become of the newly perfumed seeds?

"What do you mean by 'transformation to equality'? He replied: "When [the seeds] reach the stage of medium intensity, from those seeds of natural law (dharmatā) belonging to the medium category, there arise seeds of new perfuming that manifest as actualities; these are called 'newly perfumed seeds of medium intensity.

Furthermore, when the seeds of the lower category reach this stage, their power becomes equal [to that of the medium category]; therefore, it is called 'transformation to equality. There is another interpretation."

In various places, it is stated that those who hold the position established by the "newly perfumed" (*navābhyasta*) contradict the meaning of the treatise; this means they all contradict its fundamental meaning.

The commentary states that those who contradict the meaning established by the "newly perfumed" do so because the two schools—the "original" (*mūla*) and the "textual" (*vyañjana*)—are mutually contradictory.
*Cheng weishi lun yi yun*, Fascicle Two (Original).
*Cheng weishi lun yiyun*, Fascicle Two (End).
Compiled by Daoyi of Kaiyuan Temple in Mizhou.
Regarding the statement in the fifth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that there are "seven kinds," etc.: first, impermanent phenomena are causes; there are no permanent phenomena.

1. That which can serve as a cause for a phenomenon perishes at that very same moment; 2. Furthermore, although an impermanent phenomenon serves as a cause for another impermanent phenomenon, it serves as a cause for the nature of another [moment] and also serves as a cause for its own nature in the subsequent moment, rather than being restricted to that very same moment; 3.
Furthermore, although it serves as a cause for the nature of another and serves as a cause for its own nature in the subsequent moment, it has already arisen but not yet ceased.
1. Only when it can serve as a cause for another nature within these two meanings—namely, the meaning that this very fruit co-exists with its cause—is it so;

2. and the meaning that this very [nature] constantly follows and transforms as a cause for its own subsequent moment’s nature. 4. However, it can only serve as a cause once it has acquired other conditions;
5. and it can only serve as a cause once it has undergone transformation. These two meanings correspond precisely to this.

1. "Depending on various conditions" corresponds to this treatise’s discussion of the meaning of the determination of nature (*dharmatā-niyama*). 6. "Necessarily corresponding with functional capacity" corresponds to this treatise’s discussion of the drawing forth of its own fruit (*svaphala-ākṣepa*).
7. "Necessarily being commensurate and concordant" corresponds to this treatise’s discussion of the drawing forth of its own fruit.

Regarding the specific distinction of "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*): if one asks how it is that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and mind-and-mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are excluded from being called "exhausted," the answer is as follows:

external seeds of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) also possess the six characteristics [of seeds], as stated in the commentary itself. Furthermore, since non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are merely provisional and lack substantial reality, there is no need to exclude them separately;
or else, they have already been excluded along with material and mental phenomena.

Regarding the phrase "like the root of a lotus" and so forth: although the lotus root is comprised within the category of manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), it is metaphorically designated as a "seed" in relation to the flower and stem;
therefore, it is said to exist simultaneously with its fruit. Question: How can external seeds possess constant continuity (*anuvartana*)? Answer:
In relation to a single lifetime (*ekāvadhi*), the continuous succession of preceding and succeeding moments is also called constant transformation.
This also clarifies that for the Mahāsāṃghikas and others, there is neither taking nor giving [of seeds]. There are two interpretations of this:

first, it is said that even if one were to grant that the Mahāsāṃghikas and others assert that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) serve as seeds for dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it would still be logically untenable; for unconditioned phenomena are devoid of transformation, and thus there can be no taking or giving.
This interpretation is incorrect. Second, it is said that this clarifies that the Mahāsāṃghikas and others establish dependent origination [itself as the seed].

The factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-aṅga*) cannot be established as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because the factors of dependent origination undergo transformation and involve taking and giving.
Therefore, just like the factors of dependent origination, the unconditioned is not truly unconditioned, because unconditioned phenomena do not involve taking and giving. [Question:

Do the Mahāsāṃghikas and others teach that the factors of dependent origination are themselves unconditioned? Or is there a separate unconditioned distinct from the factors of dependent origination? [Answer: That teacher...

Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and is not itself unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); however, the principle of impermanence, arising, and ceasing within the members of dependent origination is eternal and singular, and is designated as "unconditioned.
It is by virtue of this unconditioned [principle] that the members of dependent origination are rendered distinct from one another.
If that is so, since the Mahāsāṃghikas and others maintain that there is no taking up or discarding and no transformation, how do they demonstrate that [their view] is not [the same as ours]?

This is an answer by way of negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*); because that teacher [claims] the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) can cause the various members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to be distinct and undergo transformation, this [text] demonstrates that they are not unconditioned.
Question: Since the primary subject is to clarify the seed (*bīja*), why does it demonstrate that dependent origination is not unconditioned? Answer:
Because the seed possesses the characteristic of momentary arising and ceasing (*kṣaṇika-utpāda-vināśa*), it excludes the unconditioned; therefore, this is mentioned incidentally.

The Mahāsāṃghikas and others argue that since the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) possess arising and ceasing, they must also possess functional activity (*kāritra*), and thus they should likewise exclude [the possibility] that these are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If this were so, then even the unconditioned in the Mahāyāna would possess functional activity, because all noble ones (*ārya*) are distinguished by means of the unconditioned.
In response to this objection, we say: it is not so. In our school, the essence of the unconditioned is devoid of any transformation.
It is solely due to differences in the depth of realization that there are distinctions among the various stages of the noble ones (*ārya*).
How can you cite [the case of] the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as an example, given that it can cause transformations in dependent origination and possesses distinct intervals?
The former masters say that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the seed of all phenomena because various teachings state that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the root of all phenomena;
thus it is called the "seed. This is as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "Though they grow from one earth and are moistened by one rain, the various grasses, trees, and shrubs each develop differently.
What is called "one earth" is precisely True Suchness; since it is capable of producing growth, it is so named.

To claim that this [unconditioned] serves as a seed is incorrect. This is because while the rational nature (dharmatā) of the three vehicles is identical—just as the nature of the earth is one—their modes of practice differ, and thus their growth and development differ accordingly.
Furthermore, it is not taught that the unconditioned undergoes arising and ceasing.
By this absence of nature (*abhāva*), up to the point where it is not designated as a seed: that which is co-existent with its fruit (*phala-sahabhū*) is indeed called a seed.

Since the seventh [consciousness] lacks such nature and exists simultaneously with its perfumed fruit (*vāsya-phala*) in the present, it would [otherwise] have to be called a seed; therefore, this [definition] excludes it.
It is essential that for the produced fruit to manifest in substance, the producing cause may be called a seed. The seventh [consciousness], being devoid of such nature, is the perfumed...
Because its nature is submerged and hidden, that seventh consciousness is not called a "seed. Question:
If that is so, then since the fruits of all perfuming consciousnesses are submerged and hidden, why is it only the seventh consciousness of the "no-nature" (amala-vijñāna) that is excluded? Answer:

Other perfuming consciousnesses lack not only the meaning of this fruit’s manifestation, but also the meaning of constant concomitant transformation; the seventh consciousness of no-nature lacks neither.
Because it functions as a constant accompaniment, only this [cause] is excluded.
To the question, "If it is currently existing only in the cause, how can it be said that it is not currently existing in the fruit?
there are two interpretations: first, the current fruit is not fixed, whereas the cause is always present; second, it is like the characteristics of a tortoise's hair and so forth.
Although it arises from the same seed as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), it never actually manifests because its seed definitely exists;
therefore, it is said that it "exists" as a mere cause.
As for the statement that "the cause exists until it reaches non-contradiction," this means that a single dharma exists simultaneously in two temporal states within the present.
Furthermore, this does not contradict the fact that the cause and effect coexist;

for when it is said that "the cause exists at the time of arising and the effect exists at the time of ceasing," the intended meaning is that the cause arises first and subsequently ceases, while the effect arises later.

The subsequent commentary states, "The cause exists at the time of ceasing and the effect exists at the time of arising," which means that at the moment of ceasing, the cause draws forth the effect, and at the moment of arising, the effect repays the cause. Question: Why is this so? [End of excerpt]
The preceding and succeeding sections clarify that the arising and ceasing of cause and effect differ in their temporal sequence;
this is the core intent of the Commentary, which explains that Vasumitra maintains that cause and effect are contiguous, and thus they are cited alternately to facilitate the student’s understanding.

This means that when a preceding phenomenon arises, it coexists with its subsequent cessation, and when a subsequent phenomenon arises, it coexists with its preceding cessation. This is precisely the meaning of the response regarding cause and effect.

If that is so, regarding the detailed analysis of seeds in relation to seeds, if one were to claim—as the master Vijñānavādin (or *Jiṣṇu*) does—that a seed and its manifestation coexist in the present for a single moment each, and thus name this "simultaneous existence with the fruit" (*phala-sahabhū*), then the same would apply to the preceding and succeeding moments of the seed itself; it should likewise be named "simultaneous existence with the fruit.
What, then, is the purpose of the analysis? The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "A phenomenon acts as a cause for its own nature, yet it is not identical [to it]."

Regarding this moment, for what reason does this treatise itself provide the following analysis: "It is not like seeds, which, when arising from their own kind, are contradictory in terms of prior and posterior and must necessarily not coexist"?

This addresses the objection that there would be the fault of two destinies (*gati*) arising simultaneously. If one were to allow that cessation and arising belong to the same world-period (*adhvan*), then consider, for instance, a human being.
The state of the desire realm at the moment of final cessation occupies the former position, while the state of the desire realm at the moment of imminent birth occupies the latter;
since both states belong to the present, there is the objection that they must arise simultaneously, and others all follow this [erroneous] pattern.

The objective aspect (darśana-bhāga) takes the subjective aspect (draṣṭṛ) as its object, while the self-cognizing aspect (svasaṃvitti) takes the objective aspect as its object; both are capable of cognition and are collectively termed "seeing.
As stated below, when it says that cause and effect are not subsumed under causal conditions, the objective aspect is the cause and the self-cognizing aspect is the effect.
Regarding the statement that "there is no cause or condition for [a seed] to reach the point of producing a fruit":
if a first seed is simultaneously capable of producing a second seed, by what reason is it not permitted that a third seed and so forth could likewise be produced within the same moment?

This should also apply when considering seeds in relation to their own kind (*jāti*). As for the manifest state (*pravṛtti*), in a single moment there can never be two manifestations arising simultaneously; this is how seeds relate to [their corresponding] states.
The seeds should not arise as two types simultaneously.
How could the innate (prakṛtistha) seeds and the newly perfumed (navasaṃskṛta) seeds arise together in the same moment?
Furthermore, if it is not admitted that a seed produces a seed at the same time, how could the innate seeds and the seeds produced by the massed [food] (piṇḍa-ja) arise simultaneously?

This is not simultaneous, as in the case of the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*). This explains that the increase of the originally existing seeds (*prakṛtistha-bīja*) can produce the subsequent moment of its own kind through a single synthesis (*piṇḍotpāda*).
Since these two types [of seeds] both arise together at the same time as the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is no fault of their being produced by a single synthesis within the same moment.
Furthermore, within the subsequent moment, only the originally existing synthesis exists simultaneously; since it is not a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*), it likewise does not exist [as a cause].

This is a contradiction. [Objection: Since seeds produced by grasping (*upādāna*) arise simultaneously with their own kind and all possess innate existence (*sahaja*), why is it that only seeds produced by grasping can undergo new perfuming (*navasaṃskāra*)?
[Response: It is because they arise only through the power of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) acting as a dominant condition.

This means: first, that which "originally exists" refers to its own kind of seed; second, that which is "produced" refers to the *piṇḍa-utpāda* (the production of the physical aggregate), because it is produced by what originally existed in the preceding moment.

Regarding the previous interpretation concerning the meaning of both essence and function increasing together: the aforementioned establishment of the *piṇḍa-utpāda* seed is precisely [identical to] the essence and function.
The meaning of "both increasing" is the same. Question:

Since the cause [of increase] applies to both seeds (*bīja*) and those possessing seeds (*sabīja*), what is the distinction between them? Answer: "Seeds" refers to the seeds that produce manifest phenomena (*nirmita*). "Those possessing seeds" refers to those that produce subsequent seeds after having produced seeds;
thus, they are called "possessing" (or "existent"). Therefore, there is a distinction between the two.
If that is so, how can it be called "having the characteristic of being exhausted" (*parikṣīṇa-lakṣaṇa*)?

If, because the seventh consciousness undergoes transformation and is subject to change and relinquishment, it is not called a seed—then the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma, which produce fruits only within a limited scope, would also be subject to transformation and relinquishment, and thus should not be called "seeds that perpetually follow along" (*anuvartaka-bīja*).
Since it is said that they "perpetually follow along," they should not be [considered] "exhausted."

Regarding the *Sautrāntika* position that [dharmas] serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) up to [the point of their own category], the *Abhidharmakośa* treats only the five wholesome aggregates as homogeneous causes and does not consider other natures;
one should verify this against the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and the *Nyāyānusāra*.

Regarding the universal causes (*sarvatragahetu*) and so forth as having results of a different nature: the *Abhidharmakośa* identifies the eleven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) across the two truths as the essence of the universal cause.

These consist of the seven factors under the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*)—namely, the five views, delusion (*moha*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—and the four factors under the truth of origin (*samudayasatya*)—namely, the two graspings (*parāmarśa*), delusion, and doubt.
These eleven factors universally act as causes for all phenomena belonging to their own stage (*bhūmi*) and their own realm (*dhātu*) across the five categories (*pañca nikāyāḥ*).

Because they serve as causes, the two views of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); yet, because they act as causes for the five classes of unwholesome states, they produce results of a different nature.

As explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the simultaneous cause (*sahabhūhetu*) produces the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and others; since the fruit of human effort is broad in scope, it extends to results of a different nature.
Regarding the question, "What meaning is lacking here?"—this asks what meaning is absent in the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna* such that it is not called a seed. The answer states:

"It lacks the simultaneous existence with its fruit and cannot be perfumed. If that is so, [one might ask] how the seventh consciousness (*manas*), which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), can perfume seeds since it possesses the six conditions.
The explanation says: as stated in the commentary (*śū*).
Regarding the contradiction that arises from the faults of performing what should not be done or failing to do what should be done, some say:

"If there were no internal seeds, then performing wholesome deeds would result in attaining a happy realm, while failing to perform them would result in losing it; since both cases would thus entail faults, how could there be attainment or loss in the absence of internal seeds?

Alternatively, one might perform wholesome deeds and yet lose the realm, or fail to perform them and yet attain the fruit, because of the absence of seeds; this would then contradict [the law of karma]."
It is not necessarily the case that this contradicts the sacred teachings; rather, it explains external seeds.

This refers to cases where something is produced but does not bear fruit—such as when there is a seed but no sprout, or a sprout but no earing—and cases where something is obtained without being produced—such as wild oats (*tīra*) and barnyard grass (*pāṭala*), which resemble grain yet flourish without being sown, or like the growth of mushrooms (*śuṅgavera*) from charcoal. It is because of these [factors] that [the contradiction does not arise].
Since these external seeds are not actual seeds, internal phenomena serve as their actual seeds; the heavens, the earth, space, and so forth should all be understood according to this principle.

In his brief commentary, Vasubandhu explains that only withered and perished things are termed "drawing causes" (*ākṣepa-hetu*). As for the extensive explanation by Asvabhāva, Vasubandhu considers only that which is withered and lost to be the drawing cause.

It is abbreviated because it refers to those born through transformation (*upapāduka*); the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is not distinguished from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth, as it pervades all four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), and is therefore extensive.

As for the claim that the absence of nature reaches only the cause because of its proximity or distance, since it is stated that "it gives rise to the manifest consciousnesses (*vijñapti*) and so forth," we know that this refers to what has already arisen.
This refers to the stage of maturation (*vipāka*).

It also serves to exclude those types of consciousness that reach this stage as being identical to what follows; it excludes [the possibility] that the wholesome and defiled are the same as the three natures below.
Regarding that, it is explained: "If maturation were wholesome or defiled, the processes of transmigration and cessation would not be possible. Furthermore, it says: "It should..."
