Therefore, it was asked: "What is the meaning of the mutual functioning of the five faculties? The answer is that there are many meanings. First, one says that while the faculty and the object are fixed, consciousness is not;
for example, whatever consciousness is produced by the single faculty of the eye, it perceives only green. Second, one says that while the object and consciousness are fixed, the faculty is not;
for example, whatever faculty the visual consciousness relies upon, it perceives only green. Third, one says that while the faculty and consciousness are fixed, the object is not.
"Indeterminate" means that, for example, the eye faculty gives rise only to visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) with respect to various objects.

Fourth, "the faculties are determinate while the consciousnesses and objects are indeterminate" means that, for example, whichever consciousness arises from the eye faculty and whichever object it encounters, it is simply termed "visual consciousness.

Although the latter two interpretations are correct, even though there may be confusion regarding the separation or conjunction of faculties and objects, this is reconciled as in the commentary (*śāstra*). However, the first two meanings [of the fourth point] accord with the treatise (*śāstra*).

Regarding the contradiction, the first interpretation states that if the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) were fixed, it would contradict the treatise’s statement that a single sense organ produces consciousness that takes all objects as its conditions;
furthermore, it says that the eye-organ might produce ear-consciousness and so forth—if consciousness is called "ear[-consciousness]," how can one say it follows the [nature of the] organ?

The second interpretation states that while the object and consciousness are fixed, the organ is not fixed. If this were the case, then even in the state of mastery (*vaśitā*), it would still be called "following the object," just as in the examples provided.

What treatise states that this is based on a question regarding those who have not yet attained mastery? Even if the third interpretation is granted, once the sense-faculties and consciousnesses are established, how can they be said to function interchangeably?

The answer is: it is called "interchangeable function" when one faculty perceives the object of another, and another faculty perceives its own object; it does not mean that by producing the consciousness of another, one attains interchangeable function.
There is further a different meaning, as explained in the *Dīpa* commentary on the *Yuanjue shuyao*.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that there are three types of bodily emanations (the following section is identical to the *Mishan*, so it is now omitted).

Regarding the "six objects of no meaning": "meaning" (*artha*) refers to the objective sphere, namely the six sense-objects. Sentient beings give rise to pervasive conceptual attachment (*parikalpita*) toward these;

because the objects are not real, they are called "objects of no meaning. If this is so, the same should apply to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); why then does the text not say that the four [elements] are also "of no meaning"?

Answer: Regarding that [explanation], it refers to the *pratyaya* (conditioning factors). If one takes these as the objective field (*viṣaya*), they would all be subsumed under the sense-object of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*), which would lead to the fault of [all of them] being able to produce [consciousness]. Therefore, they are excluded.

Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that "the aspect of activity (*ākāra*) is the function": if one asks what distinguishes this from the previous interpretation, the answer is that the previous interpretation... [refers to] the conditioning factors.
Regarding the statement that "the two—the seeing-condition and the appearance-condition—are each distinct in their initial cognition, yet the essence of subsequent comprehension is one;

thus the object is divided into two while the function is identical to the essence," this explains the objects of cognition. That is to say, the eighteen *dhātus* in their causal state are each [distinct].

By how many aspects of the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) are they apprehended? Because the meaning is not fixed, it is said that they are apprehended "according to what is appropriate. Regarding the statement "five have three":

this means that the five objects (*viṣaya*) are perceived by three consciousnesses, namely five, six, and eight. Regarding the statement "six have two": this means that each of the six sense organs (*indriya*) is perceived by two consciousnesses;

specifically, the five material organs are the objects of the sixth and eighth [consciousnesses], while the single mental organ (*manas-indriya*) is the object of the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses].

Because the eighth consciousness is subsumed under the mental faculty (*manas*), it is said that "six" refers to the six consciousness-elements, which are objects of perception for the sixth consciousness alone.
Regarding "one is indeterminate," this means that the *dharmadhātu* may be perceived by five consciousnesses, or by six or eight;

since unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are perceived by the sixth consciousness alone, it is called "indeterminate. Question: Within the causal state, does the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) also perceive the ten [realms]?

Regarding the eight constituents (*dhātu*), why is it said here that five [of them] are "equal" (*sama*) and so forth? The answer is: because they are equal, indeterminate, and existent, they are not mentioned.

Regarding the seventh [constituent], the term "equal" refers to the analytical discernment (*vibhāga*); when one reaches the fruit of Buddhahood, all eight consciousnesses are able to take the eighteen constituents as their objects; thus, it is called "equal discernment. Question:
Does the wisdom of accomplishing what was to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object? Answer: Even if it does not take the unconditioned as its object...
They are also able to take the dharma-realm as their object.
Regarding the verse on their basis, it was stated previously: "Five, four, six, two, seven, eight, one;
all rely [on the same], and for the leading causes, each increases by two."

As in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* and other texts (the following sections—the thirteen gates on the wholesome, twelve gates on the unwholesome, and fourteen gates on the indeterminate—are entirely identical to those cited in the *Biji*, and are therefore omitted here).
Regarding the statement that the five consciousnesses initiate karma through the concomitant mind (*anuvartaka-citta*):

this refers to the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), whether wholesome or defiled, which is termed the "turning mind" (*pravartaka-citta*) because it possesses the capacity for volitional activity and is thus called the "initiator of karma.
Since the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, arise in dependence upon the sixth mental consciousness, they are said to "initiate karma through the concomitant mind."
Regarding the statement that hearing sound within meditative concentration occurs due to two causes: first, the mental consciousness that discerns the object of concentration;

second, the mental consciousness that has various objects. Here, hearing sound within this concentration simultaneously with the ear constitutes the mental consciousness with various objects, which corresponds to the second cause.
The intention of this master is that when the mind and the ear share the same object, [the hearing of sound] necessarily [occurs].
Because their natures are different, it is not admitted that the five [sensory consciousnesses] and the three [mental consciousnesses] are determined to be simultaneous;

the mental consciousness should be understood accordingly. Alternatively, where there are four, three, or many, and one, two, or few, the former explanation refers to the equality, continuity (*nisyanda*), and suddenness (*ābhoga*) among the five sensory consciousnesses—whether they are more or less numerous—while this present explanation refers to the variation in number within those states of continuity and suddenness among the five sensory consciousnesses.
This is the general purport of these two interpretations.
If one were to follow exclusively the intention of the former master, this would merely describe his view that the five [consciousnesses] do not coexist;
it would not establish anything distinct from what is explained by contrasting them with the latter view that the three natures coexist.

Regarding the phrase "the ear-consciousness arises suddenly," etc., one asks: if the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arising within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) produces a mind of seeking (*paryeṣaka*), how could it not be included in the aforementioned [category of indeterminate]?

What prevents it from being so? Furthermore, if "sudden" (*tadātva*) can be understood as having a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*), then the answer is: the intention is that while the ear-consciousness takes hold of objects in a state of distraction (*vikṣipta*), it cannot serve as an example for what occurs in concentration.

One might object: the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that these three types of minds are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); therefore, the seeking mind in concentration must be subsumed under the wholesome nature, and since the ear-consciousness is induced by concentration, it too must be wholesome.
One should respond according to what induces [the state], rather than answering that it is non-neutral (*avyākṛta*). The inducing mental consciousness exists in a state of meditative concentration;
although the ear-consciousness does not follow what is grasped by concentration, even though the inducing mind is wholesome, what prevents it from being termed "non-neutral" when it arises suddenly?

Although this is not a direct proof (*sādhana*), it is cited as a supporting argument (*upapatti*) by the former master; however, because the former master did not cite this specific passage, it is said to be "not a proof.

Regarding the statement that the two vehicles [attain] up to [the stage of] *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana* but not the other four, some explain: "The Sarvāstivādins and others do not allow for the simultaneous arising of two consciousnesses;

therefore, only one arises. This reasoning is incorrect, for they likewise do not allow for the simultaneous arising of the ear-consciousness and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which would imply that [the latter] should not exist.

Because of this awareness, we know that in the case of those of the two vehicles, the five consciousnesses are definitely inferior; among them, only the ear-consciousness arises during meditative concentration.
For Bodhisattvas, they are definitely superior, as all five consciousnesses arise together.

If one asks: "If the first three minds of the five scattered [consciousnesses] can be wholesome, then since these initial three minds are in a state of concentration and are of a wholesome nature, should they not be considered defiled? [This would be a contradiction.]

Regarding how a pure mind can be described as "sudden" (*tatra-kṣaṇika*) and so forth, the [opponent] asks: "If that were the case, then the Buddha’s sudden minds and so forth would not be wholesome. [The respondent] replies:

"This cannot serve as a precedent; for while the Buddha’s sudden minds and so forth are admitted to be established by way of conventional designation (*prajñapti*), how could these three minds be merely conventional?
From this, one should understand that if it is a determinate mind, its subsequent discernment of an object—whether knowing it as defiled or knowing it as pure—is [the function of the mind]."

Regarding the defiled and pure minds within this meditative concentration (*samādhi*): although the object and subject have not yet been definitively determined therein, because the mind prior to the concentration is virtuous, even if a seeking (*vitarka*) should arise, it is still termed "virtuous.
Furthermore, since the mind prior to the concentration is of the nature of an outflow (*niṣyanda*), there is no logical error in explaining that sudden seeking is also [virtuous].
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the five consciousnesses [cease] because there is subsequently no vitarka or vicāra": from the first dhyāna downwards, vitarka and vicāra may exist;

however, among the eight dhyānas, the latter seven are without vitarka and vicāra. As stated in the seventh fascicle: "This indicates that [consciousness] mostly arises by means of them, rather than asserting that it is associated with them.
Thus, one knows that within the meditative absorptions, auditory consciousness does not necessarily depend upon vitarka and vicāra.
Furthermore, regarding the question of whether the desire realm can serve as the inducer [of higher states], the intent of this inquiry is as follows:

If it is accepted that the ear-consciousness of the desire realm is induced by a mind free from vitarka and vicāra belonging to the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), then when the three consciousnesses arise from the second dhyāna and above, they should likewise be induced by a mind free from vitarka and vicāra belonging to those higher stages themselves;
why then must one rely on the vitarka and vicāra of a lower stage?
Answer: When one reaches the subsequent stage, it is no longer induced by vitarka and vicāra;

thus, in the two higher meditative attainments (*dhyāna*), the initial arising of the three consciousnesses may borrow vitarka and vicāra from the lower stages, whereas in the subsequent stage, they arise even without borrowing the three consciousnesses. Question: Since this is the initial arising of the ear-consciousness while in meditative concentration, why is there no vitarka and vicāra?
Answer: Because of the distinction between concentration and distraction, as explained in the seventh fascicle.

Regarding the question of how these natures can reach a state of non-contradiction: if the five consciousnesses are predominantly wholesome or unwholesome, they can only be induced by wholesome or unwholesome consciousness;
how then can the indeterminate mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) coexist with the five wholesome or unwholesome consciousnesses without contradiction? Answer:

When the mental consciousness first induces wholesome or unwholesome states, the five consciousnesses and the five wholesome or unwholesome factors must necessarily focus their attention on the inducing mind and its fivefold nature. Thus, there is no contradiction.

After the flow of equality has been attained, there is no partiality regarding the five [objects]; thus, it is possible for them to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), as this does not contradict their distinct natures from the five [sensory] consciousnesses. Regarding the question of how the five consciousnesses can be indeterminate from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward—since from the eighth stage and above, they are purely untainted (*anāsrava*)—it is as follows: [The five consciousnesses] are indeterminate because they are associated with the mental factors of equanimity and non-conceptualization; furthermore, since they do not engage in the discrimination of objects, they are categorized as indeterminate.

Although these consciousnesses are untainted from the eighth stage upward, they are designated as "indeterminate" in the sense that they lack the specific moral quality of being wholesome or unwholesome, functioning instead in a state of neutrality. This designation is consistent with the principle that the five sensory consciousnesses, by their very nature, are indeterminate. Thus, even though they are untainted, their functional mode remains indeterminate. Regarding the objection that if they are untainted, they cannot be indeterminate: while it is true that from the eighth stage upward all mental states are untainted, the term "indeterminate" here refers specifically to the absence of karmic maturation (*vipāka*) and the lack of engagement in the three types of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Therefore, there is no contradiction in classifying these untainted consciousnesses as indeterminate. This classification is established based on their mode of operation rather than their ontological status as untainted phenomena. Consequently, the five consciousnesses can indeed function as indeterminate from the eighth stage upward.
When the five consciousnesses arise, they must necessarily be accompanied by the sixth; how then can they be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?

The answer is that this refers to the *ābhoga* (sudden) mind, where the five consciousnesses may indeed be indeterminate, unlike the mind of outflow (*nisyanda-citta*), such as when hearing sounds within meditative concentration.

Regarding the phrase "The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) is itself cultivation (*bhāvanā*)," etc.: the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done is that which is accomplished through the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Furthermore, since the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done possesses a nature associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is the wisdom of cultivation; or, it may include both the wisdoms of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*).

Because these three functions are subsumed within a single wisdom of cultivation, it is now described as "that which is accomplished. The term "accomplished" (*sādhya*) is broad in its application and all-encompassing. [Question: ...
Now, regarding this scriptural proof that among the five consciousnesses there is "preparatory wholesome" (prāyogika-kuśala) [wisdom], it is asked:
since the Tathāgata’s wisdom lacks preparatory effort (prayoga), for what purpose is it induced? The answer is: This wisdom is not something that arises without functional effort;
rather, it is indeed induced by the cultivation of meditative reflection (bhāvanā). Therefore, it is called "preparatory. If this is so, why is it said that the Buddha has no preparatory effort?
Yājñavalkya further did not advance the argument that there is no preparatory effort (*prayoga*), nor did he state that the Tathāgata lacks preparatory effort regarding wholesome states.

The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that even up to the "obscured" (*nivṛta*) [state], the craving (*tṛṣṇā*) that moistens rebirth, although it is obscured, must necessarily not be associated with the five [sensory] consciousnesses when directed toward a place of rebirth;
however, since there exists an obscured mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) at other times, it is capable of projecting all [karmic results].
It covers the five consciousnesses.

Alternatively, that which is subsumed under the category of innate minds up to the ripening (*vipāka*) mind refers to such things as the transformations produced by gods, nāgas, ghosts, and so forth in the desire realm;

these are merely transformations subsumed under innate minds and mental factors, not actual transformations. If they were actual transformations, they would involve [the application of] supernormal power (*abhijñā*).

Regarding the inclusion [of the superknowledges] within the [five] practices: in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are no artisanal skills; everything in that realm is produced through one's own transformation and does not require craftsmanship. [Question:
Since the superknowledge of craftsmanship (*śilpa-abhijñā*) consists of physical and vocal dexterity, how could it be absent there? [Answer: It exists within the First Dhyāna.

Because of vitarka and vicāra, although speech is also produced, it is not mentioned because it is minimal. Furthermore, when it is said that [the fourth dhyāna] lacks [bodily] craftsmanship, this does not mean there is no speech.

As for the four consciousnesses taking postures (īryāpatha) as their object and the five consciousnesses taking craftsmanship as their object: since postures consist of the four sensory objects (viṣaya), there is no ear-consciousness [therein].

Skillful mastery of language also possesses sound; however, what is here termed "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to these paths of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).

In reality, both are of a single kind and are all termed "paths" (*gati*) or "spheres" (*sthāna*); yet, because the meaning of "wandering and treading" is more prominent in the case of deportment, it is specifically referred to as a "path."
That which is blue is not "non-non-blue"; excluding blue itself, everything else is termed "non-non-blue. Because there are many varieties of "non-non-blue," it is called "non-non-blue.
Within this context, the expansion up to "not different" refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts that increase the erroneous interpretations, specifically the fifty-third [chapter].
If one opens up the five views while excluding wrong resolve, there are fifty-five; however, this treatise excludes wrong resolve and combines it with the five views, thus resulting in fifty-one.
Furthermore, the word "etc. (ādi) is stated to include the remaining two categories. At the beginning of the seventh fascicle, in explaining the name "indeterminate" (aniyata), it says: "There is..."

There are three reasons: first, because [the mental factors] such as the wholesome and the defiled are all indeterminate; second, because they do not necessarily pervade the mind like contact (*sparśa*) and so forth;
and third, because they do not necessarily pervade the ground like desire (*chanda*) and so forth. Here, by citing the first reason, the other two are implied.

Regarding that which is the basis for the accumulation of form and the basis for the accumulation of the formless: the five faculties are form, and they are the basis for the accumulation of the five consciousnesses; the mind-faculty is formless, and it is the basis for the accumulation of mental consciousness.

Because they are the bases for the accumulation of body and mind, they are called "accumulation" (*caya*). Alternatively, "accumulation" refers to the fact that this basis is formed by the integration of many factors:

the aggregate of form consists of the five faculties, while the aggregate of consciousness consists of the mind-faculty. Thus, because these are integrated from many dharmas, they are called "accumulation."

One explanation states: "If the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha*) are [included], while the faculty of feeling (*vedanā*) is broad and the faculties [of sorrow and suffering] are narrow"—this refers to the first interpretation.

This is because both the faculty of sorrow and the faculty of suffering pertain equally to both the projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and the projected (*ākṣipta*) [factors]. Thus, both sorrow and suffering are included within the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Although the treatise explains three types of feeling, it includes sorrow here as well because it is categorized under suffering. Regarding the statement that "feeling is broad while the faculties are narrow": "feeling" (*vedanā*) is defined as the experience of objects.

The term "root" (*indriya*) refers to that which produces a predominant effect; while that which is a root must necessarily be capable of experiencing (*anubhava*), that which is experience does not necessarily produce [a predominant effect].

Thus, there is a discussion regarding their relative breadth and narrowness. Speaking from the broader perspective, it is said that even painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*) is induced by the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the second point, concerning the statement that "the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) reaches the conventional designation of being outflow-free (anāsrava)," this interpretation further contains two meanings:

First, it is said that because the faculty of suffering is induced by the outflow-free [path], it is conventionally designated as outflow-free; however, this is not the case for the faculty of grief (daurmanasya), and thus it is not outflow-free.

Second, it is said that because the faculty of suffering can coexist with outflow-free wisdom, it is conventionally designated as outflow-free; whereas grief certainly does not coexist [with such wisdom], as in cases such as giving away one's head or eyes.

If they are mutually manifest according to what is appropriate, the seven material faculties and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), since they pertain to non-arising, are common to both those abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya) and those abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

This is because the reflection [of these] also manifests as being common to those abandoned by seeing, as in the case of the Unconscious Heaven (asaṃjñisattva) and others who, having entered the path of seeing and above, will certainly not give rise [to them] again.

Regarding the five faculties such as faith (śraddhā), when considered in terms of their conditions and bondage, they are called "abandoned by cultivation"; the reflection [of these] also manifests as being common to both conditions and bondage, as are the material faculties and the life-faculty.
The five feelings and the mind-faculty should be understood by analogy.

Regarding the statement that "one part of the twelve [faculties] is common to the non-abandonable (*aprahātavya*) and so forth": the former six refer to the fourteen faculties abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*), excluding the seven material faculties and the life-faculty;
the latter six refer to the remaining eight, excluding the two untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Regarding the phrase "because it conforms to and inclines toward the dharma of non-interruption": conforming to and inclining toward [the path] applies to both sorrow and suffering;

alternatively, "conforming" refers to suffering, while "inclining" refers to the capacity to lead toward [liberation], as it can lead to the untainted (anāsrava) through the feeling of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Applying this principle to what the treatise does not explicitly state:

the intention here is that since the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) can lead toward non-abandonment (*aprahāṇa*), it should also be able to induce the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), and thus be categorized as outflow-free.

Why, then, is the faculty of sorrow not included among the outflow-free? Therefore, the next explanation says: it is not outflow-free because its induction is unlike that of suffering (*duḥkha*); thus, it is not outflow-free.
Among the six that cannot be described [as being exclusively of one type], the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) has not yet attained the untainted (*anāsrava*);

it is not called "non-abandonable" (*aprahātavya*), because its feeling (*vedanā*) permeates both the untainted and the abandonable. Thus, when included within the preceding six, they are considered collectively as twenty-two.

Among these, seven are material (*rūpin*), and the life-faculty permeates only the abandonable by insight (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), but not the non-abandonable. The two untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) permeate only the non-abandonable, but not the abandonable by insight.

The cultivation of the six faculties, such as faith and so forth, pertains exclusively to cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and does not pertain to what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*). Furthermore, the five feelings (*vedanā*) and the mind-faculty (*manas*) pertain to both seeing and cultivation;

this is not a question [of contradiction]. If the Tathāgata possesses the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvita-indriya*), why is it said that it does not pertain to what is non-abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?

The answer is: the statement here that it "pertains to what is non-abandoned" is spoken in reference to the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Although the material life-faculty and so forth in a Buddha are termed "non-abandoned," those possessed by the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*) are indeed [abandoned].
Because they are phenomena subject to outflows (*sāsrava*) and are capable of being abandoned, it is said that form, life-force, and so forth are not called "non-abandonable.
If it were the case that greed, hatred, delusion, up to pride could also be so [regarded], this follows from the former masters.

If you do not allow that there is the sensation of suffering within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), then since the three—greed, hatred, and so forth—arise spontaneously (*svarasena*) and pertain to all five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*), they would necessarily be associated with suffering even when present therein.
Since mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can be associated with the unwholesome (*akuśala*), it is likewise possible for pride (*māna*) to be accompanied by mental grief (*daurmanasya*).

These [factors] may be said to be obtainable through the three feelings (*vedanā*). Furthermore, those [defilements] such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) that arise spontaneously (*svarasena*) are not associated with the five [sensory] consciousnesses, nor are they unwholesome.
Since it is stated that they are obtainable through the three feelings, one knows that mental consciousness can indeed be associated with physical pain (*duḥkha*). Thus...
This refers to the mental faculty (*manas*) in its entirety.

Regarding the statement that it cannot be "concordant" (*niṣyanda*) with the unwholesome and so forth: this concerns the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) induced during the state of distraction (*vikṣipta*), which must necessarily be of the same nature as the inducing mental faculty (*manas*).

This is because, for example, in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the mental faculty and the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) hearing a sound are not of the same nature. [Question: If...

If it is the case that in the state of dispersion (*vikṣipta*), the inducing and the induced must necessarily be of the same nature, why was it previously stated that among the five consciousnesses, when the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) operate simultaneously, the mental faculty (*manas*) follows its predominant focus and shares the same nature as them, whereas when there is no such predominant focus, it is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*)?
Since this is so, how can the five consciousnesses—which may lack a predominant focus and be indeterminate—be of the same nature as the mental faculty? Answer: First, regarding the induction...

Since the nature of the eye and other [faculties] must necessarily remain the same across multiple moments, and because the subsequent mental consciousness follows by focusing on one object or may be of an indeterminate nature,
the visual and other consciousnesses must necessarily be of the same nature as the inducing mental consciousness.

Regarding the fifty-seventh [point], "There is also joy and bliss, etc.": Question: If the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) exists in the stage of *anāgamya* (the threshold), why is joy not established there in the same way as it is in the first *dhyāna* stage?
Answer: Because the joy associated with that concentration is subject to fluctuation.
Question: What scriptural authority (*āgama*) serves as proof for the existence of joy in that stage? Answer: As the Blessed One said: "In this way, O Bhikṣu, having become detached from birth..."
Joy and bliss moisten his body, pervading it completely, flowing through it with such satisfaction that not even the slightest part remains unfulfilled or unsatisfied;
this is called the joy and bliss born of seclusion. Herein, the former gate describes the stage of *anāgamya* (the threshold), while the latter gate describes the fundamental stage (*maula*).
Question: How many faculties (*indriya*) are obtainable in the level of the first dhyāna? Answer: There are eighteen, excluding the male and female faculties.

Suffering (*duḥkha*) is sorrow (*daurmanasya*). However, when that [text] cites a sūtra as a corroborating proof stating that "the words 'joy' (*prīti*) and 'bliss' (*sukha*) [exist] in both the fundamental (*maula*) and preparatory (*sāmantaka*) [attainments], and they thoroughly moisten [the body]," this refers exclusively to the fundamental [attainments].
Regarding the sequence in which suffering and sorrow arise in succession, after the first arising from the eighth [level], the next six [levels] arise in turn.
Question: Since it is said that suffering (*duḥkha*) and sorrow (*daurmanasya*) continue in succession, how can it be that, according to his [the teacher’s] intention, there is only sorrow?
Answer: This master’s intention is to say that while suffering pertains to the other faculties (*indriya*), sorrow pertains only to the mental faculty (*manas*);

thus, there is no contradiction. Question: The *Śāstra* states that there is a succession of suffering and sorrow born of maturation (*vipākaja*). Since sorrow is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), how can it be of the nature of maturation?

The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* states that the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). This is based on the fact that it is obscured (*nivṛta*) yet does not obstruct the arising of maturation (*vipākaja*). How is this known?

It is known because remorse (*kaukṛtya*), which is associated with grief, does not extend to the obscured [neutral] state. Furthermore, there is another interpretation which says: "This is not necessarily so according to principle.
When the treatise speaks of "arising from maturation," it means it arises from the eighth consciousness, the true maturation (*vipāka*). Therefore, it is so named.
Although there are two interpretations regarding the fact that maturation (*vipāka*) is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the former explanation is superior. The *Śāstra* states:
"If his intention is that it is solely suffering (*duḥkha*), why does he say 'sorrow' (*daurmanasya')? This is an objection directed at the latter master.
However, regarding the point that these are not identical to the "collective retribution" (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*) and so forth:

if one were to say that because there is suffering and mental distress (*daurmanasya*), the sixth consciousness lacks equanimity (*upekṣā*), then it would follow that the eighth [consciousness] also does not coexist with equanimity, as it is a place of extreme suffering and its karma is not light. From this, the following interpretation is reached:

the substance of the eighth *gati* (destiny) is also the primary agent of retribution; therefore, it cannot be associated with suffering, for if it were associated with suffering, it would contradict the nature of a "wholesome destiny" (*sugati*). Thus, the six consciousnesses do not [coexist with it].
However, this cannot be taken as a general rule.

Regarding the extensive explanation in the *Yogācārabhūmi* as cited previously, its underlying intent is to prove that since it states "the mental level (*manobhūmi*) is associated with all faculties," one knows that the mental level possesses painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*).
The former master’s defense was that the three faculties on the mental level are actually *daurmanasya* (mental grief) and not [painful sensation] associated with the body.

The clarification regarding the three feelings (vedanā) states that they are subsumed under the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya), because in reality they consist solely of mental grief (daurmanasya). Consequently, the Treatise states that the innate view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta) and is not subsumed under the faculty of grief.

Furthermore, the Treatise asserts that the faculty of grief is not indeterminate; according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicles 57 and 58), the faculties are either exclusively wholesome (kuśala), unwholesome (akuśala), or indeterminate.
That which has the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) as its object refers to the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).

Furthermore, it says that the five faculties have the wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), and indeterminate as their objects; these refer to the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the mental faculty (*manas*).
Furthermore, it says that one faculty is named "wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate"; this refers to the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*).
Furthermore, it is said that five faculties are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and have indeterminacy as their meaning; these are the faculties of nose, tongue, body, and the two sexual organs.

Furthermore, it is said that two faculties are indeterminate with respect to both the wholesome and the unwholesome; these are the faculties of eye and ear. This is because visible form and sound, in terms of their manifestation (*vijñapti*), pertain to all three natures.
It does not mention the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because the life-faculty pertains to the seeds and lacks the sense of being an object (*viṣaya*); therefore, it is not included here.

Regarding what was said: the eight kinds of present and seeds that are cited are all established; that is, by taking the eight present [factors] as the life-force (*jīvita*) and the seeds as the root, they are combined and termed the "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*).
Thus, both the present and the seeds are established. Since this refers exclusively to the faculties (*indriya*), there is no contradiction in not mentioning the objects (*viṣaya*).

Regarding the question of whether the five faculties, such as faith, persist until the severance or non-severance of the roots of goodness: if one says they are severed, how can that be established in the present? Why does the Sūtra state:
"The roots of goodness are severed through the power of causes at the time of birth in hell; they are severed through the power of conditions at the time of death in hell"?
The answer is that the claim of their non-establishment refers to the long duration [of suffering]. At the very moment of initial birth in hell, the suffering is not yet complete.
Therefore, when one is about to die in the hells, suffering has already ceased; thus, although wholesome states may still be manifesting, they are not mentioned in brief.
As for the opponent’s defense that "if one reaches a state free from suffering, [the eighth consciousness] is definitely established," their intention in defending this is as follows:

if the five sense-consciousnesses were to continue, then the suffering associated with them could serve as the eighth [consciousness]. However, since mental distress (*daurmanasya*) does not enter into the five sense-consciousnesses, once the five have been severed, suffering is no longer present, and therefore [the eighth consciousness] is not definitively established.
Taking the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) as the eighth.

Furthermore, regarding the objection that "if this were so, it would extend to the continuity [of consciousness]," the difficulty is raised: since suffering (*duḥkha*) is already established as being grief, why is it necessary to abandon it?

If they offer the defense that "suffering exists because the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) are continuous, whereas grief does not exist because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is intermittent," the next objection follows.

It is said that there is no other distinct factor capable of causing the continuity of the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) that have been induced, while simultaneously causing the inducing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to be interrupted.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because the mind is easily aroused by sensation," this refers to the defense offered by that teacher, who claims that within the mental consciousness, because [sensation] exists...

Because equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is intermittent, it cannot be argued that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which possesses such interruptions, can project the continuity of the five [sense-consciousnesses] once they have been interrupted.

Furthermore, one may raise the objection that in the hells there is no equanimity, because in a place of extreme suffering, equanimity—which is distinct from the feeling of sorrow (*daurmanasya*)—cannot arise due to the impossibility of any change. This would be the case unless it were a place of non-extreme suffering.

Question: Just as it is permissible for the faint and weak mind at the moment of first emerging from meditative absorption to undergo the transformation of arising and ceasing within the upper and lower realms of birth and death, and thus give rise to equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), how can the former master’s position—that one cannot attain equanimity while remaining in hell—be maintained? Answer:

This objection is raised because even according to the former master’s view, it is admitted that equanimity can arise at the final stage of the state of sorrow (*daurmanasya*); therefore, this objection is not based on the actual reality of the matter.
If they were to argue that [the faculty of grief] must necessarily continue until later, the previous objection asks: "How could there be the faculty of grief during the stupor of death and rebirth?
Therefore, it is now established that grief is certainly continuous based on whether the arising of the mental consciousness has or has not been severed.

Regarding the response that "there being [feeling] up to the point of non-existence is not obstructive," there are two interpretations here; the latter interpretation is superior. As for the former interpretation:

if it is claimed that the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) can arise at the final stage of hatred, then it would follow that the feeling of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*) in hell must also have equanimity at its final stage.

If that were so, then the feeling of grief (*daurmanasya-vedanā*) should likewise not be absent there; yet even this intermediate state of equanimity is not free from the pressure of the feeling of grief.

Why is it not the case that there is suffering? Because even for a brief moment, [suffering] ought to arise. Furthermore, since anger toward an object that accords with one's desires is still accompanied by joy and pleasure, why would it be accompanied by equanimity alone?
Therefore, one cannot use the final stage of anger as an example. Alternatively, the previous explanation may also be valid.

If that is so, and you admit that equanimity exists, why does sorrow not exist as well? The answer is: because in the preceding state, the extreme suffering of hell is devoid of discrimination. Only...

It may be that there is equanimity (*upekṣā*) but not sorrow (*daurmanasya*), just as after the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*) experienced by the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), equanimity arises rather than the sensation of sorrow.

Furthermore, at the conclusion of the most intense non-conceptual mental action (*manaskarma*) of the third dhyāna, there may be the sensation of equanimity, but there can certainly be no joy (*prīti*).
A later commentary states: "The end of extreme suffering may not be the same as the end of extreme pleasure; yet equanimity still arises."
Yaśas immediately replied: "In the state of extreme suffering, if mental suffering is severed, one necessarily enters a state of fainting;
this is precisely the absence of mind, and thus there is no neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Therefore, it cannot be objected that the third dhyāna lacks pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*);
in the end, both interpretations are equal."
Alternatively, that [first] master explains it generally by including the other three realms (*gati*) among those with mixed experiences;
excluding the places of extreme suffering in hell, he takes the remaining mild states—namely, those of hungry ghosts (*preta*) and animals (*tiryagyoni*)—as the three realms.

As for the intent of the second master’s later explanation, he says that while hell consists of pure suffering and lacks both types of pleasure, hungry ghosts and animals may possess pleasure that is a result of similar flow (*nisyanda*). Between these two explanations, which is correct?
Since this is so, how can it be said that there is "outflowing pleasure" (*niṣyanda-sukha*) in the hells, where only suffering exists?

It is called "outflowing pleasure" because it is a pleasure similar [to ordinary pleasure]—that is, a light degree of suffering is termed outflowing pleasure. This previous interpretation is also acceptable.

If that is the case, why is it not called "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*)? One cannot call it sorrow because there is no distinct mental factor [of grief] present; yet, how could it be called "pleasure"? It cannot be called pleasure either.

If that is so, one might object: "Since it is clearly known that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is accompanied by joy (*saumanasya*), it follows that the faculty of satisfaction (*saumanasyendriya*) possesses pleasure (*sukha*);
or, according to the system of the three feelings (*trivedanā*), joy itself is designated as pleasure. Why, then, do you not admit that there is pleasure in those [heavens]?
This question and answer should be explained below, following the commentary on the preceding section.

This refers to the Mahāsāṃghika school’s position that suffering and pleasure continue in succession; since the various consciousnesses of that school arise simultaneously, mental joy and the five types of physical pain continue in succession.

Regarding the Sthavira school’s "nine minds," their bhavaṅga-consciousness is identical to the eighth consciousness of the Mahāyāna, hence it is called "ripening" (vipāka) and "immediate" (anantara), and so forth.
Alternatively, regarding the Mahīśāsaka school, this [text] provides a comprehensive reconciliation of both positions.
[The] Text:

Question: Regarding the statement that those who do not follow the words of others [are reborn in hell], that treatise explains that for those sentient beings born in the hells, suffering and sorrow continue in succession.

This is precisely what is meant by the phrase "following the principle of the turning wheel" (*anuvartana-yukti*). That treatise also states that in other realms of existence (*gati*), suffering and sorrow likewise continue in succession.

Why does he not follow the other’s words? The underlying intent of the answer is this: although the mental distress of other realms can truly be called "love" (*tṛṣṇā*), because it is also a form of mental oppression despite being accompanied by suffering, it is metaphorically designated as "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*).

Regarding "joy and bliss born of seclusion" (*vivekaja-prītisukha*): "seclusion" refers to being free from the defilement of desire, which is termed the "seclusion" of the category of birth in the desire realm; the same applies to the "seclusion" of birth in the first dhyāna and so forth.
Regarding "the remaining two pervade all": this refers to the two feelings other than equanimity (*upekṣā*), namely suffering (*duḥkha*) and pleasure (*sukha*).

If one takes the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as an example for this, then while it is accepted that the three dhyānas lack the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), they are not without the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Since the five sense faculties (*indriya*) do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), what prevents the existence [of untainted consciousness there]? One should further challenge this by analogy, saying: "In the three dhyānas, the material sense faculties possess the five consciousnesses;

since those born in the formless realm lack the seeds of matter and the sense faculties, by what means could [untainted consciousness] arise? The answer is: the meditative faculties (*dhyānendriya*) are capable of producing the five consciousnesses.
What prevents the five faculties from having further increase based on the formless attainments as their cause? For example, it is explained at length that they are like a lamp.
As for the statement "because those [lower stages] are excluded due to the superiority of the qualities," among the four dhyānas, the fourth dhyāna possesses the most excellent qualities.
"Victorious" (*jaya*) means "limit" (*koṭi*), or it refers to that which is most preeminent within each respective certainty; thus, it is called a "limit.

Regarding the statement that it is the basis for the qualities of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses: the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is the support for the seeds and manifestations of pure, perfect qualities;
the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) is because it is constantly associated with great compassion and so forth. Furthermore, these two wisdoms are able to manifest both self and others.

The enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and its land are called the "basis of merit. Regarding the statement in the commentary that "the Great Compassionate One dwells [in the heavens]," it means that the Tathāgata’s great compassion relies exclusively upon the fourth dhyāna.
Among the three interpretations presented here regarding the five consciousnesses: the first holds that they exist only in the first dhyāna; the second holds that they pervade all four dhyānas.
Regarding the statement that "only the fourth [explanation] applies to the seventh and eighth consciousnesses," this refers specifically to the third interpretation.

According to the response, the eight uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses exist in all eight stages (*bhūmi*). Thus, the five sensory consciousnesses have four interpretations, while the seventh and eighth have two.

As for the previous statement that "the uncontaminated five consciousnesses rely upon the four stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)," that was a general explanation and does not apply here. Now, based on the meaning, it may be inferred that...

That realm can also be further explained as a single [level], for it merely states that one relies on the four stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) without mentioning that one frequently arises in the fourth dhyāna, nor does it say that this applies to all eight stages; thus, it differs from what follows.

Regarding the initial heading that provides a general exhortation for the arising of the teaching: the *Śāstra* states, "The six categories of mental factors (*caitta*) briefly indicated previously are precisely what was stated in the initial heading.
As for the phrase, "Now one should extensively reveal their specific characteristics," this means that it generally reveals the arising of the exhortations for the six subsequent categories.
Some editions read "generally revealing" (*tongxian*), which is entirely devoid of logical meaning.

First, regarding the question posed by the Sarvāstivādins and others concerning why only five [mental factors] are universal: since the Sarvāstivādins maintain that there are ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), they now ask how one should understand the Mahāyāna teaching that there are only five.

Furthermore, since the Sautrāntikas hold that contact (*sparśa*) and attention (*manasikāra*) are merely nominal (*prajñapti*), they now ask how one should understand the claim that all five are substantially real (*dravyasat*).
This means that just as when one grasps a specific object or location, because there are various factors such as yellow and so forth other than blue, it is said to be "not non-blue.
Regarding the terms "object" (*ālambana*) and "location" (*sthāna*): "object" refers to the general sphere, while further mentioning "location" refers to a particular spot within that general sphere;
thus, the object is broad while the location is narrow.
Those objects that are "desirable" (*abhirati*) refer to objects of the three natures—both *sāsrava* (contaminated) and *anāsrava* (uncontaminated).

Although unwholesome and neutral phenomena are in fact not desirable, they are all termed "desirable" from the perspective of subjective feeling; because they pertain to all three natures, it is not only wholesome phenomena that are called "desirable.
Unwholesome and neutral phenomena are also termed "desirable" when spoken of in relation to subjective feeling.
Regarding the phrase "if one desires external objects in this state," etc., it is like the case of shackles and fetters; these also have two states, which can be understood by analogy.
As for "external objects," such as crops: before hail has fallen, one does not desire it; once it has fallen, one desires it to cease early;
yet, one does not give rise to desire for the loathsome hail itself.

Regarding the four tracks of the Dharma (*dharmapada*): non-attachment and non-hatred constitute the track of ethical discipline (*śīla*); mindfulness constitutes the track of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and meditative concentration constitutes the track of wisdom (*prajñā*).
This should be examined.

The initial arising of a single thought is called "taking that category as its object" because it resembles the *tathatā* (suchness) of the images produced during the preceding preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Question: If the second moment is a "similitude" (*pratibimba*) of the first moment, it should also be called a "similitude. Answer: This is stated provisionally based on the first moment. Question:
Previously it was said that if one has not yet attained the essence (*svabhāva*), one merely receives the name "similitude";

why is it now that even after the essence has been attained, it is still called a "condition-similitude" (*ālambana-pratibimba*)? Answer: In reality, it is the essence; however, this is provisionally named a "similitude" with respect to its initial acquisition.
In the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*, the passage beginning with "There are those who say... and so forth is the exposition of the views of other teachers by that treatise.

The passage beginning with "Because there is recollection at a later time," and so forth, is the Master of the *Nyāyabindu* (Dignāga) stating the correct position (*siddhānta*) to refute the aforementioned opposing teachers.

Regarding the arising of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), it is provisionally termed "definitive discernment" (*nirvedha*) because of the preeminence of the untainted state—just as the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is specifically called definitive discernment due to its conformity with the stages of penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*), whereas the tainted states are not. However, this does not exhaust the full meaning, as the treatise below states:

"The essence of definitive discernment consists of the wisdoms of retribution, scripture, and realization. How could the wisdoms of innate capacity, hearing, or reflection (*śruta-cintā-mayī-prajñā*) ever be categorized as untainted?

Therefore, the statement in this treatise—that the arising of decisive knowledge (*niścaya-jñāna*) universally possesses both the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the tainted (*sāsrava*)—is logically superior.

If one objects, "In that case, it would be like self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) and so forth," the intent of the opponent's challenge is as follows: "Your Mahāyāna now claims to be able to recollect by using prior self-cognition as the cause for the present desire; however, my claim that one can recollect by using a prior momentary cognition as the cause is not [the same]. To this, the response below means: [The opponent says: "If you say that because there is no self, the mind cannot remember, then since there is no self in the Mahāyāna either, how can there be memory? If you say that memory occurs through the power of the continuum (*saṃtati*), then why does memory not arise from the continuum of another person? Furthermore, if you say that memory arises from the power of the continuum, then since all phenomena are momentary, the prior cognition and the subsequent cognition are distinct entities;

how then can the subsequent cognition remember what was previously experienced? To this, the response is: "It is not the case that the prior cognition and the subsequent cognition are entirely different entities. Rather, they are related as cause and effect. Because of this causal relationship, the subsequent cognition can remember what was previously experienced. It is just as when one sees a form, even though the visual consciousness perishes in an instant, the mental consciousness subsequently remembers it. Therefore, memory is established through the continuity of cause and effect within the same stream. Thus, the meaning of the answer is stated.

If the preceding mind possesses both substance and function such that both [self and other] are established as having the prior momentary thought serve as their cause, then my school has no objection to this and allows it to be cited as an example.

As for the phenomenon of objective cognition, if the mind were already self-established prior [to its activity], then since the nature of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) is precisely to be capable of cognition, why would they require this prior [moment]?
Question: For what reason do you now claim that the non-altering of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) is called "concentration" (*samādhi*)? Questioner:

According to the masters of the *Nyāya*, since the mind does not alter its object even for the duration of a single moment, there must necessarily be concentration. Why then do you challenge [the notion of] concentration by asking when the mind does not engage in cognitive apprehension (*ālambana*)?
Answer: If one does not admit that there is concentration during this single moment such that the mind abides upon its object, then this is precisely [the case].
Regarding the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*):
some say that this refers to the mind and its concomitants (*citta-caittas*). Within this Sautrāntika school itself, there are two positions:

first, that all mental factors such as attachment (*lobha*) and so forth are identical in essence to the mind; second, that only feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) are substantially real, while feeling also includes contact (*sparśa*).

The other [afflictions] such as faith and greed have volition (*cetanā*) as their essential nature; they are exclusively mental factors (*caitta*), whereas the Sūtras speak of them as "mind" (*citta*).

What is clarified in this treatise follows the latter interpretation. Since [these factors] such as mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) have volition as their essence and are not identical to mind itself, the following serves as an analogy:
if one were to refute the former position, the thesis established in the analogy would fail to be proven.
Regarding the question of how it is that the five [mental factors] arise together when the mind and mental concomitants share a single object, yet these five take four distinct objects:
the answer is that although the substance of the object is one, it is divided into four according to the different aspects of the perceiving subject.
For example, when one encounters a single form, at the moment of desiring it, it is called "the desirable"; in relation to the act of understanding, it is called "the determined."
The rest should be understood by analogy. Just as there are four [knowledges] when taking a single object such as suffering or emptiness, so it is with respect to the thirty-one phrases;
regarding this, there are several explanations: one says that when many arise it is called "general" (*sāmānya*) and when a single one arises it is called "particular" (*viśeṣa*);
another says that when five arise it is called "general" and the remaining knowledges are called "particular"; yet another says that from one up to five all are [general].
These five are termed "particular" (viśeṣa) and "universal" (sāmānya). The first two [interpretations] explain the correct meaning.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that even when the mind reaches [the level of the Peak of Existence], these do not arise; this principle applies generally to the first master.
If it were otherwise, they would be identical to the Vaibhāṣika school, for whom these five—desire and so forth—are also universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).

Regarding the statement that "even in the case of an outflow (*niṣyanda*), this same situation occurs," the question is: since an outflow arises only after a mind of certainty (*niścaya-citta*), how can it be that there is no superior resolve (*adhimokṣa*)?

The answer is: although a mind of certainty arises, it does not necessarily involve sustained conviction (*dhāraṇā*). For example, when seeing something simultaneously with other mental states, it is not necessarily the case that superior resolve is present at all times;
therefore, these outflows may lack the five [mental factors]. Furthermore, since doubt (*vicikitsā*) is admitted to arise together within a state of outflow, even though...
Question: If there is subsequent determination (*niścaya*), does this not preclude the presence of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*)? Answer:
How can there be a mind of determination without resolute conviction? It is like when, regarding an object such as form or non-form, one generates a determination;

yet, because one has not yet reached a definitive, stabilizing judgment (*pratyavekṣaṇa-dhāraṇa*) concerning whether it is wholesome or unwholesome, or erroneous or correct, the mind of determination is distinct from resolute conviction.

Regarding this master’s position that wisdom associated with the mental consciousness exists [in the Buddha], some say that for this master, wisdom is absent in both the cause and the fruit of the five sensory consciousnesses;
others say it is absent in the cause but present in the fruit. According to the latter master, among the fifteen elements (dhātus), only those that are tainted (sāsrava) exist [for the Buddha].

Since the Buddha lacks the five sensory consciousnesses, the former interpretation is correct. If one were to claim that the five [sensory consciousnesses] possess wisdom in the fruit of Buddhahood, how could the latter master raise the following objection?
Do all five consciousnesses possess the wisdom of accomplishing activities?

This would contradict [the established] definitions. Regarding the term "equipoise-inducing" (*samāhita*): this means that because it is induced by the mind of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "inducing equipoise.
Question: If concentration comes first and tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) follows, it may be called "inducing equipoise"; however, how does this apply to the mental factor of concentration itself?

Question: Why is it called "equipoise-conducive" (*samāhita-nairyāṇika*)? Answer: Although it is not a state of prior and subsequent equality and harmony, it is nonetheless called "conducive" because it necessarily arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, in terms of preparatory application (*prayoga*), since the preceding concentrated mind induces the subsequent state of equipoise, there is no contradiction in principle.
One should understand that the subsequent attainment of equipoise follows this same logic.
Regarding the other three [faculties], they follow this principle: there is no fault in admitting that wisdom exists where hearing and seeing possess supernormal penetration (*abhijñā*).

As for the other three, since they do not function in such a way, how can they be treated as equivalent? Answer: Because the ear perceives distant objects through separation, it is said to possess two types of penetration;
however, the other three perceive their objects through conjunction, so they cannot be called "penetrating. What prevents them from possessing wisdom? There is no such obstacle.

Regarding the phrase "because it reaches the stage of hearing and reflection and belongs to that same category": this explains that the five consciousnesses possess applied wisdom (*prāyogika-prajñā*), because they are produced by that [wisdom] consisting of hearing and reflection;
since they belong to the same category as the hearing and reflection of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they are also termed "applied."
Regarding the statement in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* that [the supernormal power] reaches the point of being uninterrupted:

the intent of that treatise is to say that because the supernormal power of the knowledge of miraculous powers (*ṛddhi-viṣaya-jñāna-abhijñā*) moves the body and takes many external objects as its conditions, it is subsumed under the "knowledge of accomplishing activities" (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Alternatively, the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-abhijñā*) is subsumed under four knowledges, or it is subsumed under the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), because within the body of one who has exhausted the outflows, thirty-four knowledges are fully present. Thus, it is the exhaustion of outflows.

These are subsumed within the four types of knowledge (*jñāna*). If categorized according to the uninterrupted continuity of the dharma-characteristics of nirvāṇa through the condition of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), they are subsumed under the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and the Equality Wisdom (*samatājñāna*).
Excluding the thirty-two [types of] supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), all others are the Wondrous Contemplation Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

That is to say, the supernormal powers of the eye and ear are wisdom associated with the mental faculty (*manas-samprayukta-prajñā*). Now, this commentary reconciles this by stating that there are two types of supernormal powers associated with the eye, ear, and mind; that [previous] account was based on the *Dīrgha-āgama*.

At that time, it is simply called "wonderful observation" (*pratyavekṣaṇā*). It is not because [the mental factors] are distinguished by the modes of joy or sorrow; for some people explain it thus: among the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, greed is characterized by joy and hatred by sorrow; among the eleven wholesome factors, there are distinctions such as preparatory application (*prayoga*) and so on.

However, these five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*) do not possess such modes of activity; therefore, among these [factors], all... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a technical commentary on Abhidharma or Yogācāra psychology. The translation reflects the technical terminology and the flow of the argument as best as possible based on the available fragments.)
Regarding the statement that the "classification by way of gates" does not discuss association with afflictions, wholesome states, and so forth: this interpretation is incorrect.

The intended meaning of this commentary is simply that, because the subsequent section clarifies the internal distinctions within afflictions and wholesome states through their respective oppositions with the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyatālambana*), these are not discussed here;
it is not due to differences such as the application of joy or sorrow.
(From here down to the end of the sixth fascicle of the Commentary has been lost from the currently circulating editions;
if future worthies should find it, they ought to supplement this deficiency in the treasury of the Dharma.)
