Regarding the statement that these are absent in their entirety or for the most part in the two higher realms: among the four indeterminate factors, remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) are entirely absent in the two higher realms;

vitarka and vicāra are mostly absent in those two realms and exist only as a small portion in the first dhyāna; furthermore, within those two realms, they are entirely absent in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and mostly absent in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding the statement that "delighting in what is superior" up to "evil dharmas" is also hatred (*dveṣa*): herein, "superior" and "inferior" are not defined by virtue versus defilement;

rather, they are distinguished according to what is desired and what is loathed. Therefore, it is said that greed (*rāga*) is the evil dharma of delighting in what is superior, while hatred is the evil dharma of loathing what is inferior.
Within the category of what is desired, this also extends to wholesome things; thus, one may have love for the Buddha and also have greed for the cessation of suffering (*nirvāṇa*).
Therefore, among those things that are objects of aversion (*vidūṣaṇā*), it also extends to the defiled, because anger and resentment arise from perceiving others as objects.

Now, regarding the statement that "evil" (*akuśala*) is spoken of in terms of its fruit: one asks, since *kaukṛtya* (remorse) is itself aversion, and it was previously stated in the Mahāyāna that aversion extends across all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*)—as in the case of non-attachment (*alobha*) and so forth—then why is it now said that [remorse] is spoken of in terms of its fruit?

It is because remorse is of the nature of all three natures; however, when it arises from a defiled state, it is designated by the name of its fruit. Thus, although remorse is inherently of the three natures, it is here referred to by the term for its fruit. This is the meaning.
To answer this: since the name "cause" is applied metaphorically to the effect, the cause is described here in terms of the effect, and thus it encompasses all three moral natures (*trisvabhāva*).
If one were not to follow the perspective of the effect, but rather that of "aversion" (*vidūṣaṇā*), then even non-greed, non-hatred, and desire would encompass all three natures;

for although non-greed, non-hatred, and so forth are in essence aversion, they are not termed "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*). This is because the primary intention is to clarify that remorse regarding evil is established based on the effect.
Because it is called by this name:
"This is my evil-side action" means that when one previously did not act, one now gives rise to a mind of aversion toward that [omission] and thus calls it "action";
hence it is said, "This is my evil-side action. Alternatively, it should be stated as "This is my side-evil action," which is the literal phrasing.
This is incorrect.

The common saying that "cuò" (措) and "zuò" (作) are synonyms with different pronunciations is mistaken; "cuò" is pronounced *cāngquè* (倉各反), which is a character meaning error or confusion, and is entirely distinct from "zuò.
This popular claim does not exist in reality; the character in question is actually "cuò," which should be pronounced *zūn fàng* (尊放反).

Alternatively, there is another interpretation regarding the designation [of "aggregates"] upon a collection (*caya*): a "total collection" refers to the body as the totality of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), while a "distinct collection" refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

Regarding the statement that "sloth (*styāna*) obstructs calm abiding (*śamatha*) because it induces sinking (*laya*)," both sloth and drowsiness (*middha*) are combined [into one category] because both are characterized by a state of dullness and sinking.

To speak of "hindering *śamatha*," *śamatha* here carries the meaning of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Because various afflictions arise from factors such as lethargy (*styāna*), they hinder *śamatha*.

Since restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) are coarse and agitated, they are combined as a single hindrance. "Excitation" (*pragraha*) refers to a mode of activity that is lofty and brilliant;
because the mind is agitated by restlessness, wholesome dharmas do not arise, and thus it hinders excitation. "Equanimity" (*upekṣā*) means spontaneous [abiding].
Because when the mind is hesitant regarding the meaning of dwelling in equanimity and tranquility, renunciation (*tyāga*) will certainly not arise; therefore, doubt (*vicikitsā*) is an obstacle.

Regarding the statement "it follows that aggregate to constitute the essence of what is intended": this explains that wholesome and neutral *kaukṛtya* (remorse) and *middha* (torpor) take wholesome and neutral minds and mental factors as their essence;
they are established as a collective aggregate according to the number of those factors present. Within the wholesome, there is necessarily no *praśrabdhi* (pliancy).
It should be understood by analogy that there may also be other wholesome states, as well as indeterminate states such as contact and desire.

When it is said that they are not "indeterminate," this is a general statement; it refers specifically to those [states] whose essence consists of being either defiled or non-defiled, and which encompass both the defiled and the pure types of indeterminate states, and is therefore a general term.
Regarding the third point, from "result" to "the object of mental discourse": Question:

Is this called the "object of mental discourse" (*manojalpa-viṣaya*) because it is an object apprehended by the mind, or is it so called because the expressive words themselves are the objects apprehended by the mind? Or is it because the object expressed by the words is the object of mental discourse?
Answer: Here, we take those words as being produced by the mind; because they are the objects of the mind, they are called the "objects of mental discourse. If [it were] the words...

The explanation of the object (*ālambana*) applies universally to all phenomena; because this [object] does not arise from the activity of the mind, it lacks the sense of cause and effect and is not what is grasped by the mind. Question:
If one says that the object of the mental aspect (*manasikāra*) is called the "object of mental discourse" (*manojalpa-viṣaya*), how does this differ from the second interpretation?

Answer: Although they are identical in terms of breadth and narrowness, this [first interpretation] is based on cause and effect, while that [second interpretation] concerns the relationship between mind and its objects; thus, they differ in their intended meaning.
Regarding the statement that it "also applies to all [objects] because it reaches them all," this text comprehensively reconciles the three preceding interpretations, as each contains this meaning.
Now, concerning the phrase "this object applies to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*"), this likewise summarizes the three preceding interpretations;

however, only the first interpretation derives its name from a metaphor, for its object can indeed apply to all phenomena. As for the latter two interpretations, they take only names and terminology (*nāma-pada*) as their objects.

Thus, it is not that [the term] does not apply to all things; there is no contradiction in the principle that it refers to what is expressed by words. However, among the three previous interpretations, the first explanation is superior.

As for the statement that "a name does not reach itself, just as *nirvāṇa* [does not reach itself]," this also refers to the fact that unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena have no connection whatsoever with names or verbal expressions.
In the *Saṃgrahaṇī*, it is stated that all phenomena are ultimately beyond the reach of words.
If both body and mind reach a state where they are equally permeated by reflection (*cintā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), this implies that both vitarka and vicāra are permeated;

however, within the treatises concerning "abiding" and "non-abiding," these two are both described as being based on non-abiding, and thus are said to be characterized by agitation. The question is: do vitarka and vicāra both permeate reflection and wisdom? Both do.
Question: What is the distinction between these two, tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) and non-tranquility? Answer: They differ in terms of coarseness and subtlety.

You yourself have stated that vitarka is coarse and thus non-tranquil, while vicāra is subtle and thus tranquil. This interpretation is incorrect, for the treatise states that both take tranquility and non-tranquility as their function.

Regarding the statement that "contemplation (*vitarka*) is explained as 'settling' (*sthāpanā*) and so forth," this specific correlation between contemplation and wisdom (*prajñā*) is somewhat difficult to clarify. Why?

For instance, the treatise states that both investigation (*vicāra*) and contemplation (*vitarka*) take a portion of thought (*citta*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence. Now, since settling and non-settling cannot occur simultaneously, how could it be that thought and wisdom are not permitted to coexist?
Furthermore, even when correlating them specifically according to the depth of their inferential analysis, this same objection applies.

Therefore, I take the former interpretation as correct. Furthermore, this commentary states: "Vitarka is coarse and vicāra is subtle; in the treatises, the coarse and the subtle are respectively assigned to vitarka and vicāra.

How could it be that *cetanā* (volition) and *prajñā* (wisdom) are also to be separately assigned? However, because the characteristic of discernment (*pravicaya*) is coarse, it is specifically assigned to wisdom (*prajñā*), rather than assigning *cetanā* and *prajñā* separately to vitarka and vicāra; thus, there is no contradiction with the treatise.

Regarding the question of whether "investigation" (*vitarka*) and "analysis" (*vicāra*) both take volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence, and whether they are both superficial when taking volition as their essence or both profound when taking wisdom as their essence, the answer is: volition is shallow while wisdom is deep;

their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are fixed in this way. However, at the time when investigation arises, volition is predominant and wisdom is weak; therefore, it is said that [the former] is not [profound].

When vitarka (initial inquiry) and vicāra (sustained examination) arise, because volition (cetanā) is weak and wisdom (prajñā) is predominant, it is said that "deep investigation" refers to vicāra. Question:
If this is so, why do both vitarka and vicāra among the two—vitarka and vicāra—in the Abhidharma (Abhidharma-piṭaka) speak of "investigation" (parimārgaṇa) and "non-investigation"? Answer:

That [text] speaks of "investigation" and "non-investigation" based on the modes of activity (ākāra) of volition and wisdom; this [present discussion], however, describes them as "shallow" because it is based on the manifest characteristics of vitarka and vicāra themselves.
It is a profound and divergent view to take wisdom (*prajñā*) as the essence of vitarka; compared with vicāra, this remains insufficiently deep.
However, if one contrasts wisdom with volition (*cetanā*), it can be said that while the former involves investigation, the latter does not; thus, there is no contradiction.
However, regarding the *Abhidharma*’s inverted sequence, the first chapter of that treatise states:
"Vitarka, which relies on volition and relies on wisdom, consists of the mental verbalization of the aspect of seeking, respectively, in the states of deliberation and non-deliberation;
vicāra, which relies on volition and relies on wisdom, consists of the aspect of examining, respectively, in the states of deliberation and non-deliberation."
The mental verbalization (*manojalpa-vikalpa*) has the function of being the basis for these two types of dwelling—either in a state of composure or non-composure.
This treatise correlates [mental verbalization] with *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom born of reflection) because it does not involve deep investigation; thus, it follows the sequential order.
In that other [text], *cintāmayī-prajñā* is correlated with both investigation and non-investigation, which is why it is said to be "contrary" to this treatise.

Question: Regarding the statement "because they differ in what they oppose," since *kaukṛtya* (remorse) and *middha* (drowsiness) are both provisional, why are they not the same as *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought), yet [the latter] are called conventional (*saṃvṛti*)?

Answer: They are said to differ in what they oppose because *vitarka* and *vicāra* are categorized according to the gates of the provisional and the real, whereas *kaukṛtya* and *middha* are categorized according to the gates of the conventional and the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

Furthermore, *vitarka* and *vicāra* are called provisional because they are mutually dependent, while *kaukṛtya* and *middha* are conventional because they depend on other factors. Moreover, regarding *vitarka*: [The text continues: ...it is called conventional. Furthermore, *vitarka*...

The two [factors] of *vicāra* (investigation) combine to form *kaukṛtya* (remorse), while *middha* (torpor) and a portion of *moha* (delusion) are likewise [included]; although these are all conventionally designated (*prajñapti*), their mutual relations differ.
Regarding the attainment of that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) from the intermediate stage up to the first dhyāna:

within the first dhyāna, which encompasses two stages, the term "subduing and examining the defiled" refers to the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the first dhyāna; it does not require the complete abandonment of even one grade, let alone many.

Only when one is able to abandon defilement—specifically, when one can suppress and exhaust the delusions of vitarka (applied thought) defilement—is one said to have "abandoned vitarka-defilement" and thus enter the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).

This does not preclude the presence of vicāra (sustained thought) defilement, as that has not yet been abandoned. If one were to completely abandon even a single grade up to nine grades [of these defilements], then one would also abandon the defilement of vicāra;
how then could two distinct stages be differentiated? Furthermore, regarding the two defilements of vitarka and vicāra existing together in the first dhyāna, what is their difference?
The answer is given in terms of distinctions because of the difference between the coarse and the subtle.
Regarding the fact that the untainted meditative absorptions (*anāsrava-samādhi*) do not exhaustively encompass all phenomena:

if the distinction between the three stages were established based on the presence of vitarka and vicāra, or on being defiled or free from defilement, then the various minds and mental factors of the untainted absorptions and those who have already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna would not possess these three [stages].

Regarding the distinction of the stages (*bhūmi*), the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) states that because they belong to the class of those with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are also called the "three stages including vitarka" (*savitarkādi*).

Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter four, says: "If the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) is subsumed under the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), the first dhyāna is also called the stage with vitarka and vicāra (*savitarka-savicāra-bhūmi*);
for one enters this concentration by taking True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the object, based on the factors (*dharma*) associated with vitarka and vicāra. Regarding that:

Since the treatise states that [the mind] relies on dharmas belonging to the stage of vitarka and vicāra, it is known that those associated with defilement are also included; thus, three stages are established.
Regarding the passage from the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (56b) stating "down to the objects of that stage," this merely introduces the question, to which the text further replies:
"Because the seeds of the various consciousnesses accompanied by vitarka and vicāra follow along with the samādhi devoid of vitarka and vicāra, [the mind arises] from that."

Having arisen, this [state] becomes manifest. The intention of this Master is as follows: since that treatise states that the seeds of consciousness accompanied by vitarka and vicāra follow along, one knows that the five consciousnesses possess vitarka and vicāra.

If it were only the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), how could it be said that the first [topic] in the Great Treatises concerns the "unshared karma" (asādhāraṇakarma) of the mind, which consists of two parts: first, the discernment of the object, and second, the deliberation [of the object]?
Regarding the nine states— (1) intoxication, (2) madness, (3) dreaming, (4) waking, (5) fainting, (6) awakening, (7) the capacity to initiate bodily and vocal actions,
(8) the transcendence of desire, (9) the regression from the transcendence of desire, (10) the severance of roots of virtue, (11) the restoration of roots of virtue, (12) birth, and (13) death—

the seven types of discrimination such as "seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā*) and "investigation" (*pratyavekṣaṇā*) correspond to the first [of these], namely, the discrimination of the object (*ālambana-vikalpa*).

Regarding the statement that "the mental level (manobhūmi) reaches the point of having conceptualization": A questioner asks, "In the previous fifth fascicle, it was stated that because there is both non-conceptualization and conceptualization, the sensation of suffering (duḥkhā vedanā) is non-conceptual.

Why, then, is it said here that suffering possesses conceptualization and is similar to grief (daurmanasya)? The answer is: The intent of the previous treatise was to state that when the body as a whole is oppressed by suffering, the mind is termed "grief";

therefore, it was said that suffering is non-conceptual [in that context]. Grief, however, refers specifically to the mental factor of distress. Thus, while the former passage speaks of the non-conceptual nature of suffering in relation to bodily experience, the present passage describes the conceptual nature of suffering as it pertains to the mental sphere, which is why it is said to resemble grief.

There are those who distinguish [the matter] here by stating that since both suffering (*duḥkha*) and grief (*daurmanasya*) are said to be associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the conceptualization of suffering resembles grief and is thus called grief.

As for the claim that [the arising of the five sensory consciousnesses] in the desire realm necessarily depends on being led by the mind, it is not the case that the five consciousnesses can be admitted to arise without the guidance of the mental consciousness;
this statement does not necessarily require that they be led by the mind through applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Regarding the question, "For what reason are the five consciousnesses called 'spontaneous' (*svarasa*) only when they reach [their objects]," the intent of this inquiry is as follows:

If that which is described in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* as "spontaneous" is the very essence of the five consciousnesses themselves—and thus they are termed "spontaneous" even when not accompanied by vitarka and vicāra—then for what reason does the *Yogācārabhūmi* state that "spontaneous" refers only to those associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), such that vitarka and vicāra must be present for them to be called "spontaneous"? The answer intends to clarify that while the five consciousnesses...
Because there is no conceptual deliberation (*vikalpa*), but rather practice based on causes and conditions with respect to objects, it is called "spontaneous" (*anābhoga*) yoga.

Regarding the statement that among the seven types of discrimination it is "spontaneous," this refers to *vitarka* and *vicāra*. As for the discrimination of intense reflection, it is also called "spontaneous. Question:
If the five consciousnesses are called "spontaneous" because they lack conceptual deliberation, then the eighth consciousness should also be called spontaneous.

Question: For what reason does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* speak only of the five consciousnesses? Answer: This is because it is taught in accordance with the Three Vehicles; it does not mention the eighth [consciousness], yet this is not contradictory.

Regarding the statement that "the nature and so forth are likewise," if the nature (*svabhāva*) of the mind and mental factors is capable of cognitive reflection (*ālambana*), it is called "intrinsic discrimination" (*svabhāvavikalpa*).

The fifth type is that which possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of strong reflection; this is called "intrinsic-nature discrimination" (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), and it belongs exclusively to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

This does not contradict the hearing of sounds within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because—as previously stated—the mind in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is devoid of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).

Therefore, the explanation here does not conflict [with scripture], for what is termed "discrimination" refers to clear discernment (*pravicaya*) and does not necessarily require applied and sustained thought. Thus says the Śrāvaka Mahāmati.

Furthermore, the mind of the formless realm universally takes all phenomena of the three realms as its object. Moreover, when that [text] speaks of "the fivefold simultaneous conceptualizing mind," it refers to the distracted mind.
Even in places of extreme suffering there are those who sleep; for when one is oppressed by the pains of hell, the mind gradually becomes obscured and dull. It is a metaphorical designation.
It is taught that [these factors] are "sleep" (*middha*); furthermore, it is accepted that there is no fault in sleep occurring in the realms of hungry ghosts (*preta*) and animals (*tiryagyoni*).

All of these may coexist with the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-niyata-kaṣāya*). Question: As previously stated, regret (*kaukṛtya*) is an obstacle to calm abiding (*śamatha*), and sleep is an obstacle to insight (*vipaśyanā*).

Thus, regret and sleep cannot arise simultaneously with concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). How then can the treatise state that their modes of activity (*ākāra*) do not contradict one another? Answer: The previous statement was based on [the case where they are] equal.

Because they lead [to distraction] and because they are contrary to superior wisdom (*prajñā*), they are said to be hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). This is stated with reference to meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

however, regret (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) may coexist with inferior wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*). Question: Since vitarka and vicāra depend upon wisdom, how can they coexist with wisdom? Answer:

Because those that depend on the aspect of volition (*cetanā*) can coexist with wisdom. Question: It was previously stated that volition and wisdom together constitute the mind; since wisdom must necessarily be present, how can it further coexist with wisdom? Answer: [This objection does not apply, as the types of wisdom involved differ.]

The portion of concealment (*mrakṣa*), deception (*māyā*), greed (*lobha*), and delusion (*moha*) that is obtained in association with greed and delusion—this same explanation applies to the portion of volition (*cetanā*) associated with wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, there is no fault in considering them as mutually induced; however, the former interpretation is superior.

Regarding the claim that there is hearing during the stages of *śruta* (hearing) and *cintā* (reflection) because of the presence of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*): one asks, "Since torpor lacks auditory consciousness, how can there be hearing? The answer is: it is because of what was previously heard;

for when one is in a state of sleep, wisdom (*prajñā*) arises, and this is also termed "wisdom derived from hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Hearing refers to inference (*anumāna*).
Since there is no speaker at the time of sleep, one does not actually hear the teaching; rather, it is the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that performs the mental reflection.

Listening to the teachings is called "hearing" (*śruta*) because it resembles the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) hearing sounds; thus it is also termed "hearing. The commentary (*ṭīkā*), however, explains that while the state of sleep (*middha*) possesses volition (*cetanā*), it is based on the definitive [definition of "hearing"];

therefore, it does not mention "hearing" in that context. Alternatively, the commentary may be considered the primary treatise (*mūla-śāstra*), where the meaning of "hearing" and "reflecting" (*cintā*) includes remorse (*kaukṛtya*), whereas sleep is not mentioned.

Regarding the statement that "this mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is not actually a maturation," this explains that both the state of sleep (*middha*) and the mind born of maturation are not the eighth consciousness;

therefore, since it was previously stated in the third fascicle, within the explanation of the eighth consciousness, that there is no distracted movement (*vikṣepa*), these passages do not contradict one another.
As for the phrase "the same applies to vitarka and vicāra," the latter interpretation holds that vitarka and vicāra are neither associated with maturation nor are they themselves maturation.
It is indeed co-existent with true maturation (*vipāka*).

Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that "at that time, one reaches the state of the fundamental existence" (*mūlabhava*): if one asks what this "fundamental existence" is, there are several explanations. One says:

an unlearned bhikṣu, by virtue of having previously attained meditative concentration, possesses the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and thereby perceives those in the higher realms.

The claim that one who possesses [the intermediate state] immediately gives rise to regret is not logical. The body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) also consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If there is an intermediate state, it constitutes birth in that realm; how then could there be regret in the higher realms?

Furthermore, if the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is bound to the higher realms, how could the regret associated with it be bound to a lower stage? If the regret were indeed bound to the higher realms...

This refers to the aforementioned [state] taking the higher as its object. How can it be said here that the lower takes the higher as its object? Furthermore, there is no textual passage stating that *kaukṛtya* (remorse) extends to the higher realms.

Moreover, if one only gives rise to this remorse after having already lost the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), then since one lacks the divine eye, how could one see that intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
Therefore, this [interpretation] is untenable. Another explanation says: when the mind of the intermediate state is full, one slanders [the truth of] cessation and is then reborn.

It is likewise unreasonable to claim that one who gives rise to this remorse while already existing in hell could do so; for if it is said that wrong view and remorse coexist in hell, how could there be wrong view in the absence of discriminating afflictions?

Furthermore, another says that those who exist as "original beings" (*pūrvabhava*) in the fourth dhyāna cannot [give rise to remorse], because once one has given rise to slander in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one is born in hell and will certainly not be reborn in the higher realms.
None of these are appropriate for the present context; rather, one should explain it as follows: The commentary states, "This refers to those who possess innate wrong views together with regret.

This is said in reference to other times when one who possesses innate regret in the desire realm cultivates higher meditative absorptions; since this does not refer to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), it does not contradict reason.
Regarding the statement in the sixty-sixth [section], "because they have all been abandoned," the meaning of that passage is as follows:

because the bonds of affliction (*kleśa*) in the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles have been exhausted, all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) within their bodies are termed "already abandoned.

Since they are designated as "non-abandonable" (*aprahātavya*) by virtue of being already abandoned, these very contaminated phenomena are all termed "not to be abandoned. This sleep is also included therein.

Question: Since both remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), why is remorse abandoned upon the transcendence of desire (*vītarāga*), whereas sleep extends even to that which is not to be abandoned (*aheya*)?

Answer: Remorse is exclusively of a dejected nature (*daurmanasya-samprayukta*) and mostly accompanies mental grief (*daurmanasya*); therefore, it is abandoned upon the transcendence of desire. Sleep, however, has a nature that extends to both types of mental activity (*saumanasya* and *daurmanasya*).
Because it arises from physical food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), and because one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) still partakes of physical food, sleep is not abandoned.

Although this subsequent explanation is not as definitive as that regarding *daurmanasya* (sorrow), it means that while these *vitarka* and *vicāra* do not coexist with the fundamental or subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*),
they do coexist with the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*). Because they are able to induce that true untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) even before one has entered the true untainted path,
and because they resemble sorrow, it is said that *vitarka* and *vicāra* can be untainted.

Regarding the passage from the *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Teachings), Chapter Two, stating "extreme seeking, extreme inquiry, entry, and extreme entry," this refers to the factor of right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) among the eight branches of the path.
It means that this factor enables the mind to seek, seek intensely, enter, and enter intensely. These terms "extreme" (*ati-*) are used because vitarka and vicāra each have shallow and deep levels;
since both types of vitarka and vicāra constitute the branch of right intention, they are both untainted (*anāsrava*).

Question: Since you have cited the reason for the verbal expression, that sutra describes how the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra and others made three requests to the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha to explain the meaning of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*). Regarding the first request, the verse says:

"For what reason does the one of pure awakening, endowed with mindfulness, wisdom, and merit, proclaim the various sublime stages yet not explain them? The treatise cites this verse and explains: "Awakening..."
Regarding the statement, "Observing this, vitarka is speech; action is speech; the cause of speech is already pure awakening (*jñāna*);
this is the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) vitarka that serves as the cause of speech," why does the present treatise not cite this as proof, but instead cite *samyak-saṃkalpa* (right intention)?

The answer—stating, "If one follows the Sanskrit original, etc."—intends to convey that if one speaks of the principle of *vitarka* and *vicāra*, it logically corresponds to *vitarka*. According to the standard, [the term used here] should correspond to *vitarka*.

Since the Sanskrit original states *saṃkalpa*, which means "reflection" (*cintā*) and is fundamentally not "applied thought and sustained thought" (*vitarka-vicāra*), there has been an error in the translation;
it is truly not "investigation" (*paryeṣaṇā*). This treatise cites [the term] in accordance with the Sanskrit original, whereas it differs from the version in this land’s *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*.
Question: According to this local variation, if one follows the Sanskrit original, then these two treatises do not contradict one another. Question: Suppose [one were to ask about] *saṃgha*...
Question: The *kalyāṇa* (kalpa) is "contemplation" (*cintā*) further purified by syllables; this differs slightly from what has been cited here. How can it be said to be the same? Answer:
Pure contemplation is precisely the factor of right contemplation (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) within the Eightfold Path; since both are causes for speech, there is no contradiction.
As for using verses 73 through 74 as proof, they state: "There is contemplation of suchness, but it is not the observation of suchness."

Regarding the phrase "contemplating suchness and so forth through reasoning, as subsumed under conceptualization," this applies to both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conceptual wisdom.
When it says "there is contemplation of suchness but no conceptualization of suchness at the time of penetrating suchness," this refers exclusively to uncontaminated conceptual wisdom.
Furthermore, there is also the case where there is both conceptualization of suchness and contemplation of suchness.

Regarding the statement, "To thoroughly penetrate and subsequently contemplate non-conceptually established suchness (*apratiṣṭhita-tathatā*)," this phrase applies to both subsequent non-conceptual wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) following the stage of application (*prayoga*) and [the state where] one neither contemplates nor observes suchness—
meaning that which is free from the mental attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward suchness while contemplating various signs (*nimitta*). Regarding the statement,
"It applies to all minds that take form (*rūpa*) and so forth as their object," this phrase applies to all consciousnesses that have form and other phenomena as their cognitive objects.

If one follows the standard that the first dhyāna consists of five factors—namely, (1) vitarka, (2) vicāra, (3) prīti, (4) sukha, and (5) cittaikāgratā—then since the Buddha is devoid of vitarka and vicāra, he lacks these first two factors.
Regarding the commentary’s explanation that this refers to *cetanā* and *prajñā*:
although the Buddha lacks vitarka and vicāra, because he possesses *cetanā* and *prajñā*, these can still function as the factors that serve as the antidotes for the first dhyāna.
Just as the Buddha, although devoid of vitarka and vicāra, possesses the factor of right thought (samyak-saṃkalpa);

and regarding the "far-reaching" (*dūra-gama*) and so forth mentioned in the fourth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*: "far-reaching" means that from beginningless time it has traversed various objects;
"solitary traveler" means it is a single mental state without a second; and "without body" means that mind is not a material dharma and thus lacks accumulation.
Therefore, those who sleep in a cave do so within their own bodies.

First, the sūtras are cited as proof, and subsequently, the principles are established through reasoning; "sūtras" refers to the aforementioned *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Daśabhūmika*, and others, while "principles" refers to the extensive citations from the *Śrīkārikā*.
Regarding the statement that "there is no form and no transformation such as that of milk," "formless" refers to mental factors (*citta-dharma*), which cannot undergo transformation like milk.
That treatise cites the passage concerning greed, hatred, and so forth; it refutes the Sautrāntika school by stating: "Since it is said that greed, hatred, and so forth are defilements..."

To afflict the mind is precisely a distinct mind; it is a separate mental factor such as hatred (*dveṣa*). If its essence were identical to the mind itself, how could the mind defile and afflict the mind?

That which is called the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*), when it exists within the internal sense-spheres, is not the unconditioned space (*ākāśāsaṃskṛta*); rather, it refers to the bones within the internal body.

Within the gaps of the flesh-gate there exists this empty form, which is called the form of the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu-rūpa*). It is called "internal" to distinguish it from the external space-element.

Next, regarding the previous citation that should serve as a counter-objection: the six elements mention only "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and do not allow for the coexistence of mental factors (*caitta*);
the milk analogy mentions only "form" (*rūpa*); and while the desire realm lacks mindless forms, the formless realm’s mental faculty (*manas*) is to be understood by analogy.
If that is so, regarding the statement "within the collection of mind," this implies that if the term "mind" (citta) is accepted as including mental factors (caitta),

then both greed (rāga) and faith (śraddhā) would also fall under the first category [of being "similar"]. Furthermore, since it is said that they are "similar to greed, faith, and so forth," by what else could they be considered "similar"?

Regarding the statement that "the mind as a whole appears as greed, faith, and so forth," this refers to the general consensus that within the appearance of the mind as dual, greed, faith, and so forth each also appear as two parts resembling themselves. Therefore, the second and third lines distinguish them by stating:
"thus appearing as greed and so forth, or appearing as faith and so forth."

Furthermore, regarding the statement "because mental factors (*caitta*) should not be [identical to] the mind (*citta*)," etc.: the previous explanation distinguished between the general and specific aggregates, and within the general category, it separately identified the defiled and pure mental factors as two distinct phrases.
This current explanation clarifies that the first phrase alone shows the self-substance of the mind-king (*cittarāja*) appearing as if it were twofold;

whereas the second and third phrases show the self-substance of the defiled and pure mental factors appearing as if they were divided into two parts, because mental factors... [are not identical to the mind].
Because they are devoid of mind, such expressions resembling greed and so forth are spoken.

This single phrase concludes both verses; by taking this one phrase as a common basis, one understands that in the first verse the five consciousnesses and in the second verse the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) both rely upon the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).

[Question: Regarding the external objects, the path, attention (*manasikāra*), the five faculties, and their objects—among these mental factors (*caitta*), what is meant by "external conditions" (*bāhyālambana*) and "internal basis" (*adhyātma-āśraya*)?

Is [attention] a manifest state (*vijñapti*) or a seed (*bīja*) based on the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*)? [Answer: One interpretation states that because seeds produce [their effects] directly, they are called "internal," whereas attention and so forth are termed "external" in the *Śāstra*.
Another interpretation holds that those which continue constantly without interruption are called "internal," while those which are occasionally interrupted are called "external."
Because these seven and eight [mental factors] in their active manifestation, along with the seeds of all consciousnesses, are subsumed under internal conditions;
and because the attention (*manasikāra*) of the six consciousnesses and their objects, as well as the eye-faculty and so forth, are occasionally interrupted, they are considered external conditions.
Both interpretations are acceptable, though the commentary follows the former explanation.

Regarding "either through aversion toward the mind or through other conditions": this refers to the three states such as the non-conceptual (asaṃjñika), which arise from the intentional aversion of the mind, whereby the mental consciousness does not arise;

and the two states of fainting and stupor, which are termed "other conditions" due to causes such as extreme exhaustion. Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna, the three states such as the non-conceptual arise solely through aversion toward the mind;
whereas in the Hīnayāna, there are distinct real dharmas [that act as obstructions]. The former interpretation is correct.

Although it is stated in general that six [consciousnesses] are distant and three are near while one is both, this means that the three—eye, ear, and body consciousness—are distant from the first dhyāna level and associated with the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*), whereas the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is near because it belongs to that same level.
Furthermore, the single [consciousness] of nose and tongue belongs only to the desire realm and is thus omitted from the discussion.

Alternatively, another interpretation holds that the three [sensory consciousnesses] are distant because they first arise without the mental consciousness and subsequently cease; hence, it is said that three are distant and one is near. Question: If that is so, should it not rather be said that five are distant? Why?
The explanation of the three [types of intermediate existence] distinguishes between near and far within their respective realms; for now, we shall adopt the former interpretation.
Regarding the question of how ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) moisten their rebirth—extending even to such non-Buddhists as these—the master asks:

since it is already accepted that the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) possesses perception (*saṃjñā*), and according to the *Abhidharma*, its final mind is defiled (*kliṣṭa*), then there must also be manifest [defilement] when one passes away from the heavens to be born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "karma moistens birth," why is it said that it only moistens the seed? The answer is: it is said that it only moistens the seed because the explanation is based on the state of existence at birth (*upapattibhava*);
or else, this master does not admit the existence of a defiled mind in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and thus makes this statement.

However, regarding the statement that "even when the Elder arrives, there is no mind," this explains that while the existence of a mind in the *asaṃjñika* state is not admitted, it does not apply to other intermediate states (*antarābhava*).
Now, as for the concern that the former masters might also hold such a view, this is merely a hypothetical objection raised by the commentator;
how could it be that the former masters did not believe that the final mind in the *antarābhava* is also defiled? Or perhaps the former masters... [text fragment ends]

Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharma* that there is a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*), this refers to other realms of existence and not to the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), and thus it does not constitute a valid objection.
Otherwise, as for the claim that those born from eggs necessarily possess consciousness upon birth: when one is born from an egg and resides in the mother’s womb, consciousness has not yet arisen.

If one divides [the process of rebirth] into three parts, this is designated as "original existence" (*pūrvakālabhava*). As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Just as in the case of original existence in other realms... Since...
Since there would be nothing established within the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), one must now examine the matter and exclude that [case]. Question:

For those born from eggs, at the moment they first emerge from the egg, they are necessarily in a state of great stupor such that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) do not function. If the "three parts" are also called the "first part," what fault is there? Answer:

In the commentary (*śāstra*), because the examples all refer to the celestial realms (*devagati*), this has already been excluded. Even if one were to take up the treatise (*śāstra*), [the same applies].

In response to this, one should state that the intermediate existence (antarābhava) is accepted as being excluded from the initial moment of the prior existence (pūrvakālabhava), just like the initial moment of other prior existences;
thus, there is no fault, because at the time of emerging from the womb, it is subsumed under the state of fainting (mūrchana).

It is not the case that the mind of retribution can arise at the end of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). This means that the maturation of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka*) must necessarily be established based on the seeds of the mind of retribution.

According to the former master, since the primary stage of that heaven lacks evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), there would be no basis for establishing the maturation of non-conceptualization.
Therefore, it is said that this mind of retribution arises at the final moment of the intermediate state; the fruit is established by depending upon these seeds.

Regarding those who are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) in the third heaven from here: in reality, the three lower heavens also include noble ones (*ārya*), whereas the five higher heavens are inhabited exclusively by noble ones;
therefore, the three lower heavens are described as the abodes of ordinary persons.

Regarding the statement, "It is capable of inducing the volition (*cetanā*) for the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)," the Commentary provides three interpretations: 1. The first interpretation holds that a single present volition can induce two results:

both a collective and a specific result. 2. The second interpretation maintains that although it is a single volition, there are distinct states (*avasthā*)—one with consciousness and one without—through which it induces the two results.
3. The third interpretation asserts that two present volitions induce the two results. Question: Among these three explanations, which [is correct]?

This is an excellent answer; the first explanation is the most superior. Regarding the statement that the substance of the fruition of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is caused by the sense-field (*āyatana*) as the cause for experiencing general and specific retributions, this is because it is taught that the member of volitional formations (*saṃskāra-aṅga*) brings about these results.
The third explanation is also logically consistent: the volitions (*cetanā*) present in the preceding and succeeding moments bring about general and specific retributions;

the former constitutes the primary practice while the latter constitutes the auxiliary members, and thus there is no contradiction with reason. As for its second interpretation, it holds that [volition] in the state of mindlessness brings about [the result].

The principle of that distinct retribution is somewhat difficult to explain in detail. How could it be that a seed of volition (*cetanā*) without mind could induce rebirth in that heaven for five hundred kalpas, such that neither the mind nor its mental factors (*caitta*) function at all?
Furthermore, we have not yet seen a scriptural passage stating that a seed of volition alone can induce a fruit;

as for the claim that one is reborn there through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this should also result in a general rebirth, since it is admitted that such power is effective. Moreover, [rebirth] without mind would be merely nominal.

If meditative absorption (*samādhi*) merely has the sense of obstructing the mind so that it does not arise, how could it have the power to induce that fruit? Furthermore, this treatise states that the volition (*cetanā*) capable of inducing the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is what induces the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of that heaven; thus, it refers to the present volition and does not speak of the "induced" [seed]. However, since the seeds of the attainment of perception can induce that fruit, we know that [the opponent's view] is incorrect. Master Xu [says]: [The text continues: ...and so forth. It is not the case that the seeds of the attainment of perception are not included within the category of the attainment itself; rather, because they are the cause for the arising of the attainment, they are designated by the name of the attainment. For example, although the seeds of the eye-faculty are not the eye-faculty itself, because they are the cause for the arising of the eye-faculty, they are designated by the name of the eye-faculty. Therefore, one should know that the seeds of the attainment of perception are indeed included within the attainment of perception. Consequently, the seeds of the attainment of perception can induce the ripening fruit of that heaven. Thus, the meaning of the treatise is established. This is the intention of the Great Master [Xuanzang]. The Master of the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "The seeds of the attainment of perception are not the attainment itself. This is not correct. Why? Because the seeds of the attainment of perception are not distinct from the attainment of perception. If they were distinct, they would fall into the fault of infinite regress. If one posits the provisional fruit by taking the provisional mind as its cause, it is not necessarily the case that this is intended as the primary question.

When we say "it induces that distinct retribution," does this refer to the *ālayavijñāna* (the retributive consciousness with mind) inducing that state, or does it refer to the inducing of that provisional and substantial retribution?

If it were only the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) that induced it, one should not say it induces the "mindless" state; yet if you say it only induces the mindless state, [how can this be so?]

Question: If it is truly the case that thought induces the various bases for the maturation (*vipāka*) of those provisional states, why does it not induce them in the present state, but instead induces only their seeds?

Answer: By inference from the meaning, it induces only the maturing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of that heaven, but does not induce the state of being without mind (*acittaka*). Why is this so? Because at the initial stage of that heaven...

There must necessarily be a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) that attains [the state]; if this mind does not arise at the time of practicing meditative concentration, at what other time could it possibly arise? Question:
If it does not arise, how can one say that it "attracts" (*ākarṣati*) the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) when there is no mind? Answer:

This is a figurative designation of maturation based on the various manifesting consciousnesses born of acquisition (*upapatti-lābhika*). Thus, there is no error in saying that it attracts the principle of non-conception.

Regarding the phrase "because it is distinguished separately from within the indeterminate," the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (19) states: "Thus, there are five kinds of determinate karma: first, determinate in being experienced in the present life;
second, determinate in being experienced in the next life; third, determinate in being experienced in subsequent lives; fourth, determinate in the manner of experiencing the retribution;
and fifth, determinate in the performance of the action. Question: Since all five of these karmas are called "determinate," how is this explained in the commentary?

Question: Is the understanding [of these actions] indeterminate? Answer: Although the three times [of action] are determined, the maturation (vipāka) is not necessarily fixed; that which is heavy may turn light.

Fourth, the maturation is determined, but the time of its reception is not necessarily fixed. Fifth, the performance of the action is determined, yet neither the maturation nor the time is said to be fixed.
For this reason, although all five types of karma are said to be determined, there is mutual indeterminacy regarding their maturation, timing, and so forth.
He also asked: "Since the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that there are five kinds of karma, why is it that only the fifth is called 'karma of action' (*kriyā-karman*)? The answer is:
while the first four are described in terms of the karma that invites [a result] based on the results they invite, the fifth does not depend on an invited result and yet possesses a fixed nature.
Question: How can the karma of action be designated as 'fixed' without being defined in relation to its results? Answer: It is like the observance of precepts through long-standing habituation."
The arising of certainty is likewise followed by the cultivation of wholesome roots;

the same applies to the habituation of evil. Regarding "arising again in each stage" (*bhūmi-bhūmi-punar-utpāda*): having previously attained this meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one subsequently gives rise to it again within each stage of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
therefore, it is said that there is "re-arising. A source states: "Arising in each stage is logically permissible."
The "superior" [attainment] does not necessarily arise in each and every stage, as it is possible for it to arise [only in certain cases].

Regarding the statement that this master also establishes [the attainment] as a "subsequent-retribution" (paścātkālavedanīya) and so forth: after one has fallen away from this meditative absorption while in a body of the desire realm, one regains it within that same desire-realm body and subsequently is reborn in that heaven;
viewed in relation to the previous attainment, it is established as a subsequent-retribution attainment. [Question: What about the previous attainment?

Once one has already regressed, one does not experience the fruit; how then can it be established as a "subsequent retribution"? Although there is regression, because the power of the subsequent meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) sustains that functional capacity, it causes the fruit to be experienced; therefore, it is established as a subsequent retribution.

There is. Regarding the statement that "the meaning is such that it can induce [the meditative attainment] to manifest," this refers to one who has fallen away from the defilements of the *Śubhakṛtsna* (Pervasive Purity) heaven and below;
such a person is able to give rise to this concentration within the lower three dhyānas because they possess the moisture of delusion (*kleśa*).

If one has only fallen away from the defilements of the third dhyāna and not those of the two lower ones, then this concentration can only be induced to manifest within the third *dhyāna*. However, if one has not fallen away from the defilements of the lower three dhyānas, yet [seeks] this...
Those who have not perfected their cultivation of meditative concentration and temporarily regress from it will again give rise to this concentration in the three heavens beginning with Anabhraka;
however, those who have perfected their cultivation and do not regress will certainly be reborn in those heavens.

Although one who has become free from passion attains this meditative absorption, the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) is similar to the three lower heavens in that it is attained by being freed from the passions of the third dhyāna;
yet, because its power is not superior due to the cultivation of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), those who have not yet produced it do not arise in that heaven.
Rather, having been born in the three lower heavens and further cultivated [the practice], they subsequently experience that fruit. If one asks how it is "freed from passion":
Because the degree of detachment from defilements is equal, the same principle applies to the three dhyānas of the form realm as an illustration;
therefore, one should not be born in the two lower celestial abodes [of the fourth dhyāna].

As for the statement that "the manifestation of the non-ideational attainment (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is a defect," this is unlike the case of the cessation attainment (nirodha-samāpatti), which is induced by untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā). Thus it is said.

Regarding "those born in superior abodes": the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) are the superior abodes, and the noble ones (*ārya*) are the superior births; alternatively, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) constitutes the superior abode and birth.

As for the meaning of "cultivating the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya*) each with their respective excellences": the four dhyānas possess excellence in feeling, while the formless attainments possess excellence in perception; now, one enters the attainment of cessation.
Because it constitutes a particularly formidable obstacle, he feels a specific aversion toward it.
According to the principle that one may reach the subsequent stage by leaping over one level (*ekabhūmi-vyutkrānta*), there are two interpretations:

first, it is said that from the mind of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), one immediately takes the mind of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) and enters this leap-over of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); second, it is said that one takes the mind of the sphere of nothingness itself.
Entering that meditative absorption by means of the mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is not called "transcending one stage. This interpretation is correct.

As for the previous interpretation—if one were to call it "transcending" by entering the Peak of Existence with the mind of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*)—how could one say that one transcends [the Peak of Existence] only after having attained the mind of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)?
Question: If one has already transcended into this absorption by means of the mind of Nothingness, how is this to be explained?

It is said that one must necessarily take the contemplation of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as the outflow-free preparatory practice (*prayoga*) to enter [this meditative absorption]; regarding this, there are two interpretations within the sub-commentary itself.

As for the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi* that "one enters this absorption," this refers to the fact that there are two types of objects of focus (*ālambana*) for the preparatory practice: those involving abandonment and those not.
Initially, one enters by taking the characteristics of the mind and mental factors of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the preparatory practice;

subsequently, one enters by taking the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness) as the object of the preparatory practice. The former refers to the initial cultivation, while the latter refers to long-term habituation.

According to these two causes mentioned in the Sūtra, it should be understood that from the stage of the "subtle-subtle" (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma*) up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called "not conceptualizing any signs."

Furthermore, regarding this transition from the mindless state to the superior meditative concentration with mind: this refers to the "lower-grade" superior concentration with mind, namely the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Among the eight concentrations involving mind, this is the last, and thus it is called "lower-grade"; because it is the most subtle, it is termed a "superior concentration.
By virtue of these two meanings, it can induce the mindless superior concentration of the fourth dhyāna.
Although the mind induces the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), because it lacks two specific characteristics, it merely induces an inferior, mindless concentration.

Regarding the statement in the sixty-second [treatise], "it should be said that it is untainted (*anāsrava*) and so forth," the meaning of this passage is explained through a series of successive clarifications.
How can this concentration be called "untainted"? It is because it is dissociated from the afflictions (*kleśa*). How is this so? [The text continues: "How is this... [and so on].
Because this concentration is not associated with afflictions, the subsequent explanation states that it is "not an associated dharma. Why is it not an associated dharma?
Because it lacks an object of cognition (*ālambana*). Since it lacks an object of cognition, afflictions do not arise;
therefore, this concentration is supramundane and is subsumed under the untainted (*anāsrava*).
From the fifth *Abhidharma* [treatise] up to the point concerning "only those who transcend the single interval," this is identical to the twelve [stages] in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

That is to say: from the first dhyāna one transcends into the third *dhyāna*; from this third [dhyāna] one transcends into the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); from this sphere of infinite space one transcends into the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*);
and from the sphere of nothingness one transcends into the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Because one has not yet attained mastery, only...

One cannot skip one stage (*ekāntara*) and leap from the first dhyāna directly into the third to enter the fourth, because the distance between them is too great and the power [of the practitioner] is insufficient for this.
This skipping of one stage is also called the "lion’s stretch" (*siṃha-vijṛmbhita*).

Since both the upward and downward leaps proceed according to their respective order, if there are two interpretations regarding this point, the first interpretation asks: does the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) immediately result in this meditative absorption?

Furthermore, since the first dhyāna and others possess obstructive dharmas (*sapratigha*), how does this treatise reconcile its reliance on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)?

Answer: That [reliance] is based on initial practice and depends solely on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this [reliance], however, pertains to the eight stages as well as the Tathāgatas and others, and thus encompasses all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*). Question:
Since the final one or two moments are not established by relying on the seeds of perception (*saṃjñā-bīja*), why must that mind be aroused? Answer: Because of that perception...
Because it is subtle and easily extinguished.

Regarding the second interpretation, "reaching the stage of perception (*saṃjñā-bhūmi*) as the basis," etc.: Question: Upon what seeds is this basis of the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) established? Answer:

Since this [attainment] is sovereign, it does not require dependence on the seeds of the subtle-subtle mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*) from the initial cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*). This attainment is established solely by depending upon...

The seeds of the mind that have been habituated through practice and contemplation on that stage are established [as the basis for the attainment], because they are extremely subtle. The *Vyākhyā* (Sub-commentary) itself explains:
"This is established based on the seeds of the 'subtler-than-subtle' mind; it is the first arising, not a transcendence. Question:

If the seeds of the mind of that stage are no longer being perfumed, how can the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) be established based upon them? If it is said to be established because they were previously perfumed, then it should exist constantly.

In response to the objection that seeds exist eternally within the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is explained that through the power of the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) of the first dhyāna and other meditative attainments, the seeds of those respective stages acquire a functional capacity to prevent the mind from arising; it is on this basis that [the attainment] is established.

If there were no such preparatory effort, those seeds would lack the power to induce the attainment of cessation, and thus there would be no fault of its being eternally present. [Objection: Since that stage lacks the capacity...

Question: Does aversion have the functional capacity to prevent [the arising of defilements]? Answer: Since the minds of the first dhyāna and so forth are also capable of aversion, it is not necessary to rely on a specific type of aversion.
Regarding "pervading both the conditioned and the unconditioned": these dharmas pervade both the conditioned and the unconditioned; however, within the conditioned...

Regarding the distinction between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*): this present meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and is outflow-free, because it arises from its supporting seeds.

As for the statement that "the mind-made gods (*manomaya-deva*) [attain it] up to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), but not otherwise," this refers to the scriptural teaching that the mind-made bodies of gods who have transcended edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) are able to enter and emerge from this absorption.
This is because the followers of the Hīnayāna do not yet believe in the eighth consciousness; thus, they describe the mind-made gods as being of the realm of form.
Because the Mahāyāna refutes this [view] regarding the realms (*dhātu*), it says "it is not so. The reasoning for why it is not so is explained in sequence in the Commentary (*ṭīkā*).
Regarding the explanation of this sūtra and others: the sūtra merely states that the body of a mind-made god (*manomaya-deva*) is able to again give rise to this meditative absorption.

Because Śāriputra did not believe in the eighth consciousness, the original intent was solely to explain that [the body] subsequently arises from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); failing to understand this, he said: [as quoted in the text].
Because these formless beings have not yet believed in the existence of the eighth consciousness, the *manas* now cites this as proof.

The Sūtra states that those who have transcended material food are called "mind-made gods" (*manomaya-deva*), which clarifies that both the realm of form and the formless realm are [included therein].

Furthermore, it says that even the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" [heaven] is a mind-made god. Since the Sūtra explicitly states that they follow and dwell in one of these locations as mind-made gods...
The body can enter this state of fixed principle (niyama) even while one has attained mastery over the formless realms;

however, because those [proponents] do not know of an eighth [consciousness], they speak only of the realm of form (rūpadhātu), failing to preclude that one may attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) in the formless realms—this serves as the proof.

Question: Regarding the statement that "the manifestation does not occur" up to "it is called the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," both Śāriputra and the gods of the form and formless realms who are born by mental transformation have yet to believe in the existence of the eighth consciousness.

Why, then, did Śāriputra state that for those who fall back from the desire realm, the subsequent arising occurs in the form realm, and that this is called the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? Answer: Śāriputra stated that there are non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who fall back and give rise [to rebirth] again.
Regarding those defiled by the realm of form who attain birth in the realm of form and again give rise to this meditative absorption:

for one who does not fall back into defilement, after departing from the desire realm, they must eventually pass away and be born in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), as it is only the final stage that is admitted to have not yet been subdued.

For this reason, it is said that this [absorption] arises subsequent to that stage. Thus, Śāriputra rebuked them, because both of those two parties do not admit the existence of the seeds or the moisture [of defilement].
Because it arises.
However, the passage from the various former masters up to "this is the teaching of the Hīnayāna" is an explanation of the text from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter fifty-six.
That treatise states: "First it arises here [in the desire realm], and subsequently it manifests again in the form realm; relying upon the support of form (*rūpa*), it then appears."
Prior to this, since the teaching that establishes the *ālayavijñāna* had not yet been established, it could not manifest in all instances.

The ancient masters interpreted this passage to mean that teachings which have not yet established the *ālayavijñāna* are the sūtras of the Hīnayāna, whereas those that have already established it are the sūtras of the Mahāyāna; therefore, the Commentary refutes this.
Alternatively, if the meaning of this passage differs from that of the *Śāstra on the Fifty-six [Points]*, it is because that treatise generally refers to all noble ones (*ārya*),
and thus states that "those who have not yet established the eighth teaching" can bring it forth at all stages after arising in the form realm;

whereas this text, referring only to those who specifically believe in the eighth [consciousness], states that "once one has already believed in it, even when born in the formless realm, one obtains it."
Regarding the statement that [the teaching] does not manifest before one who lacks faith, it further states that once established, the teaching manifests everywhere;

thus, it applies to both realms and can arise subsequently in both. This could simply be said to refer to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and therefore it is called "a portion of the noble ones" (*ekadeśa-ārya*).
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that once established, the teaching arises in all places; if this were the case, it would be excessive.
