Having already granted that those in the formless realm can enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is now further stated that they do not enter this attainment because the maturation (*vipāka*) in the formless realm is not tranquil.
This constitutes the second interpretation provided in that same *Abhidharma* treatise.
As for the term "not tranquil," it means that because they lack dhyāna, [the formless realm] is not like the realm of form.

Regarding the phrase "also [attained] according to reality": although the Abhidharma states that those in the formless realm do not enter this meditative absorption, if one follows a different interpretation—that is, if one believes in the eighth [liberation]—then those in the formless realm can also enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Furthermore, the word "different" (*yi*) here is an error;
it should be the character for "real" (*shi*), and this should be further examined.

In the third fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it states that five types of persons attain [this]: those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) in the three vehicles, non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, and those who have attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin).
If that is so, regarding the fourfold classification mentioned therein, the text asks: "If one has already become detached from the desires of the form realm (rūpadhātu), is it the case that all..."

Are all those who enter the meditative absorption of the peaceful liberation of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhyāna-vimokṣa-samādhi*) necessarily free from desire for the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu-vītarāga*)?

And are all those who are free from desire for the form realm necessarily able to enter the meditative absorption of the peaceful liberation of the formless realm? The treatise answers that there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*):

The first permutation refers to one who, relying on the *anāgamya* concentration, is already free from desire for the form realm but is unable to attain entry into the meditative absorption of the peaceful liberation of the formless realm.

The second phrase regarding liberation from concentration refers to those noble ones who, having already attained the fourth dhyāna, do not seek rebirth in the formless realm and instead constantly manifest states of aversion toward the fourth dhyāna;

they abandon the path for severing fetters and, by relying on the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), are gradually able to enter the peaceful liberations of the formless realm. The third phrase refers to these very same individuals.

The practitioner diligently seeks detachment and, by relying on the path of severing the fetters, is gradually able to enter the meditative absorption of the peaceful liberation of the formless realm (ārūpya-dhyāna).
The fourth phrase means that one excludes the aforementioned characteristics.

The meaning of its second phrase is that the fruit of the Non-returner (anāgāmin) must attain the fourth fundamental dhyāna and, relying on the sixfold path of cultivation, gradually enter the liberation of the formless realm.

Regarding the arising of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), since this master maintains that one attains the attainment of cessation simply by severing all afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) through cultivation, why would it be necessary to enter the fourth dhyāna to attain it?
Because this contradicts his position, the following question is now raised.

From fifty-nine [to sixty], it says "only the third fruit. This refers to those who, having previously suppressed the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of the desire realm and realized the truths (*satya*), immediately realize the third fruit, thereby bypassing the first two fruits.
If that were so, would ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) only possess the seeds of moisture? If an Anāgāmin suppresses the afflictions, they possess only the seeds of moisture; as for ordinary beings...
Furthermore, for those who have suppressed the afflictions from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) downward, the seeds alone should be able to provide moisture.
If this were granted, then ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) would never be born in the form realm, because the seeds belonging to the desire realm would be capable of moistening their rebirth there.

However, regarding ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are destined to be born in a higher realm: just as there are ordinary beings who have attained detachment from desire and yet do not suppress the craving associated with the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm—
since they are not reborn in the desire realm through the moistening of craving and the like, yet are nonetheless admitted to be born in a higher realm—

it follows by analogy that even though non-returners (*anāgāmin*) possess the seeds of the form realm and so forth, they should likewise be born without the seeds of the form realm acting as the moisture for their birth.
It is not that they lack perception; otherwise, the noble seeds would be stronger than those of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

If the seeds of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) were able to provide nourishment without depending on the power of the untainted (*anāsrava*), then the noble seeds would be stronger than the seeds of ordinary beings, because the noble ones would be able to provide nourishment even without relying on the manifest [untainted state].
The remaining two phrases can be understood as follows: that which is below cuts off what is below, and that which is above cuts off what is above.

Regarding the statement "if one suppresses [the afflictions of] one stage or five stages, etc.," the character "一" (one) here is an error; it should be the character "八" (eight), meaning "suppressing the eight stages.

Thus, the first master refers to suppressing [the afflictions of] the first stage, while the latter master refers to suppressing those of the fifth stage. [Question: How can it be said that this suppresses the higher stages?

The answer below does not refer to the upper and lower levels of the nine stages (*navabhūmi*). It simply designates that which was previously severed as "upper" and that which is subsequently suppressed as "lower.
Furthermore, the character "lower" (*xià*) is also an error; it should properly be the character "upper" (*shàng*). Question:

If one suppresses the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the eight and five stages and attains this meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), why does the commentary state that one does not attain two types of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas? Answer: Because the perception of immovability (*āniñjya-saṃjñā*)...

Regarding the two types of cessation—cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): the statement that one does not attain these two unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) means that because one has not severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), one does not attain cessation through deliberation;

as for the other two types of unconditioned phenomena, one likewise does not attain them because they are not [attained] through non-deliberation. According to the former master, both are cessation not through deliberation;
according to the latter master, the immovable [attainment] is also subsumed under cessation through deliberation. The commentary uses the term "general" (*zong*) to indicate this.

Regarding the statement in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* that "one reaches the arousal of afflictions," this means that within the bodhisattva’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), there arises the intention and desire to benefit sentient beings;

it is only when one reaches a contaminated state of mind (*sāsrava-citta*) that afflictions actually arise. If one considers the stage where the afflictions have not yet manifested, they may coexist with subsequently attained wisdom without any fault.

Regarding those who cite the passage from the first to the third fascicle—specifically the third master’s citation from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* concerning the abandonment of the *ālayavijñāna*—it states that although Bodhisattvas on the ten stages have not yet permanently severed all afflictions (*kleśa*), they are like those [cured] by mantras or medicine.

Based on that text, it does not say they have attained cessation; however, since this treatise states that "afflictions have already been suppressed" and there is nothing further to be separated from, [the meaning is established].

Since one attains this meditative absorption while still possessing desire, we know that the statement that the ten stages can suppress all afflictions serves as proof that Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages all attain this absorption; otherwise, what would be the purpose of citing it?
Furthermore, regarding the statement that upon emerging [from meditative absorption] one contacts three kinds of contact (*sparśa*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 12, states:

"When emerging from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one contacts three kinds of contact: first, the immovable contact (*aniñjya-sparśa*); second, the contact of nothingness (*akiṃcana-sparśa*); and third, the signless contact (*animitta-sparśa*). This means that when emerging from the attainment, one generally does so by means of three types of objects (*ālambana*):
first, by means of an object of existence (*bhava-ālambana*); second, by means of an object of non-existence (*abhāva-ālambana*); and third, by means of an object of cessation (*nirodha-ālambana*).

When emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one encounters three types of contact (*sparśa*) in successive order by means of these three objects. Here, "contact" refers to the mental factor of contact.
"Possessing an object" refers to the internal body consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

Because one takes this as an object, at the time of emerging from absorption, one encounters the "unshakable contact" (*āniñjya-sparśa*), so called because it is not shaken by views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and so forth. As for the phrase "object after object": [it refers to...]

This means that the six sensory objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are not one; because one takes these objects as conditions, at the time of emerging from meditative absorption, one contacts the "contact of nothingness" (*ākiṃcanyasparśa*), and because there are no afflictions such as greed, hatred, or delusion, it is called the "object of cessation. This refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Because one takes this as a condition and emerges from absorption, one contacts the "contact of signlessness" (*animittasparśa*), which is free from the ten kinds of signs such as male and female. Furthermore, this is based on the characteristics of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
These are assigned to the three [categories] in their respective order.
Regarding the phrase "because the *marmans* give rise to fainting": the *marmans* are what is here called the "touch of death.

Because there are specific joints and apertures upon the body such that touching them causes immediate death, they are called the "touch of death. Question: Since death is insentient (*acetana*), how [can it be a touch]?

There is no contradiction, for the "fainting" (*mūrchā*) that accompanies the state of dying is produced by contact (*sparśa*). Furthermore, what resembles death is called "death," yet it is not a non-sentient entity;
it is truly fainting. Alternatively, both of these are portions of the sense-base of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
Regarding the previous detailed explanation of sleep (*middha*) and fainting, since exhaustion, wind, and heat were mentioned:

Since the "equal conditions" (samanantara-pratyaya) are the cause for the sense-base of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana), why does this general explanation further state that it is only a portion of the sense-base of tangibles?

The previous statement was based on the physical positions being cited, which thus encompass all ten material sense-bases; this present statement, however, refers specifically to the conditions that induce [the sensation], and therefore it pertains only to a portion of the sense-base of tangibles.
Question: Since all three realms involve the fainting of death and birth, how can there be such fainting in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which lacks the sense-object of touch?

Answer: In that realm, although there are no conditions such as wind, heat, or the vital points (*marmāṇi*), during the states of death and birth, the mental consciousness does not arise due to a state of profound delusion;
this is also termed "fainting."

If one asks, "The present case is indeed so; however, regarding that which is accepted as the subject of this treatise, since you have already mentioned the eighth [consciousness], how can it be mutually accepted? The answer is:
this refers to the capacity for the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which that school also establishes; it does not mean that they accept the existence of an eighth mental faculty (*citta*).
Regarding the four types of karma within a single moment of thought, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 51) states: "To speak briefly, there are four kinds of karma:
first, the karma that discerns the vessel-world; second, the karma that discerns the basis; third, the karma that discerns the self; and fourth, the karma that discerns objects.
Now, to explain the second of these, the "discernment of the basis," it refers to the sense-faculties, the body, and the seeds, which are the supports for consciousness.

Therefore, the first two [moments] and the eighth have the objects of the sixth consciousness; the next one has the object of the seventh consciousness; and the final one has the objects of all six consciousnesses.
Since that [text] states that four karmas can operate simultaneously in a single moment, we know that the eighth consciousness is present therein.
Regarding the phrase "because within the four truths, up to the characterized object, there is nothing [existent]":

this means that while ordinary people’s deluded attachments initially conceive of the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and the characterized (lakṣya) as being distinct, when one investigates the eightfold four truths, neither the essence nor the function of parikalpita (imagined nature) exists;
therefore, both the characteristic and the characterized are without distinction.

It is not meant that the "I" which arrives is what is called the "discriminating subject"; rather, this statement means that the *nimittabhāga* (image-part) is what is grasped by the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part), and is thus the "object discriminated.
It does not mean that my own *svasaṃvedanabhāga* (self-verifying part) takes the *nimittabhāga* as its object in a relationship of subject and object.
This [self-verifying part] is what is metaphorically designated as the "I."

Regarding the resolution of the provisional and the real according to the needs of the case: An-hui [Sthiramati] explains that those who have personally realized the two parts [of consciousness] understand that the self is a provisional construct and that the transformation of consciousness is the Buddha-self;

others rely on the real existence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and based on this, they cling to the grasper and the grasped as being real—these are then considered provisional phenomena.
These two interpretations are as explained in the first commentary.

Regarding the phrase "or because both [masters] prove it to be with outflows (*sāsrava*)," this interpretation holds that both masters exclude the Buddha and other untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*), because the verse states "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*), which among the five dharmas exists only as something with outflows.
According to Sthiramati’s commentary, the subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) of a Bodhisattva also possesses the two grasps (*dvaya-grāha*);
in reality, these are entirely non-existent, and it is not only the case that they are with outflows. This is stated merely according to their predominant presence. And so it is said.

Regarding the statement that "outflowing [phenomena] and external objects encompass both the grasper and the grasped," this means that the false attachment to real grasper and grasped is collectively termed "external objects"; for instance,
although the mind of another is an external object, it is also termed a "grasper" when one so conceives of it.
"Corresponding with the fetters of craving for desire and so forth" means that all three realms possess these fetters of craving for desire and so forth;
that is, the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms are associated with and bound to these fetters of craving, such as greed, and thus it is said that "the three realms are mind only.
Alternatively, the phrase "craving for desire and so forth" refers here to the Desire Realm and the other two realms.
This refers to the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) that pertains to the mind and mental factors belonging to this realm.

Furthermore, regarding the Sautrāntika position that [the mind] reaches the basis for manifestation and so forth: the Sautrāntikas maintain that the mind and mental factors of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) observe only space;
this observed space is a characteristic of formlessness and lacks any substantial reality as an object of apprehension (*grāhya*).
The meaning of "object" (*viṣaya*) is defined as being free from all obstructions; this is what is called "manifestation.

Since those minds and mental factors take only this manifestation of empty space as their support, once the meaning of "object" is absent, they become identical to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Therefore, fearing that the Sautrāntikas might hold [these] to be non-mental phenomena, [the author] states this.

Furthermore, regarding the previous two masters' statement that it refers only to the "three realms": in both of their preceding expositions of the verse’s term *vibhāga* (differentiation), they explained it as referring to false and out-flowing (*sāsrava*) minds and so forth;
therefore, here it is stated that the three realms are "mind-only" (*cittamātra*).

Regarding the statement that "the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) is solely emptiness and not a single real entity," etc.: the object observed by the concentration observing emptiness is that all things are empty;
it is not a real person, nor is there a real entity that is observed as empty. If [emptiness] were itself a real entity that is empty, it would constitute a contradiction.
Furthermore, it is not the case that what is seen by humans, ghosts, and so forth is real and mutually contradictory. Moreover, many editions read "not one" (*naika*) instead of "not a real entity."
The substantial entity (*dravya*) is superior from the perspective of principle.

As for the phrase "contemplation through mental resolution" (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) and so forth, it refers to cases where something that is not actually gold or a jewel is mentally resolved upon as being gold or a jewel;
since this involves a transformation of substance (*bhāvānyathātva*) and lacks the functional utility of gold, it is not what is being discussed here.

That which takes the substance of consciousness as its object means that it takes the substance of consciousness as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This nature is of two kinds: first, the thing (*vastu*), and second, the principle (*artha*).
"Thing" refers to the substance of consciousness; "principle" refers to the underlying meaning, namely the basis for such concepts as "self" (*ātman*) and so forth.
Both of these take consciousness as their own essence; the objects apprehended by the mind and other faculties do not depart from this intrinsic nature of consciousness.
Regarding the fear that this constitutes the fallacy of the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*): in reality, this is not inconclusive.

It is feared that the opponent might consider [the example] to be a case where the direct condition (*pratyakṣa-pratyaya*) is separated from its own dharma; therefore, this is refuted. Question: The opponent accepts that the five consciousnesses directly perceive external objects, and that these objects are themselves dharmas.

Since this is now used as an analogy, it would follow that the "probandum" (*sādhya*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). Answer: There are two interpretations. The first says: "This refers to a distinct dharma-object (*viṣaya-dharma*)."
Regarding the five objects (*viṣaya*) being non-dharmas: just as the visual consciousness is established, the auditory [consciousness] serves as the analogy.
Second, even if all five were dharmas, since the previous formal argument has already established that they are not separate from consciousness, there is no deficiency in the thesis (*sādhya*).

The meaning of this passage—that "this direct object of cognition reaches the same state as its corresponding subject"—also includes the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) that cognizes the aspect (*ākāra*);
for within the pair of subject and object, it is one of the two, just like self-cognition itself.

By virtue of these dharmas, one arrives at that which cannot serve as a cause; this refers to the statement in the treatise that "the dharma which is the object-condition (ālambana) is the causal dharma.

Now, in establishing a thesis (pakṣa) that possesses substantial existence, one must necessarily employ a reason (hetu) that possesses substantial existence. Therefore, this present reason is a dharma possessing substantial existence.
Since empty flowers are non-existent dharmas, they do not enter into the reason, for they are not objects of cognition.

However, because it is stated generally as "associated," it applies to the mind; for if the treatise speaks of "dharmas associated with the mind" (*cittasaṃprayuktadharma*), this refers exclusively to mental factors (*caitta*), whereas if it simply speaks of "associated dharmas" (*saṃprayuktadharma*), it includes both the mental factors and the mind-king (*cittarāja*). This is the meaning of the treatise.
Regarding the statement that "first one leaves existence and later one leaves non-existence," do not take the ultimate truth and conventional phenomena as being first and last;

for in this treatise, the initial mention of "self and dharmas" constitutes the departure from existence, while the subsequent mention of "emptiness and consciousness" constitutes the departure from non-existence.

Regarding the statement that "the three characters in the middle are all in the seventh case (locative)," there are two interpretations: First, it is said that the three characters in the middle are all in the seventh case. In the context of the term *ālambana* (object), they are placed in the middle according to the locative case (*adhikaraṇa*).

This is like saying "consciousness within the eye" (*cakṣuṣi vijñānam*), where "within" (*madhye*) is also used in the locative sense. Second, it is said that the character "middle" (*zhōng*, 中) is an error and should be "equal" (*děng*, 等).

That treatise uses the word "place" (*chù*, 處), whereas this verse says "middle. Therefore, it should read: "The three characters in the middle are all equal to the seventh case. This is because that treatise states "place," while this verse says "middle. Thus, the meaning is that these three characters are equivalent to the seventh case.
Regarding your inquiry as to why the latter interpretation is considered correct for the character "zhong" (middle) between the two passages:

from the perspective of principle, although all four matters are generally applicable, the *dharmakāya* cannot be said to apply to non-sentient things; therefore, when it is said that they are all applicable, this refers to sentient beings.
This is because both place (*sthāna*) and time (*kāla*) are also applicable to sentient beings, as in the expressions "the king’s place," "sovereign time," and so forth.
As for those who claim it is "pervasive" (*vyāpya*), this can be inferred from the pervasive concentration (*vyāpya-samādhi*) and reflection (*manasikāra*).
Regarding the statement in the old *Tattvārtha-śāstra* (Paramārtha’s translation) that "place and time are entirely without fixedness," etc.: "place and time" refers to fixed concentration;
that treatise challenges [the notion of] a fixed continuity by asserting it is non-fixed, whereas our current challenge asserts there is no such non-fixity. The rest may be explained accordingly.

The external inference states: "That which reaches another place cannot be seen by others. This inference is consistent with the facts, for instance, when ghosts, humans, and gods occupy the same location at the same time, only one sees water while the others do not;

therefore, this inference should state: "When many continuums occupy the same location at the same time, such as on Mount Zhongnan, it must necessarily be that only one sees it while others cannot see it. This constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*). This is the reason (*hetu*).
This is illustrated by the commentary (*śāstra*).

However, it should be stated that there are mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), because both [schools] agree that these are not separate from the mind.

Second, regarding the five material sense faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) and so forth: this refers to the five faculties and the eighth [consciousness], the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of which the Hinayānists have not yet accepted.
Therefore, for now, let us set this aside and simply discuss the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*). If that is so, since the seed is not established in the Hīnayāna, how can it be spoken of?
The answer is: although they do not admit seeds within the eighth consciousness, seeds are indeed mentioned in the sūtras of the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*;
thus, they speak of them as "roots. The "two" mentioned here refers precisely to the second meaning among the twenty meanings in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and is not the former category.

Regarding the second section within the "Dispelling External Doubts," because the phrase "not explaining the intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*)" and so forth constitutes the second [point], it does not state that there are truly existent beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
As for the question: "Since the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is produced by karma and is composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), why is it not real?"—the answer is:
because the body of the intermediate state arises instantaneously and ceases instantaneously; it is not like the characteristics of existence in the [subsequent] life (*pūrvakālabhava*).
Furthermore, because there is a concern that they might grasp [the self] as a real sentient being or a real "I" over a long period of time, it is not the actual truth;
rather, it is taught cryptically as being similar to what exists for them from the beginning.

Regarding the statement that "the wisdom of the true essence (*tattva-jñāna*) reaches the realization of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)," this means that while the previous fundamental question concerned the nature of consciousness as the dependent, the present treatise provides the answer.

To say that it is not the case that there is no correct cognition (samyagjñāna) realized through that which is beyond words, and that the correct cognition which realizes [it] is itself suchness (tathatā), would contradict the intent of the question;

therefore, this interpretation states that the self-realization and the objective aspect of the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (mūlaprajñā) are also the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā).

Regarding the statement "present cognition is like a dream," etc.: although this dharma and its metaphor are not entirely similar, it is used as a metaphor because, just as in a dream one does not clearly grasp [objects] as real while they appear externally, present cognition is likewise.

Regarding the phrase "when present cognition arises," etc., it means that when a grasping mind arises from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the object seen by that direct perception is [simultaneously] absent; this is because schools such as the Saṃmitīya maintain that the object is long-lasting.
At that time, when only the mind remains in an intermittent state, it cannot be said that the object of perception has ceased; rather, it is because the "mind-only" that perceives has ceased.
This is stated by combining the views of both masters.

However, the actual explanation—that the five [consciousnesses] up to the *vijñāna* involve false attachment—is particularly distinct from the common interpretation and also contradicts the treatise, as it would likewise apply to the five consciousnesses.

Since the simultaneous consciousness (*sahaja-vijñāna*) that arises together with innate afflictions (*kleśa*) cannot give rise to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), how could it be possible for the five sense-consciousnesses to possess false attachment?
The preceding treatise itself states: "The subsequent mind discriminates and falsely gives rise to external perceptions.

Why is this so contradictory [to your claim]? However, according to the correct interpretation of the former masters regarding vitarka and vicāra, the five [sense-consciousnesses] are without vitarka and vicāra.

Since the conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is indeed admitted to exist, what fault is there in the false attachment of the mental consciousness that arises simultaneously with the five [sensory] consciousnesses?
This merely clarifies the correct principle and does not refute others; this has already been established by following the masters previously.

Now, since the Hīnayāna opponent objects, saying that it is only the five consciousnesses that apprehend external objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and that the mental consciousness is not said to grasp external objects, we now explain: the five consciousnesses...

The objects of perception appear as external things grasped by the mind, yet in reality they do not apprehend an external world; rather, they are like objects in a dream, which are not truly external.
This is the correct interpretation that establishes the true meaning without refuting the Hīnayāna.

Regarding the question: "Just as when one takes another's mind as a condition, one sees only the appearance of one's own mind and can thus be said to see one's own mind again, how can it be said that one sees the original object again when a mirror-image appears in a mirror by taking the original object as a condition? The answer is: The mirror has no real image; it is simply because of the mirror that [the reflection arises]. By means of the mirror, the original object is made manifest. Just as the face is not actually inside the mirror, yet by virtue of the mirror, the face is seen outside; so too, although the mind does not go out to the external object, by virtue of the object, the mind perceives the object. Therefore, it is said that one sees the original object again. Furthermore, because the mind perceives the object, it is called "seeing"; because the object is perceived by the mind, it is called "being seen. Thus, there is no fault in saying that one sees the original object again. It is like a person looking at their own face in a mirror: although they do not see the face within the mirror, they see the face outside. Likewise, although the mind does not go out to the external object, it perceives the object by virtue of the object. Therefore, it is said that one sees the original object again. This is the meaning of the statement that one sees the original object again. Question: When a facial image appears upon one's own consciousness, resembling the original object, it is called "seeing the object.
Does visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) also take a mirror-image as its object? Answer: Visual consciousness, being direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), does not take false objects as its domain;

however, because mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes the eye as its gateway to apprehend the reflected image, some also allow that the five consciousnesses can take such [images] as their objects, according to the two previous explanations.

Regarding the phrase "the outflow [of that] and so forth" (*tad-anvaya-ādi*), some editions use the character *jian* (簡), which is an error; it refers back to the "transforming cause" (*pariṇāma-hetu*) mentioned previously, hence the term "that interval" (*pi jian*).

However, according to the first interpretation, "outflow and so forth" refers to the initial part of the explanation of outflow, namely: first, the production of seeds from seeds and seeds [from seeds].
The first interpretation is that "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) refers collectively to both the produced (*jāta*) and the manifest (*pratyutpanna*).

If one were to provide a separate explanation later, it would mean that only the preceding and succeeding seeds are outflow-seeds, while the production of the manifest is the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and sovereign influence (*adhipati*). This is the latter interpretation.
Here, according to the first interpretation, "outflow" is broad and inclusive; this "maturation" (*vipāka*) encompasses all seeds, which is precisely as stated previously.

In the second fascicle, regarding the explanation of the two causes—*niṣyanda* (outflow) and *vipāka* (maturation)—the熏習 (*vāsanā*, habitual tendencies) are as stated below; the preceding and succeeding [sections] should all be understood accordingly.

If one follows the latter explanation—that [they arise] because they reach the mind and so forth—then, according to this latter interpretation, since it concerns only the preceding and succeeding seeds, [the text continues as follows].
The outflow (niṣyanda) is the arising of the manifest from the seed, which may be termed "human effort" (puruṣakāra); since this has already been explained previously, it is not mentioned again here.

Rather, it is stated that attention (manaskāra), in relation to the mind, constitutes human effort, because it exerts a superior influence despite being somewhat remote. This [definition] refers to the human effort of dharmas.

If, according to the former interpretation, the name "arising" refers to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), then since the former interpretation already takes the arising of the manifest from the seed as a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*), it is by looking back at that distant [cause] that the activity of the person is designated as the fruit of human effort; this is the human effort of that person.
If subsequent liberation is called the "dominant fruit" (*adhipatiphala*), then since that subsequent liberation is itself a result of its own seed, it is a "flowing-on fruit" (*niṣyandaphala*);

thus, the arising of the manifest from the seed is designated as the dominant fruit. The word "also" in this context also includes the "virile fruit" (*puruṣakāraphala*), as this has already been explained previously.
The subsequent passage, "the same applies to the pure dharmas," serves as proof that the preceding interpretation holds that *vikalpa* (conceptualization) is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
By this principle, since it is stated that [only] the seeds capable of producing [results] are taken, one should know that in the subsequent analogy regarding the pure,
the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) is likewise not included.

Regarding the statement that "the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [dharmas] do not exhaustively include their results": among the uncontaminated results, the result of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is excluded; thus, there are four results.
As will be explained below, all seeds of the conditioned uncontaminated are not included within those four results because they exclude the result of disconnection (*visamyogaphala*);

therefore, it is said that they are not exhaustive. How is this known? Because within the subsequent pure dharmas (*śuddhadharma*), the result of disconnection is mutually not included. Prior to this...
Since the subsequent passages all contain the sense of "being able to produce," we know that even within the pure [dharmas], the fruit of disconnection (visamyoga-phala) is not included.
As the treatise itself later states: "Because pure seeds and manifest activities arise with [other factors] as conditions. Therefore, it is said here that the fruit of disconnection is excluded;
by this standard, the four fruits pertain to the contaminated (sāsrava), while the uncontaminated (anāsrava) possesses only three.
Regarding those that function through three conditions, the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) is excluded.

As for "the cause of manifest activity and the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and so forth," this means that the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which act as manifest perfumers (*vāsana*), are not subsumed under the causal condition when viewed in relation to their ripened manifest fruits, because they do not occur successively. Likewise, present karma is also not a causal condition in relation to its fruit.
Because they do not belong to the same category.

Regarding the statement that "in the Buddha-fruit, [the seeds] do not even reach the point of being perfumed to form seeds," one should say here that the eight consciousnesses of the Buddha-fruit do not perfume to form seeds;
the word "only" refers to the eighth [consciousness], as the commentary is abbreviated.

In the *Sarvāstivāda*, when discussing causes as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are six types of causes: first, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); second, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); third, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*);

fourth, the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*); fifth, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*); and sixth, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*). Only the first, the efficient cause, is not said to be a causal condition.
In the eighteenth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, these five causes are extensively refuted; fearing prolixity, they are not cited here.
Regarding the question of how the preceding extinguished single mind and the subsequent minds and mental factors can have equal objects when their quantities are unequal:
the answer is that because the mind and its mental factors are conjoined as if they were one, they are termed "equal" despite their numerical differences.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "equal" up to "equal to only one": the question is, what is the difference between this and the meaning of being designated as a *śramaṇa*?

The answer is: in that case [of the *śramaṇa*], it is merely that feeling (*vedanā*) serves as the condition for feeling, and perception (*saṃjñā*) serves as the condition for perception, without looking toward other dharmas.

In this case [of the "equal"], although it is a single mind and a single object, it can look toward other dharmas because it functions as a condition-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Therefore, it differs from that; however, because it is not multiple dharmas, it constitutes "equality."
Furthermore, regarding those who enter the state of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) but do not pass away while in an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind:

this refers to Arhats liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*) who, through the power of their vows, attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and then pass away. Others who are not liberated both ways, as well as those lacking such vow-power, do not [attain it].
If one can ask such a question, it must be that at the time of death one abides in a distracted state of mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), not in a mindless meditative absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*).

Having already raised this point, why is it said here that one dies from the cessation absorption (*nirodha-samāpatti*)? The answer is: for an Arhat, within the cessation absorption, there are the seven and eight consciousnesses;

since these are exclusively *sāsrava* (tainted), they cannot coexist with the meditative absorption itself, and thus they are indeed a distracted state of mind. To say that one dies "not in a mindless absorption" refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those who lack the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
Because it is so stated, there is no contradiction. As for the distinct interpretation of the "gate," it is as explained in the third [chapter].
Regarding the phrase "the benefit of subsequent retribution leading to birth in the abode of wisdom":

the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* states that "the benefit of subsequent retribution" refers to the attainment of benefit by the final body and mind; "birth in the abode of wisdom" refers to the palace of Maheśvara.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the place where beings of great wisdom dwell is visited by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, and it is called 'Birth There' because one receives the status of a Buddha as a reward in the present life":
receiving the status of a Buddha in one's current body is what is meant by "benefit in the present life."

However, regarding the phrase "because their maturation belongs to the same stage": this means that when a Bodhisattva who has attained the sudden teaching reaches the eighth stage, they undergo the transformation of rebirth (*pariṇāmiki-jāti*) and must be born in one of the three lower levels of the fourth dhyāna.
The statement here that they are "born in the abode of wisdom" refers to what is called "birth" because they go there;
it is called "birth" because the three lower heavens and the Palace of Sovereignty (*Vaśavartin*) belong to the same stage.
Regarding the phrase "reaching as far as the three heavens of receptivity," some editions read "according to reality" (*yathābhūta*), which is superior from a logical standpoint.

Regarding the phrase "the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that it reaches the abode of mastery": if one asks whether there are further abodes beyond the Śuddhāvāsa [heavens] such that the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*) would then consist of nineteen heavens, some offer this explanation:
although it is said to "surpass" them, it is still subsumed within Akaniṣṭha; therefore, [the count remains seventeen].

Regarding the eighteen [abodes], some say they are comprised within the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) and the Heaven of Vast Fruit (bṛhatphala); thus, by opening up the stage of mastery (vaśitā), there are eighteen.
This interpretation is correct.
If it is admitted that the Buddha also goes there, it is as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*: "From the Bodhi tree at the Vajrāsana, he taught the ten periods of time."
In the ocean of realms, he further proceeded to the palace of Śakra and even to the first and second dhyānas, preaching the Dharma throughout them all.

Regarding those born in the Form Realm who are reborn in the Desire Realm: this refers to those Non-returners (anāgāmin) who resolve their minds in the Desire Realm and receive a body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*) there;
it does not refer to those born in the Form Realm who necessarily resolve their minds in the Desire Realm and undergo rebirth, for such individuals lack the moisture of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because the power of past karma has been exhausted. Regarding the question: why was the first fruit mentioned previously, yet here the non-returner fruit (*anāgāmin*) is discussed? The answer is:

the previous question concerned those who can be born in the higher realms; since the non-returner is also included among those who have attained the first and second fruits, etc., it is mentioned here as well within that category.

This differs from those who have attained the first and second fruits; for after generating the resolve for enlightenment, those in the first and second fruits may still undergo one or many more births within the desire realm, yet they must necessarily experience a transformation of the body within the desire realm.
For those who have not yet attained the meditative absorption of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*), the fourth dhyāna serves as that ultimate limit.

Regarding the statement that "defiled consciousness acts as both condition and result": "as condition" refers to the fact that being contaminated (*sāsrava*) acts as the condition capable of inducing the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);
"and result" refers to the contaminated states induced from the uncontaminated. This refers to the seventh [consciousness] throughout these preceding and succeeding phases of existence.
However, regarding the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [dharmas] induced by the Desire and Form Realms, it may be argued that they can also extend to the Formless Realm.

As for why this treatise states that contaminated [dharmas] induce uncontaminated ones, yet here it speaks of contaminated fruits induced by the uncontaminated—the meaning of the commentary is as follows:

the contaminated dharmas of the lower realms induced by the seventh [consciousness] allow the uncontaminated to extend to the Formless Realm; subsequently, when uncontaminated [dharmas] arise later, they in turn [induce] the latter.
It is said that they are "fruits" because they induce the seventh consciousness with outflows (*sāsrava*) belonging to the lower realms.

However, they do not mutually induce one another through a single acquisition (*prāpti*); for the lower realms lack the untainted (*anāsrava*), while the upper realms lack the unwholesome (*akuśala*), and thus these cannot be mutually induced between the upper and lower realms.

Furthermore, although the wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*) and the resultant mind (*vipāka-citta*) exist in both the upper and lower realms, they likewise do not [mutually induce one another].
Because it gives rise to no difficulty, the eighth [consciousness]—the mutual induction of the upper and lower realms as maturation—is not what is being discussed here.
As for the phrase "it is permissible," the treatise merely states that each is permitted to act as a condition of equal immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the other;

it does not mean that every single instance of the outflowing (*sāsrava*), non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), wholesome, or unwholesome [states] within the three realms is capable of mutually inducing one another. There is a commentary that provides three [explanations].
Each of these [interpretations] is an error.

Regarding the view that "the five [consciousnesses] can arise interchangeably," one asks: how does this master allow for uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) to rely upon contaminated faculties (*sāsrava-indriya*)?
The answer is that this does not rely on contaminated faculties; it follows the position of the first master regarding the five faculties, such as the eye, as presented in the fourth fascicle.
If the seeds of the five consciousnesses are already untainted (*anāsrava*), then their seeds are likewise untainted;

furthermore, since these five consciousnesses take the untainted mental consciousness as their simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), this does not contradict reason. [Objection: Although this interpretation is logically consistent, it contradicts the subsequent treatise.
Since this master does not admit that they rely on tainted (*sāsrava*) faculties, how can he establish that the tainted five sense-faculties do not give rise to untainted consciousness?

Regarding the charge of "contradiction with what has already been established" (*sādhya-sama*), this former master establishes his thesis based on his own fundamental tenets, whereas the latter master relies on the fact that the existence of the five material sense-faculties has already been proven; therefore, there is no fault of contradiction.

Regarding the argument that one should establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) [stating] that "untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) and so forth must arise," this inference is subject to the fallacy of being counterbalanced by a contradictory inference (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*). [The counter-inference is:

"The five untainted sense-faculties (*indriya*) should give rise to untainted consciousness, because they are untainted and non-common faculties (*asādhāraṇa-indriya*), just like the sixth [consciousness] in the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-darśana*) or the seventh consciousness.
Since there is this fault, how can the original inference be established? [Answer: Within the inference that puts forward the fault, you yourself have committed the same error.

If one asks: "How is it that even when the original measure is exceeded, the same fault remains? The answer is: The thesis (pakṣa) commits the fault of contradicting scripture and contradicting its own tenets;

the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntika). For example, [the opponent argues]: "Because the seventh consciousness (*manas*) in the state of emptiness of sentient beings is with-outflow (*sāsrava*), do the five sense organs (*indriya*) not likewise give rise to outflow-free (*anāsrava*) consciousness?
Or, because the seventh consciousness in the state of being with-outflow is with-outflow, do the five outflow-afflicted sense organs not likewise fail to give rise to outflow-free consciousness?"
Furthermore, when establishing a thesis based on valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one should state: "The five contaminated sense faculties do not give rise to the five uncontaminated consciousnesses.
Since the word "five" is added within this formulation, there is no fault of contradiction.

Regarding the statement, "If one follows the former master, there is no contradiction with principle," etc.: since the former master maintains that the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) possesses the five consciousnesses and allows for them to be untainted (*anāsrava*), there is no contradiction with principle.
The latter master, however, holds that the transformation body lacks the nose and tongue consciousnesses.

This is explained in terms of those of sudden enlightenment, who attain the transformation body at the eighth stage (*bhūmi*); thus, it is said that they project [the next life] from whichever realm they depart, as appropriate.
Regarding the statement "the five untainted consciousnesses (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) and so forth," there are two explanations. The first says it is in terms of the body (*kāya*):

according to the former master, when the untainted five consciousnesses first arise, they must do so within a body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because only a body of the desire realm enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Therefore, those eighth [consciousnesses] and so forth arise within a body of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). The second says it is in terms of the consciousness (*vijñāna*): when the untainted five consciousnesses first arise, they must necessarily be in the desire realm.
Regarding the realms, the subsequent arising of the five contaminated consciousnesses occurs because the five consciousnesses are fully present within the desire realm;

the subsequent arising of the uncontaminated [consciousnesses] also extends to the form realm, as that realm possesses its own uncontaminated five consciousnesses capable of inducing them. Between these two explanations, the latter is correct.

The previous clarification regarding the three consciousnesses did not take the physical bases (āśraya) into account; therefore, the statement "according to what is appropriate" refers to the nose and tongue consciousnesses.
Because two consciousnesses do not belong to the higher realms, and because within the three realms there is no formless realm [where such would apply], it is said that they "correspond accordingly.
When these eight consciousnesses are combined to serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), there are four types of mind in the desire realm:

the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the two types of neutral. In the form and formless realms, the unwholesome is excluded, and the two untainted minds—the learner’s (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner’s (*aśaikṣa*)—are added.

Thus, there are twelve [minds] in total: within the wholesome, the preparatory (*prayoga*) and innate (*upapatti-lābhika*) are distinguished; within the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*), four types are distinguished. Specifically, in the desire realm there are eight minds;
in the form realm there are six, excluding the unwholesome and the artisanal (*śailpasthānika*);

in the formless realm there are four, further excluding the deportment (*airyāpathika*) and transformation (*nairmāṇika*). To these are added the two minds of the trainee (*śaikṣa*) and the non-trainee (*aśaikṣa*), which are not bound to any realm (*apratisaṃyukta*). In sum, there are [twelve].

Twenty moments of mind serve as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). However, since the desire realm lacks the transformational mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*), which is not a [mental] state, there are actually only nineteen or more;

in the two upper realms, the untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) replace those of the trainee and the non-trainee, their number being the same as previously stated, as explained in detail in the *Dīpa*.
Regarding the statement that the "perceiving aspect" (*darśana-bhāga*) is also called an "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) because it reaches [the object], a question is asked:

"What is the difference between this remote object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana*), which also transforms into an internal image, and the immediate [object-condition]? The answer is: With respect to the immediate object-condition, the perceiving aspect and its objective essence are not separate;

since the objective essence is precisely what is internally reflected upon by the perceiving aspect, it is called "immediate. Now, as for what is called "remote," although the primary substance (*bimba*) acts as a condition capable of giving rise to a reflected image (*pratibimba*), [it is remote] because...
Furthermore, because the transformational aspect (nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa) resembles its material cause (upādāna), and is described in terms of that cause, it is called "distant" (*sū*).
Regarding the phrase "because the seeds of sentient beings are not all equal," the *Śū* commentary explains: "The three vehicles and five lineages are each distinct and unequal in their numbers;

how, then, can they serve as mutual supports? [This] asks: since the eighth consciousness with outflows (*sāsrava-aṣṭama-vijñāna*) does not take uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) as its object, how can this be established?
Question: Is it difficult to establish the five natures? Answer: This is stated in reference to both ordinary beings and sages; therefore, there is no fault. Question:

When a Buddha’s eighth consciousness conditions that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*), the substrate (*bimba*) and the image (*pratibimba*) differ in being contaminated or uncontaminated, yet they are still able to rely upon one another.

Now, although the quantity of seeds belonging to oneself and others differs, what logical contradiction is there in taking the other as the substrate? Answer: It is said that the former master maintains that [the eighth consciousness] must necessarily rely upon...

Since the principle that the substantial entity (*dravya*) and its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) must necessarily be equal in number, this objection is raised: "The Buddha allows for the support of outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) [dharmas] by others, yet their numbers remain equal; thus there is no logical fault. Since the sense organs (*indriya*) of self and other are equal, you should allow for the production [of dharmas] supported by others. My original intention was to refute the opponent, not to turn back and expose their position as being incapable of withstanding scrutiny; furthermore, it reveals that the reasoning of the former master is also contradictory.

One should challenge the former master as follows: "While you may allow for the mutual functioning of the number of sense faculties (*indriya*) belonging to oneself and others as conditions, how can you allow for such mutual dependence when the seeds (*bīja*) of self and other are not equal?"
Regarding the phrase "because the five factors of the Buddha-fruit lack independent power," this meaning is difficult to explain in detail.
Furthermore, when untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) directly realizes *tathatā*, how could it rely on the transformations of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as its objective support?

Moreover, since the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) can manifest all bodies—the reflections of the five wisdoms—how could it not be able to transform the reflections of the past and future itself? Why, then, must it rely upon the mind-king? Furthermore, there is no... [text continues].
If, in the state of outflows (*āsrava*), wisdom is strong and consciousness is weak, how can it be that mental factors themselves lack power? Therefore, they are certainly not similar to their cause.

The *Śū* (the *Vyākhyā*) states: "Being similar to the cause refers, for the time being, to cases such as the appropriation of seeds where [mental factors] rely on the objects transformed by the sovereign mind-king;
it does not mean all [cases]."
Since it is not the case that [the seventh consciousness] arises depending on an objective basis (*ālambana*) merely because it is not the result of karma, this point means the following:

Because the eighth consciousness is the fruit of karma, its own power is superior and it does not necessarily require an objective basis. However, because the co-emergent [seventh consciousness] lacks such power, it must rely on the power of an objective basis to arise.

Question: In the case of the man-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), as well as wholesome minds that take the past or future as their object, these too are not the fruit of karma; how could they possibly have an objective basis?

Yaśomitra replies: These [minds] also possess their own superior power and differ from the seventh [consciousness], which arises spontaneously and simultaneously; therefore, they are not mentioned here.

Regarding the preceding five classes of mind, that which necessarily has a real object (*bhāva*) is easy to understand and is thus called "coarse" (*audārika*); because it is not profound, it is called "dull" (*mṛdu*);

because it lacks the power to arise by itself and is induced by another, it is called "inferior" (*hīna*). This statement—that in the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one must rely upon a real object—refers for the time being to karma.
This is because it takes the eighth consciousness induced by the power [of meditative concentration] as its objective support (*ālambana*).

However, if one considers the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of meditative absorption, they do not necessarily have an objective support, as in the case of the divine eye seeing the three calamities of the lower realms; such examples are numerous. Some say that this [divine eye] also has an objective support, taking the three calamities transformed by the eighth consciousness of the lower realm as its support.
Regarding the statement that "the five consciousnesses within the causal stage reach the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)," this refers to their own nature:
it is asserted that the subjective cognizer and its objective aspect mutually serve as the substantial basis (*bimba*) for one another.

As for the phrase "capable of [serving as] the preceding object-condition for others," the preceding object-condition is established solely in relation to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), acting as their support.

Therefore, with respect to all things that are not concordant—that is, those which are contrary—it is not the case that there is no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because [the mind] does not lack an object.

As for the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) in relation to phenomena that have not yet arisen up to those that have not yet ceased: since it has passed away and lacks substantial existence (*avastu*), it cannot serve as a condition;
however, it does serve as a condition for phenomena such as the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth.
Alternatively, the phrase "only the third [kāraka] reaches the point of having no function" refers to the establishment of the third [kāraka].

Just as when accomplishing tasks such as craftsmanship, there must necessarily be an agent (*kartṛ*) and an instrument (*karaṇa*), and because the causal role of the instrument is most prominent, it is specifically said that the third has a function, while it is not the case that the others lack it.
Furthermore, another commentary states: "Alternatively, 'only the first three' is superior in terms of logic; the character 'third' (*di*) is an error."
Furthermore, those who grasp objects and continue the lineage are the six sense faculties, such as the eye, as well as male and female; the rest may be understood by analogy.

Third, regarding "not grasping the preceding stage": the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) does not grasp the stages of the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the application (*prayoga*).
Since this [text] concerns only those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and asks specifically about those that are "unbound" (*apratisaṃyukta*), it does not include them.

As stated in the *Pañcāśatikā* (Treatise on the Fifty): "Regarding the phrase 'the first untainted faculty' (*anāsrava-indriya*) up to 'and those unbound,' [it refers to the untainted faculties]; as for the phrase 'bound to the form realm' (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), it is because the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are bound only to that [realm].

However, even within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), one also cultivates those meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), and thus they are also bound to the form realm. This is the commentary.

In this context, only those [faculties] determined to be wholesome are selected; because the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) mostly involves abiding in the external gates, they are omitted here.

Question: In the preceding text (at verse 57), it was stated that three faculties are entirely unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*); why then does the subsequent text state that these faculties also pertain to the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?

Answer: In the aforementioned treatise, the question asked was "How many faculties pertain to the unbound? and thus it answered "three faculties," namely the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

Because the faculties (indriya) extend to the untainted (anāsrava), and because these faculties subsequently extend across the three states, it is said that one [faculty] is bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-baddha) and is also unbound (apratisaṃyukta).

The *Pañcāśatika-śāstra* (Treatise on Fifty-seven [Verses]) states that seven faculties enter the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu): the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā), along with the mind (manas), equanimity (upekṣā), and the latter three [faculties].

There are those who can enter [the formless realm] and those who cannot. This refers to those who have transcended the first two fruits, as well as those liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) and bodhisattvas;

this class is able to enter the formless realm by means of three faculties. Others, such as those who attain the fruits through gradual succession and those liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta), are of a class that cannot enter the formless realm by means of these three faculties.

Regarding the statement that eleven faculties can be obtained in the spheres of Infinite Space and so forth, up to the Sphere of Nothingness—when it says "eleven faculties can be obtained," it refers to the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), the faculty of mind (*manas*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*). Question:

In the text following verse 57, it states that only seven faculties enter the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), yet it does not mention the life-faculty. Why is this, given that the preceding text speaks of eleven being obtainable?

The answer is that the attainment [of the formless realm] includes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). If one’s body belongs to a lower realm and attains that meditative absorption, there is no life-faculty;
thus, seven faculties enter the formless realm. However, if one is born in that realm with a body belonging to it, then the life-faculty exists.
Therefore, the statement that "eleven faculties can be obtained" differs from this meaning of "obtainable," and thus the two passages are distinct.
Regarding the statement that "the Stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (asaṃjñi-bhūmi) possesses only eight [faculties]": Question:

Since one who enters the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) must necessarily take the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) as the preparatory stage (prayoga), and since this entry involves the untainted (anāsrava), one would then enter via the latter two faculties (the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure and the faculty of equanimity). Why, then, is the Stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception not mentioned in this context? Answer:

According to the formal classification (*saṃgraha*) in the treatises, the untainted [faculties] of that stage also possess these two faculties. However, the term "faculty" (*indriya*) carries the sense of being preeminent and productive; therefore, [it is not mentioned here].
Because their investigation of the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) is extremely weak, that treatise mentions only eight [kinds of patience].

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the term "superior" (*viśeṣa*) refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); that is to say, when a certain class of followers of the Two Vehicles first attains the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamādhi*), thereby suppressing the afflictions of the desire and form realms, they enter the path of seeing and leap over the first two fruits.
This is called the "superior path of seeing" because it is superior to its immediate predecessor.
This is "auxiliary cultivation" (*pārśvabhāvanā*).
It is not like the Sarvāstivāda position that one cultivates the four truths through the six preparatory stages (*prayoga-mārga*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)—

whereby one suppresses the afflictions— and then, upon reaching the path of seeing, can also cultivate these three types of knowledge (the knowledges of origin, cessation, and the path) at the conclusion of the subsequent classes of knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

In that [Hīnayāna] system, the capacity of the three types of contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*) increases until they ultimately cease to function; however, in this [Mahāyāna], one cultivates the seeds of contaminated knowledge as a secondary practice and later allows them to manifest—therefore, it is not the same as that system.
Question: Why does the Hīnayāna not cultivate the knowledge of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya-jñāna*)?

Answer: Because that system asserts that the six modes of practice (*ṣaḍ-abhyāsa*) are capable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), the power of the knowledge of the Path increases naturally, and thus there is no need for further cultivation.
It is only threefold.
There is only the cultivation of attainment (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and not the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*). Regarding "attainment," it should be written as "virtue" (*guṇa*).

When virtues are nurtured and increased upon the seeds, it is called the "cultivation of virtue" (*guṇa-bhāvanā*); when the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) increase, it is termed the "cultivation of practice" (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*). Now, there is...

Regarding the statement that the seeds of the knowledge of the outflows (āsrava-jñāna) are cultivated "sideways" within the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), this refers solely to the cultivation of qualities because those qualities increase;
subsequently, upon reaching the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), it is also called "cultivation by practice" (caryā-bhāvanā).
If one follows the Abhidharma, even though it does not accord with ultimate reality, when one enters the path of seeing based on the fourth dhyāna, [the seeds] are cultivated.

Regarding the three lower dhyānas, whether they are with-outflows (sāsrava) or without-outflows (anāsrava), their principle is fixed; those who practice gradually are also capable [of this]. Therefore, these are specifically discussed.
As for the cultivation of the higher [dhyānas], it requires transcending the fruits [of the śrāvaka] and is attained by Bodhisattvas; because this is not fixed, it is not discussed therein.
This refers to those who have already attained the third fruit and beyond. One might ask: how do we know this does not refer to those in the first two fruits? The answer is:

those in the first two fruits frequently give rise to the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) concentration, yet they certainly cannot give rise to the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) regarding the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*) across the nine stages.

If they were to give rise to that wisdom regarding the emptiness of arising, they would have severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the form realm; how then could they be called those in the first or second fruits? Therefore, [this] refers to the third.
The Three Fruits have already been discussed.

Regarding the term "basis" (*āśraya*), it possesses two meanings within the seventh case (*saptamī-vibhakti*): the meaning of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) and the meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*).
In this treatise, when the word "basis" is used, it takes the sense of "locus," meaning that [the cause] is established upon the words as its ground.
Fearing that there might be confusion regarding the meaning, this distinction is made.
As for the three kinds of ten causes, each possesses the natures of wholesome, defiled, and neutral.
However, in reality, they possess only two natures because the causes are neutral and the Buddha-nature is wholesome; thus, there are only two natures.

Regarding the phrase "merely because the three characteristics reach the same basis," this means that the Hīnayāna school only admits the three characteristics and their acquisition (*prāpti*) as pervading the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) according to the phenomena they depend upon;
it does not admit that names follow sounds, and thus it is cited as an illustrative example.

Regarding the statement that "the ineffable characteristic is a common cause (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*) and so forth," their defense is as follows: because characteristics such as form (*rūpa*) pervade all phenomena, they are common causes;

thus, depending on what they rely upon, they may be designated according to the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). However, the term "sound" (*śabda*) alone is not a common cause and therefore does not pervade the three natures.
As for the statement that "in the Mahāyāna, the meaning of 'common cause' applies to all," even the name "Mahāyāna" relies upon the wondrous light.

Because [the sense objects] such as odor and fragrance are common to all, they function as a "common cause" (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*); since their meanings are equally applicable to the three characteristics and to acquisition (*prāpti*), they are analogous to the characteristic of "form" (*rūpa*) in that they pertain to all three moral natures.
As for establishing the meaning based on the substance, the substance of speech is taken as the basis; thus, that which can express meaning is the "conforming cause" (*anuvāda-hetu*) of speech.
It is not different from that which expresses [the object].
There are those who take the capacity to receive as the cause and that which is received as the effect; this refers to the mind first seeking something and the object subsequently responding.

There are also many cases where one takes that which is received as the cause and that which is received as the effect; this refers to depending on feet for coming and going, or depending on hands to grasp objects.
Generally, that which takes what has been received as the cause and that which is capable of receiving as the result is like the arising of a perception after an object has first arrived.

Without questioning whether they are identical or different, that which arrives is called its own result. Regarding "identical nature," this refers to the seeds of verbal designation (*nāma-karma*); regarding "different nature," this refers to the seeds of karma (*karma-bīja*). Question:

Since the seeds of karma and their results are of different natures, how can they be said to correspond? Answer: Virtuous karma invites a fortunate rebirth (*sugati*), while non-virtuous karma invites an unfortunate rebirth (*durgati*).
The "feeling" of the three miserable realms is also called "correspondence.
Furthermore, among the pure causes, that which is the most remote cause refers to the innate untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) within the pure cause;

these are moistened by hearing the teachings from virtuous friends and so forth, subsequently giving rise to the untainted [states] capable of realizing *nirvāṇa*. Thus, one regards these innate seeds...
The untainted wisdom capable of realizing [nirvāṇa] serves as a remote cause, not in the sense that it anticipates nirvāṇa itself.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that a person who abides in the lineage (*gotra*) and is fully endowed with that lineage is able to act as the primary leader in realizing both types of nirvāṇa, including the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder;
this [wisdom] serves as a drawing-in cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) for purification. Fearing that people might not understand this passage, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "Do not... [fear].
Regarding "seeing" and so forth:

however, as for these two and up to the exclusion of the "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) and so on—this means that when the first six consciousnesses induce the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), they necessarily possess neither an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nor a fixed-wholesome (*niyata-kuśala*) nature;
therefore, the six indeterminate faculties (*indriya*) are likewise incapable of producing the six outflow-free consciousnesses. As for the seventh...

The eighth [consciousness] and the preceding thought-moment serve as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*); although they are neutral (*avyākṛta*), they are capable of inducing uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousness.
Regarding the faculties among the sense organs, if the fruit is a neutral material faculty, its cause must necessarily not be an uncontaminated mental faculty;

this is possible because the eighth [consciousness], though having a neutral fruit, is permitted to have the seventh [consciousness] as its faculty, since it is uncontaminated. As for the other consciousnesses...
Since that is not the case, one must make a distinction.

Regarding the passage in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Great Treatise), fascicle 5, which states that "the wholesome and the defiled act as causes," etc., this refers to the reconciliation of apparent contradictions in other texts.

That treatise speaks of seeds sharing the same nature as the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) in terms of being indeterminate; however, it maintains that the manifest activities (*samudācāra*) produced from them do not necessarily follow the nature of the fundamental consciousness, and thus they may be wholesome.

Regarding the statement that "defilement arises from this," it is said that the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and the wholesome (*kuśala*) serve as causes for defilement because this treatise considers the seeds in accordance with their manifestation;

thus, they are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). However, if one examines them by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this cause is narrow, consisting only of seeds of outflow (*niṣyanda-bīja*) and lacking the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*).
It is not said that they obtain a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Regarding the phrase "because this alone is superior among the six contradictions," the six contradictions are explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 38) as:
first, contradiction by verbal expression; second, contradiction by reasoning; third, contradiction by origination; fourth, contradiction by coexistence; fifth... [the text continues].

The six obstacles consisting of enmity and opposition are the counteragents to their opposites; as explained in the *Pradīpa*, that treatise clarifies the basis for hindrances solely by relying on the third type, the opposition of arising.

Regarding the Mahāyāna principle that the characteristic of cessation serves as the cause for the extinction of phenomena: it is like the descent of autumn frost, whereby the green of grasses and trees turns to yellow.
The frost is not the cause for the extinction of the green; rather, the extinction of the green is non-existence (*abhāva*), while the frost is existence (*bhāva*).

Since existence cannot serve as the cause for non-existence, the frost merely serves as the cause for the arising of the yellow. Thus, the frost and other such factors function as causes for the mutual exclusion between green and yellow.

This is the interpretation of the *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*). However, judging by reason, since frost and snow are able to cause greenness to perish, what fault is there in their serving as the cause for that very perishing of greenness?
If this is so, how can it be said that existence has non-existence as its cause? The answer is:
the statement that "an existent dharma cannot serve as a cause for a non-existent dharma" refers to cases where they are not contradictory dharmas; here, however, they are indeed contradictory.
Because it is the opposite of that, it can be established as cessation without cause (*ahetuka-vināśa*), which does not depend on a cause;

this should also be explained accordingly. Otherwise, how could they be called "contradictory"? Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "This [distinction between] conforming and opposing causes operates in four respects.

'Conforming' means causing a phenomenon to arise, abide, be accomplished, and be attained; 'opposing' means causing a phenomenon not to arise, not to abide, not to be accomplished, and not to be attained. Since that...

Granting this, why is it not so? For this reason, the *Vyākhyā* states: "To say that [cold] acts as a cause for the production of subsequent phenomena is merely a provisional explanation regarding the existence of phenomena;
