it does not exhaust the full reasoning. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that while frost and snow can cause greenness to perish, this is because they are incompatible with greenness itself, rather than being incompatible with the perishing of greenness.
Thus, to say they act as causes for the production of phenomena is also consistent with the principle of contradiction.
If this is contradicted, it is because it follows the preceding [analysis]: both the locus (*āśraya*) and the cause (*hetu*) are explained by the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

Why, then, is this contradictory cause alone explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound? If one follows the latter interpretation, it should not contradict the previous examples; thus, one should examine this matter with care.

Answer: Regarding the statement, "Based on the predominant [condition], up to the projecting and producing [causes]," since this asks about the many karmic seeds that project and produce [results], there is no logical contradiction.

As for the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) mentioned below, it does not state that it obtains a matured fruit (*vipāka-phala*); rather, it conforms to the principle that one only obtains a flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
How, then, can it be said here that the projecting cause is subsumed under the predominant condition? [The answer is: Within the context of the projecting cause...

It is also stated that the present [factors] induce the present, as well as the attainment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); all of these are subsumed under the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). Question:
Regarding the intent of that treatise, even if the twelve links were to attain the unconditioned, although it would be a dominant condition, it would not be a "link" (*aṅga*).

What is the proof for this? Answer: It is just as within the links themselves: ignorance (*avidyā*) in relation to wholesome and unwholesome karma, and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in relation to grasping (*upādāna*) and so forth, are already the same.
Since "mutual induction" is also subsumed under the "inducing cause," one should know that there is no contradiction between those questions and answers.

Furthermore, the principle governing the phrase "up to the seeds of karma existing" is as follows: in the preceding question, it was not asked about the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*), but rather only about the "arising cause" (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*).

This is because the text itself later states that the "basis of habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā-adhiṣṭhāna*) obtains its maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) through the projecting cause; therefore, this [present discussion] does not [concern the projecting cause].

Question: Now, judging by this principle, since it is already admitted that there are seeds of unmoistened habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), why would there not also be seeds of karma within those that are moistened?

Furthermore, regarding this passage from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, it should be stated therein that both the projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and the actualizing (*abhinirvartaka*) seeds are productive causes (*janakahetu*).
Who says that the actualizing seed is exclusively a condition-cause (*pratyaya*) and not [a productive cause]?

The *Zengshangyeshu* (Commentary on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*) states: "That this passage is [the one referred to] refers to what was cited immediately prior from the tenth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, namely:
'Based on the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), there are the projecting and actualizing [causes], etc. Furthermore, it says:

"That this passage is [the one referred to] means that throughout the upper and lower sections of this treatise, the explanations regarding the causes of actualization and so forth all refer to internal and external seeds, as well as karmic seeds, etc."
Therefore, one should know that when the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* speaks of "arising" (*utpāda*), it does not refer solely to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Question:

Why is it that here only "arising" is mentioned, while the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*) is not? Answer: Since this refers to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and so forth, it must correspond to the *Vitarkavicārābhūmi*.
Furthermore, because there is no projecting cause in that [latter] stage, it is not mentioned here. Alternatively, some commentaries state that this should be understood by analogy with that [stage].
The term "yan" (言) is a transcription error for "zhuan" (准).

Regarding the statement that the "determining cause" (*niyata-hetu*) leads to the "equal-flow fruit" (*niṣyanda-phala*): the question asks how the equal-flow [fruit] is excluded. The answer is that this explains the seed as the productive agent;
it excludes that which is currently arising and removes seeds such as external barley and the like.

Regarding the statement, "Or it is also included within the 'inducing cause' (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) up to the 'generating cause' (*janaka-hetu*)," this refers to the meaning of "inducing. It includes both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and other factors.

Among these two causes, the manifestation (*pravṛtti*) that perfumes the seeds is both a "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and, within the context of these two causes, is subsumed under the "generating cause," because that manifestation perfumes the seeds.
Although [factors such as] "common activity" (*sahabhū*) share this same sense, they do not correspond to this [specific classification].

Since this has already been combined with the preceding [section], it is not explained in detail here. Regarding the statement that "there are two interpretations below," although there are two interpretations, the intended meaning adopts the latter solution;
for even that which directly produces the fruit is established by the name "seed" because it serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Question: Why does it say that both the present and the seeds are exhausted? Answer: It is because the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* speaks only of the seeds that draw forth (*ākṣepaka*) and produce (*abhinirvartaka*), and thus does not include the seeds of the active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
Furthermore, the *Savitarkādi-bhūmi* speaks only of the cause of production (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*) and does not mention the seeds of production.

Among the six causes, those which are the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for both the present and the seeds are termed "production" (*abhinirvṛtti*); thus, there is a difference in their breadth and narrowness.
Because they are equal, the intent of the present question and answer can be inferred.

Regarding the statement that "one who commits evil does not receive the retribution immediately," this refers to the fact that the fruit of karma is distant; the same applies to its projecting power (*ākṣepa*).

Although the seeds exist due to causes and conditions, because the fruit is remote, the karma is manifest while the name is latent. For this reason, it is not said to be "projecting" (*ākṣepaka*) in the stage of investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra-bhūmi*).
It is cited as the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) because that karma acts as the牵引 (*ākṣepa*, projection).

As for the remaining points regarding the experience (*anubhava*) and the arrival at the two conditions (*pratyaya*), according to the present context of the "bases of the faculties" (*indriyāśraya*), the mental faculty (*manas*) and the basis conforming to true vision (*tattva-darśana-anukūlāśraya*) also possess the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*); however, only the experience and so forth are mentioned here.

The reason why the others are not mentioned is that although there is an immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) in the case of the conforming [condition] and so forth, it lacks an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);

therefore, it is omitted for brevity. Since the treatise speaks of "two conditions" among the [six] conditions, if one considers the functional efficiency (*puruṣakāra*) of phenomena—that is, the efficiency of their activity (*kāritra*)—then the basis of that activity also possesses the immediate condition.

This means that, with the exception of the "conditioning" (*apekṣā*) [condition] up to the "dominant" (*adhipati*) condition, because the three causes [among the six conditions] possess the conditions of immediate succession (*samanantara*), object (*ālambana*), and dominant [conditions], with the exception of a small portion, all others are dominant conditions.
This clarifies that the "conventional expression" (*anuvyavahāra*) and the "contradictory cause" (*virodha-hetu*) are included within the dominant condition.

Regarding the understanding of the essence of non-reaching conditions (*aprāpti-pratyaya*), the treatise states: "Although, as a skillful means, the latter three conditions are internally possessed... and so forth.

This is based on the predominance of non-confusion; if it were based on the predominance of confusion, one would have to speak only of the single predominance of inclusion by means (*upāya*), because the other three conditions are also predominant.

If it were not so, then regarding the statement "this refers to the predominant [condition] (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and so forth," those who do not interpret this as referring to the predominant condition in the sense of being non-confused would argue that the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) is also a predominant condition;
since they do not state that the productive cause is the predominant condition, it is known that this refers to the body [of the cause] in its non-confused aspect.

Therefore, one should know that within the efficient cause (*upāya-hetu*), the three conditions are fully subsumed, and because the predominant condition is most prevalent therein, it is mentioned specifically.

Furthermore, herein, those who follow the Sarvāstivāda school—specifically the Mahīśāsaka sub-sect who hold views similar to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna)—assert that wholesome states which do not serve as causes for the three realms of existence and instead lead to rebirth as humans or devas are merely minor unwholesome states;
this is because their essence is still tainted (*sāsrava*). Thus says Master Daosheng of the Gu Dao school.
For this same reason, it is said that "wholesome [karma] does not receive retribution.

That "only this one instance" refers entirely to a figurative designation (*prajñapti*). This means that only when a result corresponds to its preceding karma—both in cause and effect—is this single dharma termed a "figurative outflow" (*prajñapti-niṣyanda*).
This clearly shows that even when patience or anger results in pleasant or unpleasant retributions, the relationship between cause and effect remains the same.
Question: If that is so, how can there be the retribution of good and evil when they are not similar? Answer:

It is as with a single word of angry slander that causes one to suffer for long kalpas, or a brief period of diligent austerity that yields much fruit of happiness; such disparities between cause and effect cannot be designated as "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) by way of mere convention.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the single act of taking life alone causes the life-span of others to be shortened and one’s own life-span likewise.
Because they are extremely similar in their brevity, although these are nominally termed "ripened" (*vipāka*), other causes and effects also possess some degree of similarity;
however, none of them are like this. Therefore, it is said that "none of the others are so. The former interpretation is superior.

Because *yoga* and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are similar, the general treatise takes killing and so forth as "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) results based on the similarity between cause and effect across preceding and succeeding moments.

Third, regarding "the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) up to unconditioned wholesome phenomena": this refers to space (*ākāśa*) and the like; although they are unconditioned, they are non-existent.

Because it is recorded [in the treatises], the term "wholesome" is used to distinguish it from the immovable [attainments] of perception and feeling; there are those that are permanent and those that are temporary. Regarding the attainment of the temporary suppression of afflictions, this is not the attainment of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*);

the same applies to True Suchness (*tathatā*). Some claim that even if True Suchness has not yet severed the afflictions, it is still called "dissociated" because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is dissociated;
however, this interpretation is incorrect, as it contradicts this treatise, which maintains that the attainment of severing the fetters must necessarily arise through the manifest path (*mārga*).

If that which is known as an obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) is also [an obstacle to omniscience], then "obstacle to concentration" refers to inferiority in concentration; this is subsumed under the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
As the Abhidharma treatise states: "Because of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), one attains the two unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*); therefore, there is dissociation (*visamyoga*)."
Regarding those who obtain the fruit of co-arising up to the fruit of non-arising, among the fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), there are these four types: 1. **Co-arising** (*sahaja*):

This refers to cases such as the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) producing derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), or mental attention (*manasikāra*) startling the mind. 2. **Immediate** (*anantara*): This refers to cases such as the preceding moments of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) inducing the subsequent ones.
3. **Separated** (*vyavahita*): As explained in the *Vyākhyāyukti*, this refers to divination, agriculture, and so forth. 4. **Non-arising** (*anutpatti*): This refers to...
Regarding these four kinds of unconditioned fruits (*asaṃskṛta-phala*), they mostly refer to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) in terms of phenomena (*dharma*).

As for the remaining two [fruits] based on reaching all contaminated things (*sāsrava*): among the three types of "appropriation" (*parigraha*), the first three take only mind and mental factors as their fruit;
therefore, they lack "ripening" (*vipāka*). Their functions—the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and the fruit of dominance (*adhipati*)—are explained in terms of phenomena and apply universally.

The attainment of all results, such as those of form and mind, follows this same principle; thus, the maturation (*vipāka*) is also attained. This includes the previous five, making a total of seven bases.

The statement in the commentary that there are six is an error. Alternatively, based on the fact that the maturation cause is remote and only takes its functional activity into account, there are only six bases.
Regarding the statement that "the basis of reception does not obtain the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*)," it is like the case of the shin waiting for the foot.
Although the shin is indeed what the foot depends upon, it is not the fruit of human effort because it is merely that which is brought about [by the foot]. Question:
In this context, one should say that the "basis of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-āśraya*) also does not obtain the fruit of human effort; why then do you speak of the "basis of reception"?
Answer: In the lower section of the commentary, it is stated that among the bases for human effort (*puruṣakāra-āśraya*), there is none that does not obtain the fruit of human effort;

therefore, one cannot speak of them as "bases of human effort" [in the strict sense]. In the preceding text, this master asserts that human effort is obtained across five bases, namely, those such as experiencing (*anubhava*) and so forth;

thus, these can only be spoken of in terms of the bases of experiencing and the like. This is because within the base of experiencing, there exists that which is not obtained by the person (*puruṣa*).
Regarding the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*):

the phrase "it is not said that the latencies [exist] up to the point where this cause is absent" means that the word "not said" from above flows down to the middle of the subsequent section on the "remaining bases."

In this context, if reaching another [dharma] constitutes predominance (*adhipati*), it refers to the present producing the present; those that are of the same category (*sabhāga*) are also results of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
This is the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

However, regarding "that which does not produce the activity of a man" (*puruṣakāra*): "that which does not produce" refers to unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*); the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) maintains that these obtain the activity of a man.
The application of the fruit in the Mahāyāna is not like this; there must be that which produces and that which is produced for it to be called the "land of application" (*bhūmi-prayoga*).

This differs from the Hīnayāna, where even the five fruits have causes. For instance, in the Sarvāstivāda school, although the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is a productive cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), it is not the cause of the five fruits;
and although disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*) is a fruit, it is not the fruit of the six causes. Now, in the Mahāyāna...

Although the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is without taking or giving, it is nevertheless not a discordant cause (*virodhahetu*), for it is able to produce a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) because it does not obstruct others.

That which is "likewise" in the statement regarding "conformity to what is taught" (*yathādeśanānugama*) and so forth means that there is no confusion; the dominant fruit is precisely the cause that conforms to what is taught.

In the context of the "complete dependence" (*paratantra*), with the exception of the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), all other [causes] are included as the cause of dominance (*adhipati-hetu*) because they are contrary [to the result];
thus, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is used.

Although these are also subsumed under the category of "contrary causes," this refers to the fact that while the various untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are indeed dominant among the four conditions, [they do not produce a result].
Among the ten causes for superior objects, this is subsumed under the non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*), as it is capable of producing manifest conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

This is because manifest conceptualization is *āsrava* (tainted). Alternatively, one might say it is subsumed under the contradictory cause (*virodha-hetu*); the word "non-" (*a-*) has likely entered erroneously.

Question: Regarding seeds that take space (*ākāśa*) up to the characteristics of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as their objects—since space lacks substantial reality, how can the sixth [consciousness] take it as its object alone?

Question: Since shadows are known to arise from the seeing [faculty], one should know that there are only seeds for the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*). Why, then, does the Commentary state that the perfuming agent produces seeds for that image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*)?
Answer: The Commentary does not say that, apart from the seeing-portion, there are separate seeds for the image-portion of empty space.

Although it is a "solitary shadow" object (*kevala-chāyā-viṣaya*), because the image and the seeing are perfumed by the same single type of seed, what contradiction is there in principle in speaking of "image-seeds"?

Regarding the statement "the sixth [consciousness] taking the seventh as its object, etc., should be understood accordingly": one should know that the sixth consciousness conditions the seeds of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) and *darśana-bhāga* (perceptual aspect) of the seventh consciousness, which are formed through mutual perfuming;

these correspond respectively to the objects of the *darśana-bhāga* and the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying aspect) of that [seventh consciousness]. This principle should be applied to other cases as well; therefore, the treatise does not explicitly state it.
Regarding the statement that the self-cognizing aspect (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) leads only to the latter fault:

it is now explained that when the self-cognizing aspect of feeling (vedanā-svasaṃvitti) and the other [aspects], namely the seeing aspect (darśana-bhāga), take the same object, there is no fault of their objects of cognition being different. This is because the seeing aspect does not share the same object as the other seeing aspects regarding feeling;
otherwise, it would contradict the following treatise. Since the objects of the seeing aspects must not differ in substance, this constitutes the latter fault.

Another interpretation states: "Since it is granted that self-cognition takes the feeling-aspect (*vedanā-bhāga*) as its object, there would be the fault that the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of mindless states would likewise take itself as its object.
Furthermore, if the seeing-aspect of the feeling does not take the feeling-aspect as its object, there remains the error of having different objects of cognition.
Although there are these two interpretations, the latter explanation is considered correct.
Regarding why the "reaching" (*prāpti*) is divided into two meanings: the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) transforms reality to serve as the objective essence (*bhāva*).

Since that which is transformed by the mental factors (*caitta*) neither arises as a manifest form nor relies upon the essence transformed by the mind-king, its own transformation lacks an objective essence. Thus, it is said to be without an essence.

Regarding the statement, "Now, based on what is possible, it does not necessarily require this": it is indeed possible to rely on the five categories, such as contact (*sparśa*), which take the seeds transformed by the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as their objective basis (*ālambana*).

However, it is not necessary that all minds and mental factors (*caitta*) must invariably possess an external objective basis (*mūla-vastu*), because the mind-king does not take the characteristics of mental factors as its objective basis.

If even as a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*) it is not [the case], then for the *nimittabhāga* (image-part) and the other two parts, they cannot serve as an immediate object-condition (*sākṣātālambana-pratyaya*);
even by way of the principle of a remote object-condition, why would it be so?

It is because a remote object-condition must necessarily manifest an image resembling the substance (*bimba*). Now, if one were to take the *nimittabhāga* as the substance and the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part) as...
Regarding the claim that this aspect of the object (nimittabhāga) serves as the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) and so forth:
since the reflection of the perceiving aspect (*darśanabhāga*) and the substance of the objective aspect are not similar, it is also not established [as such].

As for the statement that it "may be said to obtain" [the status of a condition] and so forth, this is merely explained in terms of the perceiving aspect arising from the objective aspect; in reality, it is not so, because the perceiving aspect is not the reflection of the objective aspect, and thus they are not distinct.

"Because it is a transformed aspect (nimitta-bhāga)," and "furthermore, because it can take that objective aspect as its object," and so forth—this has two meanings: first, regarding the self-witnessing consciousness (svasaṃvitti) taking the objective aspect as its object;

second, regarding the mutual taking of objects by associated mental factors (saṃprayukta-dharma). In both cases, it is necessary to transform a reflected image (pratibimba) in order to take it as an object.

Regarding the question, "If it were the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) itself, what would be the distinction [between them]?"— if the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) were to take the seeing portion as its object,

what difference would there be between that cognizing seeing and the self-cognizing portion? If the seeing portion did not take the seeing portion as its object, it would contradict the preceding text, because it would follow that the objects of the seeing portions are not of the same substance.

Although this meaning is superior because those with vision see it as having the same objective substance (*ālambana-vastu*), it is difficult to know because [the others] all take themselves as their own objects.

As for the "shadow" previously mentioned regarding what has been reached and obtained: that which was previously taken as an object before the stage of Buddhahood is called "previously obtained" (*pūrvapratilabdha*), just like the aspect of self-realization (*svasaṃvitti*).
Regarding the fourth object, the first two are the seeing-parts (*darśana-bhāga*) and the latter two are the objects; these all become manifest only upon attaining Buddhahood.
For this reason, it is said that all newly acquired [karmic results] take transformed appearances as their objects.

When the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that "one may experience [the results] in other realms of existence," this means that, for example, karma belonging to the animal realm of the desire world may, upon encountering particularly intense adverse conditions, result in experience within the hells;
conversely, if one encounters favorable conditions, it may instead result in experience among humans.

This refers to the indeterminacy of maturation (*vipāka*) within indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*). Question: Regarding the statement that one "transfers to receive [maturation] in other realms," does this refer to the total maturation (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*) or the individual maturation (*asādhāraṇa-vipāka*)?
Answer: One view holds that it applies to both total and individual maturation, because among indeterminate maturations, both types are included.
Another view holds that it refers only to individual maturation. How is this known? The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that it is like [the case of] others within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Regarding the statement that one who is heading toward the full maturation of wholesome or unwholesome karma may, upon encountering conditions, undergo the maturation of another realm:

since this refers only to "fulfillment" (*pūrana*) and does not mention "projecting karma" (*ākṣepaka-karma*), it is known that this refers exclusively to distinct retributions (*vipāka*). This interpretation is correct.
Regarding the ten factors that accompany the mind (*cittānuvartin*) as distinct from the Lesser Vehicle, the *Abhidharmakośa*, chapter six, states:

"All mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*), the two types of restraint (*saṃvara*)—those of dhyāna and the untainted (*anāsrava*)—as well as the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) such as arising (*jāti*) of those dharmas and of the mind itself, are all called 'dharmas that accompany the mind.
The current commentary explains this as follows: "Mental concomitants" refers to all the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).

Regarding the two types of restraint—those of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and those that are untainted (*anāsrava*): these refer to the morality of meditative absorption (*samādhi-śīla*) and the morality of the Path (*mārga-śīla*).

These are indeed material form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) associated with that mind, as well as the four characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth that exist upon the mind—all such phenomena are called "mind-concomitant factors" (*cittānuvartaka-dharma*) because they function simultaneously with the mind. Question: How is it that these factors are named "mind-concomitant"?
That treatise explains: "Because of time, fruit, and so forth; because of being wholesome, and so forth, this dharma is said to be 'concomitant with the mind' (*cittānuvartin*).
Regarding the phrase "because of time," it means that this [dharma] shares the same four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) as the mind and falls within the same time period (*adhvan*).

Regarding "because of fruit," it means that this [dharma] is of the same category as the mind in terms of its maturation (*vipāka*) and its uniform outflow (*niṣyanda*). Regarding "because of being wholesome, and so forth," it means that this [dharma] [shares the same quality as the mind].
Because they share the same nature—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—these ten factors are called "concomitants of the mind" (*cittānuvartin*). These ten are as follows:
five in terms of time, two in terms of fruit, and three in terms of the wholesome and so forth; taken together, these ten are termed "concomitants of the mind.

In the Mahāyāna, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of both the past and the future are not substantially real, as they do not project a future fruit; thus, it is said that this differs from the Hīnayāna.

Regarding "there is that which expresses and that which excludes": "expresses" refers to the seeds of karma; "excludes" means to distinguish them from those that were previously or currently [active], such as the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) and so forth.

Second, regarding the statement "taking name-and-form up to attaining external dharmas," the question is: why was it previously stated that within the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are taken in a general sense?

Taking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its essential nature, this name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) internally takes only the direct conditions; the answer is that both the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) are subsumed under the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).
While unconditioned name-and-form may be included [in these], it is explained here solely in terms of the aggregates (*skandha*); therefore, it refers only to the direct aspect.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "transformations of the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) are also included within the "appropriated" (*upātta*): Question: The four aggregates (*skandha*) are called "name" (*nāman*); under which aggregate is the characteristic of the unconditioned subsumed? Answer:

The manifesting aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). As for the seeds of the aspect of characteristics (*nimittabhāga*), they are subsumed under the category of "dharma-sameness" (*dharmasabhāgatā*).

Because these seeds follow the nature of the transforming consciousness (*pariṇāmika-citta*), they are generally subsumed under all four aggregates; there are no separate seeds [for the unconditioned].

This refers to "clinging" (*upādāna*) as that which, through craving (*tṛṣṇā*), takes up its objects. This explains how the maturation (*vipāka*) of both the root and the branches, although not itself defiled, can still be termed "clinging.
That is to say, because one craves, clings to, or takes as an object that maturation of the root and the branches, it is all designated as "clinging.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that one clings to the maturation of the root due to the seventh consciousness’s craving, while one craves the maturation of the branches due to the sixth consciousness.
Grasping (*upādāna*) is collectively termed "clinging" (*parigraha*) because of its nature of attachment.
Regarding the question of whether the associates of karma are also designated by the name "karma," the answer is: not all five aggregates are associates of karma;
rather, it is only those that assist tainted (*sāsrava*) wholesome or unwholesome karma and are capable of summoning both general and specific retributions that are so designated.
These "retinues" (parivāra) specifically exclude all untainted (*anāsrava*) five aggregates and include the pure (*śubha*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) five aggregates.
Within the aggregate of form (*rūpa*), one takes the wholesome or unwholesome bodily and vocal actions that are produced as the "form" of restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).

Among the remaining four aggregates, one takes only those that are tainted (*sāsrava*) and wholesome or unwholesome; the rest are excluded. Question: Is the defiled seventh consciousness a retinue of karma? Answer: [It is].

Regarding the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—they belong exclusively to the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*). Since the seventh consciousness (*saptama-vijñāna*) does not share the same aggregate (*naikāya-samudāya*), it lacks the power to assist [the sixth] and is not included among its retinue (*parivāra*).

There is, however, a view that it is also called "retinue" because the mental consciousness arises depending upon it; thus, although they constitute separate aggregates, they must necessarily exist simultaneously.
Since it can indeed assist the karma, why would it not be considered part of the retinue? The former interpretation is superior, provided one accepts it as the basis (*āśraya*).

Because they arise simultaneously, they are termed "retinue" (*parivāra*). The five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are the eighth [consciousness] taken as an example; it should be understood accordingly.

As for the remaining consciousnesses, all phenomena that constitute individual retribution (*pratiniyatavipāka*) up to the end of all dharmas—namely, the eight [consciousnesses] and the five categories—are collectively termed the "category of total retribution" (*sāmānyavipākapakṣa*).

Within the other seven consciousnesses, all phenomena of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*) belong to the category of individual retribution. Although the two natures of wholesome (*kuśala*) and defiled (*kliṣṭa*) are not [exclusively] individual retribution...

Because they are categorized as both retributive and non-retributive, and since they do not all fall under the category of the "specific" (bheda), these two categories—the general and the specific—comprehend all phenomena exhaustively.

As for the reason why only the maturation (vipāka) is excluded because it is extremely narrow: if one takes only the eighth consciousness-king (*citta-rāja*) from among the primary [categories], and from among the secondary [categories]...

If it is argued that the previous explanation is extremely narrow because it takes only a portion of the six consciousnesses as being produced by karma— without mentioning the general and specific categories of retribution—

and asks how the "root" and "branch" could be explained as *vipāka* (maturation), this [passage] reconciles such contradictions. If one says, regarding the eight appropriations (*upādāna*) among the previous [categories]:

Regarding the statement that "all possess both the sense of being the producer and the produced," the first interpretation holds that since the root and the branches are exclusively *vipāka* (maturation), they cannot be perfumers (*vāsaka*).
Since there is no perfumer, seeds do not exist; if seeds do not exist, how could the relationship between producer and produced be established? Therefore, the commentary explains:
"Taking [them] as the grasped (*grāhya*), etc. This means that it is by means of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, etc., that those roots and branches—the *vipāka*—are grasped.
It is held that because that which is grasped (*grāhya*) consists of the seeds perfumed within the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect), it possesses both meanings.

That is to say, the seeds of names and words (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-bīja*) arise from the grasping of the two [aspects] because the seeds of names and words are perfumed by grasping both the fundamental and the derivative;
thus, it is said they "arise from the grasping of the two. Even if these seeds of the fundamental and derivative are perfumed and activated by defiled or pure minds and so forth...

Furthermore, because the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the determinate-unspecified (*niyata-avyākṛta*) follows its substrate (*vyañjana*) and is exclusively unspecified, other meanings may be inferred accordingly.

Regarding the statement that "this should be understood as reaching the three periods of time and so forth in future lives," although there are two kinds of the three periods of time, this treatise specifically clarifies the three periods of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
How is this known? Because the preceding external objection asked: "By what means do sentient beings undergo birth and death?"

The continuity [of karma] is not restricted to specific states; furthermore, the lower treatise states that when a previous matured fruit (*vipākaphala*) has been fully experienced, it can again separately induce other matured fruits, whereby one revolves through birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, it is known that [karma] definitely takes up [rebirth] across the three periods of time.
The *Shu* (Commentary) says: "It should be understood that this is the intended meaning."
However, because the *niṣyanda* (outflow) is necessarily broader than the *adhipati* (dominant),
and because the dominant [cause] further reaches the nature of the outflow— this explanation in the commentary regarding the non-distinct nature of the outflow and the dominant,
and the statement that they "easily induce" [results], does not mean that all faculties produce consciousness; rather, this refers to cases where it is the dominant cause and not the outflow.
Regarding the previous statement that although the first three conditions are also sovereign (*adhipati*), why is it that here, when excluding those [three] and taking up the remainder, one asks:
"If these are necessarily both maturation (*vipāka*) and sovereign, why is it stated specifically as 'outflow' (*niṣyanda')? Answer:

Although they are indeed produced by sovereign conditions, because the majority of sovereign fruits are easily summoned, they are omitted from the discussion of maturation. This is because they are of a different nature. Question: [Why is this so?]

If one asks: "Just as the five faculties give rise to consciousness, and seven [faculties] produce six or eight [results], although these are predominant (*adhipati*), why must they be of the same nature?
Answer: Here, for the time being, we speak in terms of those that are of the same substance as their outflow (*niṣyanda*). This is not contradictory.

According to the second interpretation in the *Śāstra*, assigning them individually to the nature of outflow while maintaining their predominance is easily established; thus there is no fault, and this is superior in principle.
If one asks: "If an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) perfumes seeds based on the names and so forth of the Tathāgata, would these not be untainted (anāsrava) wholesome states?
Answer: They are designated as "untainted wholesome" because they are untainted wholesome, but in reality they are tainted and are subsumed under the category of manifest objects (*viṣayālambana*).
However, the statement here that "based on untainted names, one perfumes only untainted wholesome states" refers to this [specific case].
This refers merely to the seeds perfumed by the *pṛṣṭalabdha-jñāna* (subsequently attained wisdom) of a Bodhisattva. [Question:

As for the previous statement that names are fundamentally derived from sound and are thus classified as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), since the voice of a Bodhisattva is exclusively *sāsrava* (with outflows), names derived from sound should likewise not be *anāsrava* (without outflows).

Furthermore, the Buddha does not perfume seeds; this is not what is being discussed here. Why, then, is it said that seeds are perfumed by means of names that are *anāsrava*, and that these are also *anāsrava*? Moreover, the previous commentary...
Question: If it is said that "names" (nāma) depend on the external, why is it called "that which expresses meaning," and why is it said here that "names are internal"? Answer:

The former refers to the substance of names within the five categories (*pañcadharma*), which is *sāsrava* (with outflows) and fundamentally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). The latter refers to names as they transform according to an *anāsrava* (without outflows) mind, and thus are said to be "without outflows.
Furthermore, the former refers to hearing names from others as being external, while the latter refers to all sounds as being internal; therefore, there is no contradiction.

These two [grasping subjects] cannot be designated as "appropriation" (*upādāna*). Although the seeds for the linguistic expressions of "I-grasping" (*ahaṃkāra*) and "mine-grasping" (*mamakāra*) are also perfumed, they are merely termed the two types of perfuming;

they are not yet termed the "habitual tendencies of the two graspings. Only when there is a distinct grasping subject that grasps these two, thereby perfuming them into seeds, are they termed the "habitual tendencies of the two graspings.
Furthermore, the seeds perfumed by the grasping of "I" and "mine," as well as by taking names and objects as conditions, are likewise [not yet the habitual tendencies of the two graspings].

Regarding these two types of grasping (*grāha-vāsanā*), the statement that they do not possess the capacity to perfuse (*vāsana*) by their own nature refers to the fact that the grasped objects—the self (*ātman*) and the [five] names (*nāma*)—cannot perfuse seeds on their own;
rather, it is only through the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) that seeds are perfused.

Therefore, according to the preceding principle, these two should likewise have the perfuming of grasping (*grahaṇa-vāsanā*). However, because the treatise does not explicitly mention that grasping, it is not discussed here.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the remaining text, such as 'together' (*saha*), is as explained previously," the questioner asks: "In the previous [explanation], it was stated that the aspects (*nimitta*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), as well as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, are all seeds of conventional expression (*nāma-vyavahāra*).

Because they are induced by karma, the word 'together' (*saha*) refers to the fact that the seeds of karma and the seeds of the two-grasps (*dvaya-grāha*) assist one another through their mutual relationship as remote and immediate conditions.
Now, since the seeds of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) taken here as the 'two-grasps' are not induced by karma, they do not assist one another; why is this?"

Because it has been established as previously answered that the seeds perfumed by the grasping at a self and their objective bases are of the same genus and directly produce their own future fruits, which can only arise through the auxiliary power of karma;
therefore, this principle does not contradict what was stated before.
Regarding this, one should first understand the afflictions and only then resolve their delusions. Here, "grasping" (*upādāna*) is designated by the names of the afflictions and suffering;

the verse first mentions karma and only later explains the afflictions. Some say that according to the sequence of "moistening birth," since the afflictions follow after karma in that process, [the verse's order] is logically untenable.

In the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, regarding the "obscured-unspecified" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), this serves as proof that the ignorance (*avidyā*) which initiates wholesome actions in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is categorized as obscured.

If it is by means of "desire for sensual pleasure" (*kāmārāga*) and so forth, this clarifies the delusions that initiate karma; furthermore, by including "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) and "grasping" (*upādāna*), it also clarifies the delusions that nourish rebirth (*janmopabṛṃhaṇa*).
Because they are subdued by faith, both are subsumed under the category of the obscured. Question: What are their characteristics? Answer: It is, for example, like a person who loves...
In the Heaven of Contentment (*Tuṣita*), craving for sensual pleasures arises; thereupon, ignorance (*avidyā*) is activated, which gives rise to these meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

Due to the teachings and so forth, deep faith is produced, and through the formation of a resolute conception, the various afflictions are subdued, resulting in that which is "enveloped" (*nivṛta*). Question: That text merely mentions "craving for sensual pleasures" (*kāmatṛṣṇā*) and so forth;
how can this be used as proof for the existence of ignorance? Answer: Because one does not clearly understand the suffering inherent in those happy realms (*sugati*) and the like.

Because attachment arises [from it], there must certainly be delusion (*moha*). If someone were to say that the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) states in the desire realm lack superior efficacy in initiating various formations (*saṃskāra*), one may use this as proof to show that the obscured [states] are also capable of initiating formations.
Regarding the eleven excellences in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*: first, excellence of object (*ālambana*), because it universally takes both the defiled and the pure as its objects;

second, excellence of aspect (*ākāra*); third, excellence of causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); fourth, excellence of motivation (*samutthāna*); fifth, excellence of transformation (*parivarta*); sixth, excellence of wrong practice (*mithyā-pratipatti*); seventh, excellence of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*);
eighth, excellence of activity (*karma*); ninth, excellence of obstruction (*āvaraṇa*); tenth, excellence of conformity (*anuvartana*); and eleventh, excellence of antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Regarding these ten [types of] ignorance down to the six, if we provisionally take nineteen as the basis, the *Mahā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Vehicle), fascicle nine, states:
first, ignorance regarding the past; second, ignorance regarding the future; third, ignorance regarding both the past and the future;

fourth, ignorance regarding the internal; fifth, ignorance regarding the external; sixth, ignorance regarding both the internal and the external; seventh, ignorance regarding karma; eighth, regarding... [text truncated].
1. Ignorance regarding maturation; 2–9. [Ignorance regarding] the nine [factors]; 10. Ignorance regarding karma and its maturation;
11. Ignorance regarding the Buddha; 12. Ignorance regarding the Dharma; 13. Ignorance regarding the Saṅgha; 14. Ignorance regarding suffering;
15. Ignorance regarding the origin; 16. Ignorance regarding cessation; 17. Ignorance regarding the path; 18. Ignorance regarding causes.
Ignorance regarding the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) produced by causes (19); ignorance regarding the thorough penetration of the spheres of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) as they truly are (7).

Regarding ignorance, there are seven types: first, ignorance concerning the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); second, ignorance concerning entities (*vastu*); third, ignorance concerning the process of evolution (*pravṛtti*); fourth, ignorance concerning the supreme (*agra*); fifth, ignorance concerning reality (*tattva*); sixth, ignorance concerning defilement and purification (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna*);
seventh, ignorance concerning overweening pride (*abhimāna*). Regarding the five types of ignorance, there are: first, ignorance concerning meaning (*artha*); second... [text fragment].

1. Delusion regarding views; 2. Delusion regarding the three [types of] negligence; 3. Delusion regarding the meaning of reality; 4. Delusion regarding overweening pride—these names and meanings may be understood by reflecting upon them;
6. Ignorance, which has not yet been examined.
Furthermore, regarding the initiation of karma, that which is both unwholesome (*akuśala*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) pertains to the actual arising of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Since this [ignorance] is exclusively abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), it follows that within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), the factor of "ignorance" (*avidyā-aṅga*) alone is capable of initiating the three types of formative forces (*saṃskāra*). These are categorized as exclusively unwholesome. The sixth fascicle states:

"The discriminative afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) of the Desire Realm are exclusively unwholesome; those of the two higher realms are exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*), yet they too are capable of actually initiating [karma]."

Question: Since the two higher meditative attainments (*dhyāna*) and above are all initiated by the ignorance belonging to those higher levels, does the obscured-ignorance (*nivṛtāvidyā*) co-arising with the meditative states of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) serve as the actual initiator of future-retribution-formations (*vipākakarma*)? Answer: The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states:

"If one creates various meritorious formations (*puṇyakarma*) through desire for sensual pleasures, and acts upon them based on that faith, I designate this as 'obscured' (*nivṛta*). Thus, it is established that such obscured-ignorance can indeed initiate future-retribution-formations.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that because the principle of performing various meritorious actions (*puṇyakriyāvastu*) encompasses both the "correct" (*samyak*) and the "auxiliary" (*upakāra*), one knows that even obscured [neutral] states in the desire realm can correctly initiate such actions.

Based on this text, we derive the following meaning: regarding external phenomena in the desire realm, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) initiates various formations, those capable of initiating ignorance are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).

However, if an ordinary person who belongs to internal phenomena is heedless (*pramatta*), even if they initiate meritorious formations, these pass through both natures (wholesome and unwholesome). If not...

Regarding the question: "Is it only the obscured [ignorance] that is said to correspond to active manifestation (*samudācāra*), while for those who say it is not so, it is only the seeds of non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) that give rise to unwholesome states?
The answer is: Because it serves as a remote cause (*dūre-hetu*). If one seeks meritorious karma (*puṇya-karma*) and takes delight in birth among humans or devas, this is the case.

That which can give rise to ignorance is subsumed under the unwholesome (*akuśala*). If one seeks birth in a pure land or the sight of a Buddha and so forth, that which gives rise to ignorance is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
it is necessarily not simultaneous with the action it initiates, because that [action] is exclusively wholesome. Question:

According to the correct meaning of the subsequent treatise, the branch of ignorance that actually initiates an action is only abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*). Why, then, is it said here that they coexist?

Question: Can those born as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) also correctly initiate [karmic] formations? Answer: The lower treatise, referring to external phenomena, states that the correct initiation of ignorance by ordinary beings is solely discriminative (*vikalpita*).
Now, based on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), we speak according to internal phenomena; thus, there is no contradiction.

Alternatively, since dependent origination often pertains to the cultivation of meritorious conduct, saying they "create various meritorious formations" is likewise not contradictory. The former interpretation is correct.
However, regarding the statement that "meritorious [karma] arises up to the three types of ignorance," the three characters here are to be connected with the preceding text;

it is not intended that there are three distinct types of the ignorance link. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Through delusion regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*), one initiates non-meritorious formations;
through delusion regarding the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha-moha*), one initiates meritorious and immovable formations. Thus, it is known that ignorance consists of only two types.

The text states: "Furthermore, as for the phrase 'that which is followed by what is reached,' etc., the 'consciousness' mentioned here refers to the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
As for 'following' (*anubaddha*), it means that because this consciousness serves as a condition, it draws forth future name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); thus it is called 'following.

This applies analogously up to feeling (*vedanā*) following contact (*sparśa*). Question: Does the "this consciousness" mentioned here refer to the seeds of the present consciousness, or does it refer to the future consciousness?

Question: Although the seeds of this [consciousness] are present in the current life, they are in reality the seeds of future consciousness; thus, the seeds of present consciousness and the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) of the future would lack the relationship of condition (*pratyaya*).
How can it be said that they "follow along" (*anubandha*)? Furthermore, when it is simply stated that "this consciousness" exists, how do we know it is specifically the eighth consciousness?

Answer: If one takes the seeds of consciousness as the object of cognition, they are already included within "name" (*nāman*); why then could one further say that "name-and-form" follows along? If there were such a thing, it would be redundant. Therefore, it must be understood that this refers to the eighth consciousness.

To claim that consciousness holds the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth, and is thus called "that which follows along" (*anugata*), and from this to conclude that it is the eighth [consciousness], is logically untenable.
Furthermore, even regarding the factor of contact (*sparśa*), it is said to be "followed along" by what is to be felt (*vedanīya*); would you then say that contact supports the seeds of feeling?

Regarding the "suffering of the embryonic matrix" (*garbhasthāna-duḥkha*), some say that the seeds of the five fruits are called suffering because they reside within the eighth consciousness, and thus their meaning is the same as that of the "matrix.

This reasoning is incorrect. That treatise explains that the five [aggregates], beginning with consciousness, are called the "suffering-matrix" (*duḥkha-garbha*) because birth and old age/death are properly termed "suffering," and these five types—consciousness and so forth—are the causes capable of producing them; therefore, they are called the "suffering-matrix. For this reason...

The commentary cites scriptural evidence that [feeling] is the seed, and so forth, up to the statement "all should be understood according to this. The *Mahāśāstra* (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya), Chapter Ten, states:

"There are two kinds of feeling, termed 'mixed portions': first, that which pertains to future lives and has contact as its condition; second, that which pertains to the present life and serves as the cause for craving."

Regarding the "fruition-feeling" (*vipāka-vedanā*) within these two types of feeling: both the preceding seed and the subsequent manifestation are to be understood accordingly. This is stated either with reference to what will arise in a future birth or to what arises in the present life;
thus, it is said to encompass both the manifest and the seed. However, strictly speaking, it refers only to the seed.
Regarding this treatise’s statement that it extends downward to include all three natures (*trisvabhāva*), according to the following text, the five causes (*pañca-hetu*) are collectively subsumed;
however, while there is the sense of their being intermingled with the other four branches (*aṅga*), it does not explicitly state that they extend to all three natures.

Now, the commentary concludes by stating that "taking all three natures as its essence" has two interpretations. One says: citing the five causes below merely proves the sense of their intermingling and extending to all three [natures].
Regarding the nature (*svabhāva*), it combines with the preceding text; it does not prove the subsequent text, yet it is permitted to pervade all three natures.

Second, according to the "Gate of Distinguishing the Three Natures" below, within the seven stages (*avasthā*) there also arise wholesome and defiled states; therefore, it pervades the three natures. The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "The 'subsequent' in this treatise simultaneously reveals two passages:
the former clarifies the intermixture of factors (*aṅga*), hence it is said to 'comprehensively subsume' the five causes; the latter clarifies the intermixture of natures, hence it says 'pervades'."
Regarding the grasping of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), both interpretations are valid; however, the former explanation is taken as the primary one.

As for the grasping of the discourse on self (*ātmavādopādāna*): it refers to the desire to follow along with conventional designations and conceptualizations to construct the characteristics of a "person" (*puruṣa*).
It is called the grasping of the discourse on self because one clings to words or gives rise to speech based upon them; this is precisely the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Regarding "if one can [be equal]," the grasper refers to the arising of desire and so forth based on the four [objects]; the grasped refers to the four objects of the desire realm and so forth;
and the action refers to the union of these two as its essence. For those four objects, there is another interpretation found in the *Gāthā-ṭīkā*.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "also" (*yòu*) in the commentary on the passage beginning with "relying on conditions" (*yīyuán*), the word "also" is an error and should instead be read as "this interpretation.

This merely serves to conclude the preceding explanation of the term based on the character "relying" (*yī*); it does not constitute a separate interpretation. Rather, the phrase "arising from the characters 'relying on conditions' (*yīyuán')" refers to the fact that the afflictions which bind one to the various realms of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) are themselves the conditions.
Thus, it is "arising from the characters 'relying on conditions'."
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the various conditions have passed away yet are not abandoned," that treatise says:
"Because the various conditions, though having passed away, do not abandon [their influence] and arise based upon one's own continuum, it is called 'dependent origination' (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

This meaning explains that "condition" (*pratyaya*) signifies the sense of the uninterrupted flow and revolution of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Since that treatise states that the various conditions arise in succession after having passed away, this present [text]...
The meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) explained here is exactly the same as that [previously mentioned]. Question:

What is the difference between this interpretation and what was previously stated regarding [the nature of phenomena] relying on various conditions and perishing rapidly? Answer: The point concerning rapid perishing at every moment (*kṣaṇa*) applies universally to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
This [present] explanation concerns the long-term continuity of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), referring exclusively to sentient beings; therefore, it differs from the former.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "awakening to the nature of conditions in past lives," it means that because one awakens to the dharmatā of causes and conditions in the past,
the subsequent arising of verbal expressions in a continuous succession is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).

There are two senses of "changeable and obstructive" (*rūpa*): first, the sense of being transformed and damaged when touched by hands and the like; second, the sense of having various characteristics distinguished by spatial location.

The intent of that treatise is that the former necessarily implies succession and replacement, which is the meaning of "change," while the latter refers to mountains, rivers, and so forth, which possess the quality of "obstruction.

Regarding the phrase "because one gives rise to wrong conduct, it causes the mind to become inverted," a question is raised: there are three types of conduct, such as merit (*puṇya*), non-merit (*apuṇya*), and [neutral conduct]. Is this not the case?

Question: How can movement be called "perverse" (*mithyā*)? Answer: Because all contaminated actions (*sāsrava-karman*) arise from ignorance (*avidyā*) and are thus part of the process of saṃsāric flux (*pravṛtti*), they are all termed perverse.

Alternatively, here it is spoken in reference to non-meritorious action (*apuṇya*). Question: Why is the eighth link, consciousness (*vijñāna*), called "inversion" (*viparyāsa*), when the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) occurs after consciousness, yet is called "linking birth" (*pratisaṃdhi*)?
Answer: This follows the perspective of the Hīnayāna, according to which it is not the eighth [consciousness]. There is no [eighth consciousness].
Because the initial arising of consciousness, which is stained by craving and aversion, is designated as the limb of "consciousness," it is said that there is a reversal [of the process].

Since the state of "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) is subsumed under the blue-black *kalala* stage and name-and-form exists at the very beginning, it is stated that name-and-form constitutes the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*).
The second [category], the objects of enjoyment, refers to contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
Regarding the statement that within the first six members there are internal conditions and so forth: the first six members do not yet manifest external objects but serve as internal conditions;
the latter six, when active, mostly take external objects, and thus they are divided into two [categories]. Both contact and feeling are capable of experiencing objects.

What is the reasoning for this difference? The answer is: Contact merely causes the sense organs and so forth to come together; it has not yet apprehended the object as definitively belonging to oneself.
Because the act of experiencing (*anubhava*) is superior, [the faculties] are divided into internal and external.
Regarding the "cessation of dependent origination and the increase of pure dharmas" (*nirodha-pratītyasamutpāda-śukla-dharma-vardhana*):

this refers to those who delight in the supramundane, who practice the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-vipaśyanā*), thereby ceasing this contaminated (*sāsrava*) dependent origination and increasing uncontaminated pure dharmas (*anāsrava-śukla-dharma*). Consequently, they perform the contemplations of the forty-four knowledges (*jñāna*) and the seventy-seven knowledges, as detailed in other commentaries.
The latter two types of dependent origination may be understood as previously explained.
Answer: Regarding the sequence according to the Truths (*satya*): within the categories of defilement and purification, suffering (*duḥkha*) comes first and origination (*samudaya*) later.

Old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) and birth (*jāti*) constitute suffering; grasping (*upādāna*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) constitute origination; the five fruits constitute suffering; and the performance of formations (*saṃskāra*) constitutes origination. Because one contemplates suffering first, one contemplates [the others] in reverse order.

Regarding the two periods of cause and effect: the former ten belong to the past and the latter two to the present; or alternatively, the former ten belong to the present and the latter two to the future.

The future [existence] is explained here in terms of karma that ripens in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*); if it refers to karma that ripens in subsequent lives, it concerns the causality of the three time periods.
Regarding "delusion with respect to the object": this refers to the arising of delusion regarding the objects of the three realms of existence; this is called "delusion with respect to the object.
Because of this, one cannot clearly comprehend the object, causing sentient beings to frequently give rise to doubt and confusion.
Because it is not perceived or known, that which continues in an uninterrupted succession at the moment of death— since the six consciousnesses do not function during this state—
is not seen to pass from the present death into the subsequent rebirth; thus, the statement that it is "uninterrupted" reveals that old age and death have further results.

Furthermore, regarding the arising of the notion of an antidote where there is no knowledge: due to revulsion toward the suffering and coarse obstructions of the three evil realms and the lower realms, one subsequently cultivates meritorious conduct and immovable conduct.

Although these practices are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and are not actually antidotes to such obstructions as suffering and coarseness, one nonetheless gives rise to the notion that they are antidotes;
this occurs because of ignorance, which fails to penetrate reality, leading one to cultivate meritorious conduct and the like.
If that were so, then for one who generates non-merit (*apuṇya*), there would actually be no destruction within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

One should not object on the grounds of the formless realm; rather, because both the upper two realms lack non-merit, they are treated as a single category in the text. The underlying objection here is:
if the name "suffering of change" (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) refers to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), then since the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is not conventional, it should likewise be without change.

If suffering is also deluded regarding the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) in the form realm, it should likewise be said that one is deluded regarding conventional suffering (*saṃvṛti-duḥkha*);
thus, would not the cultivation of immovable karma (*āniñjya-saṃskāra*) arise?

How could it be that only non-meritorious karma arises? Regarding the statement that "one cultivates the subsequent factors based on the preceding factors," this term "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) here carries the meaning of "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*), and is not [the usual sense of mental development].

This means that while one wishes to sever ignorance (*avidyā*), one first eliminates old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*); yet, it is precisely for the sake of eliminating old age and death that one severs ignorance.

Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "When ignorance ceases, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) cease. Question: Regarding the relationship between feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), why is the latter severed before the former is cultivated?
Answer: It is because one wishes to sever craving that one first does not grasp at sense objects; this is likewise an instance of severing a later link by cultivating an earlier one.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is of two kinds; that it has these two is stated in the tenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. There are two types of feeling:

first, that which is the cause-feeling (*hetu-vedanā*), which takes contact (*sparśa*) as its condition and pertains to future lives (*paraloka*); second, that which is the effect-feeling (*phala-vedanā*), which serves as the condition for feeling and pertains to the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*).
Regarding "future lives," this refers to the seeds of future worlds; thus it is called "cause-feeling. Regarding "present life," this refers to...
This refers to the experience (*vedanā*) of the stages of birth and aging in the present life; this is precisely the active manifestation (*samudācāra*), which is the past result. Question:
Since *vedanā* applies to both seeds and manifestations, it is described as being "mixed" [with them]. The same principle applies to the other four [aggregates], such as consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Why, then, is it not stated that they apply to both cause and effect? Answer: *Vedanā* conditions craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and since craving must necessarily be manifest, *vedanā* applies to the present as the condition for the other four, such as consciousness.
Since the principle that the branches have only the seeds as their conditions is not at all obstructed, they are not termed "mixed.
Regarding the five [factors], ignorance takes only the preceding four: this refers to the ignorance that initiates karma within the four abodes. Question:

If one takes only that which directly initiates karma, it should apply only to the first [abode]; how can it be said to apply to all four? Answer: Since it takes all four universally, the principle encompasses both the direct and the indirect.
Because they assist one another and do not merely take up the primary [factors], they are not contradictory.

Regarding the statement that "the Abhidharma has two kinds of delusion" and so forth: first, due to being deluded regarding internal matured results (*vipāka-phala*), the "delusion of maturation" arises, which gives rise to non-meritorious formations (*apuṇya-saṃskāra*).
Due to being deluded regarding the principle of the Four Noble Truths, the "delusion regarding the true meaning" (*tattvārtha-moha*) arises with respect to them.
Not understanding the sufferings of humans, devas, and others, one creates meritorious, immovable karma (*puṇya-aninjya-saṃskāra*).

According to this principle, since all such karma is said to be "karma of distinct retribution" (*vipāka-karma*) and not designated as the "limb of formations" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*), it is also not the substance of the limb of formations;
rather, it is what is called "karma to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya-karma*).
If it were not so, there would be the fallacy of confusing distinct retributions with one another;

this [objection] uses retribution as an analogy for karma, arguing that if an action capable of inducing a distinct retribution is indeed a "branch of formation" (*saṃskāra*), then the distinct retribution resulting from it should be called an "induced fruit."
If it were not so, then that which is to be experienced as a separate maturation would not be induced by volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

If only those actions resulting in separate maturations were not designated as the limb of volitional formations, then name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) resulting only as a separate maturation would likewise not be induced by volitional formations. Since it is indeed induced by volitional formations, actions resulting in separate maturations may be called the limb of volitional formations, though they are not the primary limb of volitional formations.
Within the limb of name-and-form, the eighth [factor], the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), are termed "general," while the remainder are termed [specific].
Although the term "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) also applies generally and specifically within other factors, it is mentioned here specifically because it is the most extensive.
Otherwise, there would be an obstacle to the principle as previously stated—namely, the obstacle regarding the analogy between karma and its fruit.

The reason they are excluded is that since the distinct retribution (*pratiniyata-vipāka*) is not the primary karmic action, the treatise excludes it; likewise, both the karma concordant with the present life and the auxiliary karma are not [the primary] actions.

Thus, from the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to this point, that which constitutes the substance of the total retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*)—namely, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth—is taken as the mental intention (*manas-karman*) consisting of the volition (*cetanā*) associated with the eight [factors].
Regarding the phrase "taking the preceding thought from among those in the middle," the rest can be understood accordingly.
As for the objection raised here that will be addressed in the section on "defining the essence" (*svabhāva*), this does not refer to the specific location where the essence was previously cited;
rather, it refers to the location within the first ten gates where the essences of the five fruits were explained.
Regarding the point that each [feeling] acts as that which is produced at the stage of its own arising, there is a commentary manuscript that reads "named the producer" (*nengsheng*);
this character "producer" (*neng*) is an error. If both types of feeling were both producers, why would it be called "one part"?

Regarding the essence of these factors, there are five distinct seeds that project and produce [results]. At the time when these seeds give rise to manifest phenomena and at the time before they have arisen, their essence is one;

it is only in terms of their different states (*avasthā*) that they are said to be "produced" and "projected. Now, based on the state of manifest production, it is said that production and projection occur simultaneously.
This means that the produced and the projected are simultaneous, referring here to the five factors—consciousness and so forth—within the state of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The manifest [result] refers to the five types of consciousness, such as the visual consciousness, which are produced; the "induced" refers to those seeds that have not yet been moistened.

Since production and induction do not occur simultaneously, when the seeds have been moistened and the manifest [result] arises, the seed and the manifest must necessarily coexist; therefore, they are simultaneous.
From delusion regarding the internal up to the performance of the three types of karma, these two forms of suffering are both conventional and ultimate. Question:

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter ten, states that because one does not understand conventional suffering, one initiates non-meritorious karma; and because one does not understand ultimate suffering, one initiates meritorious and immovable karma.
The *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*, chapter seven, speaks of two kinds of ignorance: first, ignorance regarding the meaning of maturation (*vipāka*). [End of excerpt]
Regarding the two types of delusion concerning reality: the latter gives rise to merit and the immovable [karma], while the former gives rise to non-merit.

Based on these two passages, it follows that the delusion regarding maturation (*vipāka*) results in the performance of non-meritorious actions alone because it does not comprehend conventional suffering, whereas the delusion concerning reality results in the performance of meritorious and immovable actions because it does not comprehend ultimate suffering.
In this treatise, the delusion regarding the fruit of maturation corresponds to what is termed "delusion" (*moha*) in the *Abhidharma*.

Question: Since the term "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is the same [in both cases], why is it said here that it is "delusion regarding maturation" (*vipāka-avidyā*), while later it is said that one "performs the three types of formations according to their respective conditions"?
Answer: Here, the delusion regarding the fruit of maturation refers specifically to that which is contrasted with external fruits;

however, all instances of being deluded regarding the fruits of suffering within the three realms are collectively termed "delusion regarding internal maturation. It is because of this comprehensive [definition] that [the former] is so designated.

Delusion regarding the two [types of] suffering generally gives rise to the three types of conduct. In the *Abhidharma*, this refers specifically to those who are deluded regarding the three evil destinies and, being consistently devoid of faith, perform all manner of unwholesome deeds;

this is termed "delusion regarding maturation" (*vipāka-moha*). If one is deluded regarding the objects of the Four Noble Truths and, failing to know the suffering of humans and devas as it truly is, performs wholesome deeds, this is termed "delusion regarding the true meaning" (*tattvārtha-moha*). These are combined into one [in the *Abhidharma*], whereas that [text] analyzes them into two.
Although the names of these two delusions are the same, their meanings differ.

Otherwise, regarding the phrase "up until it is unable to produce a fruit," if one does not speak of the *vipāka* (maturation), then it would simply mean that the seeds of nomenclature (*nāma-vāsanā*) themselves can produce subsequent seeds and present fruits.
Now, the intention here is to say that if one does not rely on ignorance (*avidyā*), the force of the impelling action (*ākṣepa-prayoga*) cannot arise; thus, [it is called] "delusion."
It is said that the seeds lack power and are thus unable to produce the future ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).

Regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is also stated that there is "planting of seeds" and "arising," etc.; within the womb, there are five stages, the first of which is called "planting of seeds and arising," while the remaining four are called "gradual growth.
Within the stage of being born from the womb, the initial infant stage is called "arising from the womb," followed by the stage of childhood.

In the stage of infancy, one is called "gradually growing" (*anupūrva-vardhamāna*). In the stage of flourishing roots, where one is able to experience various objects and so forth, one is called "growing fully" (*paripūrṇa-vardhamāna*).
There are six kinds of death: that which occurs according to the power of karma is called "ultimate" (*atyanta*); that which is untimely and premature is called "abrupt" (*akāla-mṛtyu*).
The ultimate death and the death at the very moment of dying are called "death by its own characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa-maraṇa*).

Within the categories of ultimate and non-ultimate death, there are many distinct types with differing characteristics; these are called the "differences in states" (*avasthā-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Sixth, regarding death:

dying after one has already aged and one's lifespan is exhausted is called "timely death"; dying before one has aged is called "untimely death. Now, how does this differ from ultimate and non-ultimate death?

Regarding the distinction between those who die at the end of their lifespan and those who die prematurely: it is not contradictory for one who dies at the end of their lifespan to have not yet reached old age, because their karma has been exhausted;

whereas one who dies prematurely does not necessarily reach old age, because their karma has not yet been exhausted. When death occurs at the appointed time, it is necessarily at the end of one's lifespan; however, death that is not at the appointed time (untimely death) is not necessarily at the end of one's lifespan.
This may be understood by analogy.

Regarding the passage from "Fifty-sixth: the basis of the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and so forth": both that which projects (*ākṣepaka*) and that which is projected (*ākṣipta*) are termed the "projecting cause.

This is because, within the present state of birth, the active *nāmarūpa* and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) can give rise to ignorance (*avidyā*), set in motion the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and thereby invite the five [aggregates] of the future.

Therefore, *nāmarūpa* and the six sense bases are said to be the cause; as for the projecting cause, it belongs to the subsequent fruit, while the six sense bases belong to the preceding cause. Is this not so?
